paragraphs: The paper studies how coarse-coded symbol memories scale as the demands on them increase. These memories appear in neural models of symbol processing, so understanding their mathematical properties is necessary for assessing larger versions of those systems. The authors begin by defining their general structure.

The analysis derives relationships among three essential quantities: memory size, the size of the available symbol set, and storage capacity. These quantities describe different aspects of the problem. A system's physical memory, the vocabulary it must represent, and how much it can store must be considered together when reasoning about scale.

For one of the schemes, the calculated capacity agrees well with measurements from the working memory of DCPS, Touretzky and Hinton's distributed connectionist production system. This connects the mathematical analysis with an implemented symbol-processing model. The contribution is a framework for relating representation choices to storage requirements, backed by a capacity calculation that matches observed behavior in a concrete coarse-coded memory.
summary.tldr: The paper derives scaling relationships for coarse-coded symbol memories and checks one capacity prediction against DCPS measurements.

title: Scaling Properties of Coarse-Coded Symbol Memories

abstract: Biological neurons have a variety of intrinsic properties because of the large number of voltage dependent currents that control their activity. Neuromodulatory substances modify both the balance of conductances that determine intrinsic properties and the strength of synapses. These mechanisms alter circuit dynamics, and suggest that functional circuits exist only in the modulatory environment in which they operate.
originalAbstract: Biological neurons have a variety of intrinsic properties because of the large number of voltage dependent currents that control their activity. Neuromodulatory substances modify both the balance of conductances that determine intrinsic properties and the strength of synapses. These mechanisms alter circuit dynamics, and suggest that functional circuits exist only in the modulatory environment in which they operate.

paragraphs: This paper explains why a neural circuit’s behavior depends on the chemical environment in which it operates. Biological neurons possess many voltage-dependent currents, and the balance among these currents helps determine each neuron’s intrinsic activity. A neuron’s contribution to a circuit therefore depends on its own electrical properties as well as its connections.

Neuromodulatory substances can change that balance of conductances and also alter synaptic strength. These provide two routes for changing network behavior: modifying how individual neurons respond and modifying how strongly neurons influence one another. The resulting changes affect circuit dynamics, linking cellular properties and interactions within the network.

The authors argue that functional circuits should consequently be understood in relation to their modulatory environment. A description of which neurons are connected does not, by itself, capture the conductance balance and synaptic strengths under which those connections operate. The paper’s central implication is that understanding circuit function requires considering the modulatory conditions that shape both neuronal activity and communication.
summary.tldr: Neuromodulators change both neuronal properties and synaptic strength, making circuit function dependent on its chemical environment.

title: Dynamic Modulation of Neurons and Networks

abstract: This paper describes a new approach to extracting 3D perspective structure from 2D point-sets. The novel feature is to unify the tasks of estimating transformation geometry and identifying point(cid:173) correspondence matches. Unification is realised by constructing a mixture model over the bi-partite graph representing the correspon(cid:173) dence match and by effecting optimisation using the EM algorithm. According to our EM framework the probabilities of structural cor(cid:173) respondence gate contributions to the expected likelihood function used to estimate maximum likelihood perspective pose parameters. This provides a means of rejecting structural outliers.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional perspective structure from two-dimensional point sets involves two connected questions: which points correspond, and what geometric transformation relates them. The paper proposes estimating these together. This matters because the geometry depends on the matches, while deciding which matches are plausible also depends on the geometry.

The method represents possible correspondences with a bipartite graph and places a mixture model over that representation. It then uses expectation-maximization to optimize the model. Correspondence is treated probabilistically, allowing the geometric estimation to account for uncertainty about which point pairings represent the same underlying structure.

Within this framework, the probabilities of structural correspondence control how much candidate matches contribute to the expected likelihood used to estimate perspective pose. Matches with little support can therefore have less influence on the geometric solution. The abstract identifies this as a mechanism for rejecting structural outliers. The contribution is a unified estimation procedure in which uncertain matching and pose recovery inform one another.
summary.tldr: A joint EM model estimates perspective pose and point correspondences while reducing the influence of structural outliers.

title: Recovering Perspective Pose with a Dual Step EM Algorithm

abstract: Hierarchical learning machines are non-regular and non-identifiable statistical models, whose true parameter sets are analytic sets with singularities. Using algebraic analysis, we rigorously prove that the stochastic complexity of a non-identifiable learning machine (ml - 1) log log n + const., is asymptotically equal to >'1 log n - where n is the number of training samples. Moreover we show that the rational number >'1 and the integer ml can be algorithmically calculated using resolution of singularities in algebraic geometry. Also we obtain inequalities 0 < >'1 ~ d/2 and 1 ~ ml ~ d, where d is the number of parameters.

paragraphs: Hierarchical learning machines can be non-identifiable: different parameter choices can describe the same underlying statistical model. The paper studies this setting through the geometry of the parameter sets representing the truth. These sets contain singularities, so their structure is more complicated than a smooth, regular parameter space.

Using algebraic analysis, the author proves an asymptotic expression for stochastic complexity. Its dependence on training sample size includes a leading logarithmic term and a correction involving the logarithm of the logarithm. The coefficients are a rational number and an integer tied to the singular structure. Thus, the analysis describes complexity through more than simply the number of adjustable parameters.

The paper also shows that these coefficients can be calculated algorithmically using resolution of singularities, a technique from algebraic geometry. It bounds the positive leading coefficient by half the parameter count and places the integer between one and that count. These are asymptotic theoretical results, providing a way to analyze the statistical complexity of non-regular learning machines.
summary.tldr: Algebraic geometry yields an asymptotic characterization of stochastic complexity for non-identifiable learning machines.

title: Algebraic Analysis for Non-regular Learning Machines

abstract: We discuss an information theoretic approach for categorizing and mod(cid:173) eling dynamic processes. The approach can learn a compact and informa(cid:173) tive statistic which summarizes past states to predict future observations. Furthermore, the uncertainty of the prediction is characterized nonpara(cid:173) metrically by a joint density over the learned statistic and present obser(cid:173) vation. We discuss the application of the technique to both noise driven dynamical systems and random processes sampled from a density which is conditioned on the past. In the first case we show results in which both the dynamics of random walk and the statistics of the driving noise are captured. In the second case we present results in which a summarizing statistic is learned on noisy random telegraph waves with differing de(cid:173) pendencies on past states. In both cases the algorithm yields a principled approach for discriminating processes with differing dynamics and/or de(cid:173) pendencies. The method is grounded in ideas from information theory and nonparametric statistics.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to summarize a process's past while retaining information useful for predicting its future. Its information-theoretic approach learns a compact statistic from past states. That statistic serves as a condensed representation for modeling and distinguishing dynamic processes, making predictive information central to what the representation preserves.

Prediction uncertainty is described nonparametrically through a joint density over the learned statistic and the present observation. The method therefore learns both a useful summary and a probabilistic description relating that summary to observations. The authors consider noise-driven dynamical systems as well as random processes whose sampling distributions depend on their histories.

For the first setting, reported results capture both random-walk dynamics and the statistics of the driving noise. For the second, the method learns summaries of noisy random telegraph waves with different dependencies on past states. Together, these examples support a principled way to distinguish processes through their dynamics or historical dependencies. The contribution links compact predictive representations with an explicit account of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic method learns compact predictive summaries and nonparametric uncertainty descriptions for dynamic processes.

title: Learning Informative Statistics: A Nonparametnic Approach

abstract: We consider the question of predicting nonlinear time series. Kernel Dy- namical Modeling (KDM), a new method based on kernels, is proposed as an extension to linear dynamical models. The kernel trick is used twice: ﬁrst, to learn the parameters of the model, and second, to compute preimages of the time series predicted in the feature space by means of Support Vector Regression. Our model shows strong connection with the classic Kalman Filter model, with the kernel feature space as hidden state space. Kernel Dynamical Modeling is tested against two benchmark time series and achieves high quality predictions.

paragraphs: The paper proposes Kernel Dynamical Modeling for predicting nonlinear time series. It extends linear dynamical modeling through a kernel feature space, providing a way to represent dynamics beyond the original linear formulation. The method has a strong connection to the classical Kalman filter, with the feature space serving as the model’s hidden state space.

Kernels enter the procedure twice. First, they are used to learn the model parameters. Second, they help convert predictions made in feature space back into the space of the observed time series. The authors perform this second task, described as computing preimages, using Support Vector Regression.

That second stage matters because a prediction in a hidden representation must be translated into the quantities being forecast. The method therefore addresses both learning the dynamics and recovering usable outputs from those dynamics. Tests on two benchmark time series yield predictions described as high quality, providing empirical support for the proposed modeling approach on those examples.
summary.tldr: Kernel Dynamical Modeling learns time-series dynamics in a kernel feature space and uses Support Vector Regression to recover observable predictions.

title: Dynamical Modeling with Kernels for Nonlinear Time Series Prediction

abstract: We present an efﬁcient algorithm to actively select queries for learning the boundaries separating a function domain into regions where the func- tion is above and below a given threshold. We develop experiment selec- tion methods based on entropy, misclassiﬁcation rate, variance, and their combinations, and show how they perform on a number of data sets. We then show how these algorithms are used to determine simultaneously valid 1 − α conﬁdence intervals for seven cosmological parameters. Ex- perimentation shows that the algorithm reduces the computation neces- sary for the parameter estimation problem by an order of magnitude.

We develop experiment selec- tion methods based on entropy, misclassiﬁcation rate, variance, and their combinations, and show how they perform on a number of data sets. We then show how these algorithms are used to determine simultaneously valid 1 − α conﬁdence intervals for seven cosmological parameters. Ex- perimentation shows that the algorithm reduces the computation neces- sary for the parameter estimation problem by an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate the boundary between inputs where a function lies above a chosen threshold and inputs where it lies below. The goal is specifically to identify that separation. The authors develop an active learning algorithm that chooses which function queries to make, directing computation toward learning the threshold boundary.

Several query-selection methods are investigated. They use entropy, misclassification rate, variance, and combinations of these quantities to guide experiment selection. These criteria express different ways of deciding which observation would be useful for distinguishing the two regions. The paper examines their behavior across multiple datasets rather than presenting only a single selection rule.

The authors then apply the algorithms to construct simultaneously valid confidence intervals, at confidence level 1 − α, for seven cosmological parameters. In that parameter-estimation application, experiments show an order-of-magnitude reduction in required computation. The result illustrates how actively identifying a threshold boundary can make a substantive inference task cheaper, with the reported reduction tied to the application studied.
summary.tldr: Active selection of function queries learns threshold boundaries and reduces computation by an order of magnitude in a cosmological parameter-estimation application.

title: Active Learning For Identifying Function Threshold Boundaries

abstract: Hybrid “CMOL” integrated circuits, combining CMOS subsystem with nanowire crossbars and simple two-terminal nanodevices, promise to extend the exponential Moore-Law development of microelectronics into the sub-10-nm range. We are developing neuromorphic network (“CrossNet”) architectures for this future technology, in which neural cell bodies are implemented in CMOS, nanowires are used as axons and dendrites, while nanodevices (bistable latching switches) are used as elementary synapses. We have shown how CrossNets may be trained to perform pattern recovery and classification despite the limitations imposed by the CMOL hardware. Preliminary estimates have shown that CMOL CrossNets may be extremely dense (~107 cells per cm2) and operate approximately a million times faster than biological neural networks, at manageable power consumption. In Conclusion, we discuss in brief possible short-term and long-term applications of the emerging technology. 1 Introduction: CMOL Circuits Recent results [1, 2] indicate that the current VLSI paradigm based on CMOS technology can be hardly extended beyond the 10-nm frontier: in this range the sensitivity of parameters (most importantly, the gate voltage threshold) of silicon field-effect transistors to inevitable fabrication spreads grows exponentially. This sensitivity will probably send the fabrication facilities costs skyrocketing, and may lead to the end of Moore’s Law some time during the next decade. There is a growing consensus that the impending Moore’s Law crisis may be preempted by a radical paradigm shift from the purely CMOS technology to hybrid CMOS/nanodevice circuits, e.g., those of “CMOL” variety (Fig. 1). Such circuits (see, e.g., Ref. 3 for their recent review) would combine a level of advanced CMOS devices fabricated by the lithographic patterning, and two-layer nanowire crossbar formed, e.g., by nanoimprint, with nanowires connected by simple, similar, two-terminal nanodevices at each crosspoint. For such devices, molecular single-electron latching switches [4] are presently the leading candidates, in particular because they may be fabricated using the self-assembled monolayer (SAM) technique which already gave reproducible results for simpler molecular devices [5].

The motivation is to explore hardware that could extend microelectronics into dimensions below ten nanometers, where the supplied text describes growing challenges for purely CMOS technology.

This assigns different neural functions to different hardware components. The authors show how such networks may be trained for pattern recovery and classification despite constraints imposed by the hardware.

These are projected capabilities of an emerging technology. The paper's contribution is to connect a proposed physical architecture with trainable neural functions and to discuss possible near-term and longer-term applications.
summary.tldr: Proposed CMOL CrossNets combine CMOS and nanodevices for trainable neural circuits, with preliminary estimates suggesting high density and speed.

title: CMOL CrossNets: Possible Neuromorphic Nanoelectronic Circuits

abstract: We consider the machine vision task of pose estimation from static images, specifically for the case of articulated objects. This problem is hard because of the large number of degrees of freedom to be estimated. Following a established line of research, pose estimation is framed as inference in a probabilistic model. In our experience however, the success of many approaches often lie in the power of the features. Our primary contribution is a novel casting of visual inference as an iterative parsing process, where one sequentially learns better and better features tuned to a particular image. We show quantitative results for human pose estimation on a database of over 300 images that suggest our algorithm is competitive with or surpasses the state-of-the-art. Since our procedure is quite general (it does not rely on face or skin detection), we also use it to estimate the poses of horses in the Weizmann database.

paragraphs: This paper addresses estimating the pose of articulated objects from a single static image. Such objects have many independently varying parts, creating many quantities to estimate. The authors follow a probabilistic approach to pose inference, while emphasizing that the quality of visual features often strongly influences how well these methods work.

Their main contribution is to treat inference as an iterative parsing process. As the process proceeds, it learns increasingly effective features tailored to the particular image being analyzed. Feature learning thus becomes part of interpreting the image, allowing the representation used for inference to improve over successive steps.

Quantitative experiments on a database of more than 300 human images suggest performance competitive with, or better than, the state of the art. The procedure does not depend on detecting faces or skin, and the authors also apply it to horse pose estimation in the Weizmann database. Together, these applications show how the image-specific parsing approach can extend beyond human bodies.
summary.tldr: An iterative parsing method learns features tailored to each image to estimate human and horse poses.

title: Learning to parse images of articulated bodies

abstract: We study the problem of parameter estimation in continuous density hidden Markov models (CD-HMMs) for automatic speech recognition (ASR). As in support vector machines, we propose a learning algorithm based on the goal of margin maximization. Unlike earlier work on max-margin Markov networks, our approach is specifically geared to the modeling of real-valued observations (such as acoustic feature vectors) using Gaussian mixture models. Unlike previous discriminative frameworks for ASR, such as maximum mutual information and minimum classification error, our framework leads to a convex optimization, without any spurious local minima. The objective function for large margin training of CD-HMMs is defined over a parameter space of positive semidefinite matrices. Its optimization can be performed efficiently with simple gradient-based methods that scale well to large problems. We obtain competitive results for phonetic recognition on the TIMIT speech corpus.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to estimate parameters for continuous density hidden Markov models used in speech recognition. The learning objective follows the margin maximization idea associated with support vector machines. Its aim is to train the speech model through separation between alternatives, while retaining a representation suited to real-valued acoustic observations.

The approach specifically accommodates Gaussian mixture models for observations such as acoustic feature vectors. Its training objective is defined over positive semidefinite matrices and leads to a convex optimization problem. The authors emphasize that this formulation avoids spurious local minima, distinguishing it from the cited discriminative speech training frameworks.

Simple gradient-based methods can optimize the objective efficiently and scale to large problems. The reported phonetic recognition results on the TIMIT corpus are competitive. Taken together, the contributions connect a margin-based learning goal with an observation model appropriate for speech and an optimization formulation with favorable mathematical structure; the empirical claim is competitive performance, rather than a stated across-the-board improvement.
summary.tldr: Large-margin training for continuous density HMMs yields a convex optimization problem and competitive phonetic recognition results.

title: Large Margin Hidden Markov Models for Automatic Speech Recognition

abstract: Is accurate classification possible in the absence of hand-labeled data? This paper introduces the Monotonic Feature (MF) abstraction--where the probability of class membership increases monotonically with the MF's value. The paper proves that when an MF is given, PAC learning is possible with no hand-labeled data under certain assumptions. We argue that MFs arise naturally in a broad range of textual classification applications. On the classic "20 Newsgroups" data set, a learner given an MF and unlabeled data achieves classification accuracy equal to that of a state-of-the-art semi-supervised learner relying on 160 hand-labeled examples. Even when MFs are not given as input, their presence or absence can be determined from a small amount of hand-labeled data, which yields a new semi-supervised learning method that reduces error by 15% on the 20 Newsgroups data.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether text classification can be accurate without hand-labeled training examples. Its proposed source of guidance is a monotonic feature: as the feature’s value increases, the probability of belonging to a particular class increases monotonically. Such a feature supplies directional information about class membership.

The authors prove that, given a monotonic feature and certain assumptions, learning without hand-labeled data is possible in the PAC framework. They also argue that these features arise naturally in many text applications. The guarantee is conditional: the feature and the assumptions provide the structure that makes this form of learning possible.

On 20 Newsgroups, a learner using a supplied monotonic feature and unlabeled data matches the accuracy of a state-of-the-art semi-supervised learner using 160 labeled examples. The authors also consider discovering whether monotonic features are present using a small labeled sample. That route yields a semi-supervised method reporting a 15% error reduction on the same dataset, extending the idea beyond situations where a suitable feature is supplied beforehand.
summary.tldr: Monotonic features can enable text learning without labeled examples under assumptions, and can also support a label-efficient semi-supervised method.

title: Look Ma, No Hands: Analyzing the Monotonic Feature Abstraction for Text Classification

abstract: We present a novel regularization-based Multitask Learning (MTL) formulation for Structured Output (SO) prediction for the case of hierarchical task relations. Structured output learning often results in difﬁcult inference problems and requires large amounts of training data to obtain accurate models. We propose to use MTL to exploit information available for related structured output learning tasks by means of hierarchical regularization. Due to the combination of example sets, the cost of training models for structured output prediction can easily become infeasible for real world applications. We thus propose an efﬁcient algorithm based on bundle methods to solve the optimization problems resulting from MTL structured output learning. We demonstrate the performance of our approach on gene ﬁnding problems from the application domain of computational biology. We show that 1) our proposed solver achieves much faster convergence than previous methods and 2) that the Hierarchical SO-MTL approach clearly outperforms considered non-MTL methods.

paragraphs: The paper combines multitask learning with structured-output prediction when task relationships form a hierarchy. Structured outputs require predicting related pieces together, as in sequence segmentation, and learning accurate models can demand substantial training data. The proposed formulation uses hierarchical regularization to let related tasks contribute information to one another.

Sharing information creates a computational challenge as well as a statistical opportunity. Combining the example sets of structured prediction tasks can make training prohibitively expensive. The authors therefore develop an efficient optimization algorithm based on bundle methods for the problems arising from their multitask formulation. The solver is an integral part of making hierarchical sharing practical at larger scales.

The evaluation uses gene-finding problems in computational biology. In these experiments, the solver converges much faster than previous methods, and hierarchical structured-output multitask learning clearly outperforms the non-multitask methods considered. These findings support both components of the approach: exploiting hierarchical task relationships can improve prediction, while the specialized solver helps manage the accompanying training cost.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical regularization shares information across structured prediction tasks, with an efficient bundle-method solver and favorable gene-finding results.

title: Hierarchical Multitask Structured Output Learning for Large-scale Sequence Segmentation

abstract: Skill discovery algorithms in reinforcement learning typically identify single states or regions in state space that correspond to task-specific subgoals. However, such methods do not directly address the question of how many distinct skills are appropriate for solving the tasks that the agent faces. This can be highly inefficient when many identified subgoals correspond to the same underlying skill, but are all used individually as skill goals. Furthermore, skills created in this manner are often only transferable to tasks that share identical state spaces, since corresponding subgoals across tasks are not merged into a single skill goal. We show that these problems can be overcome by clustering subgoal data defined in an agent-space and using the resulting clusters as templates for skill termination conditions. Clustering via a Dirichlet process mixture model is used to discover a minimal, sufficient collection of portable skills.

paragraphs: Skill discovery in reinforcement learning often starts by identifying useful subgoal states or regions. However, several different subgoals may represent the same underlying skill. Treating every subgoal separately can create an inefficient collection of skills, while tying each skill to a particular state space can restrict its reuse across tasks.

The paper proposes clustering subgoal data expressed in an agent-space. Instead of making each discovered subgoal its own skill goal, the method uses the resulting clusters as templates for skill termination conditions. These conditions specify when a skill has achieved its purpose, allowing corresponding subgoals to be represented through a shared template.

A Dirichlet process mixture model supplies the clustering mechanism used to discover a minimal, sufficient collection of portable skills. This addresses the question of how many distinct skills are appropriate alongside the question of which subgoals matter. The contribution is a way to consolidate redundant subgoals and support transfer without requiring every task to have an identical state space.
summary.tldr: Clustering subgoals in an agent-space produces shared skill termination templates and a minimal, sufficient collection of portable skills.

title: Clustering via Dirichlet Process Mixture Models for Portable Skill Discovery

abstract: By developing data augmentation methods unique to the negative binomial (NB) distribution, we unite seemingly disjoint count and mixture models under the NB process framework. We develop fundamental properties of the models and derive efficient Gibbs sampling inference. We show that the gamma-NB process can be reduced to the hierarchical Dirichlet process with normalization, highlighting its unique theoretical, structural and computational advantages. A variety of NB processes with distinct sharing mechanisms are constructed and applied to topic modeling, with connections to existing algorithms, showing the importance of inferring both the NB dispersion and probability parameters.

paragraphs: Count models describe how often events occur, while mixture models describe observations through combinations of hidden components. This paper connects these seemingly separate approaches through negative binomial processes. Its central technique is data augmentation tailored to the negative binomial distribution: introducing additional hidden quantities that make the models easier to analyze and support efficient Gibbs sampling inference.

The authors develop fundamental properties of this framework and establish a specific connection to hierarchical Dirichlet processes. Normalizing a gamma–negative binomial process reduces it to a hierarchical Dirichlet process. This relationship places the two constructions within a common account and helps explain the theoretical, structural, and computational advantages discussed for the negative binomial formulation.

The paper also constructs several negative binomial processes with different mechanisms for sharing information and applies them to topic modeling. These models connect to existing algorithms while offering distinct ways to organize shared components. The stated findings emphasize that inference should address both the negative binomial dispersion and probability parameters, rather than leaving either parameter outside the learning process.
summary.tldr: Negative binomial data augmentation unifies count and mixture models and enables efficient inference for models with different sharing mechanisms.

title: Augment-and-Conquer Negative Binomial Processes

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of clustering data points into low-dimensional subspaces in the presence of outliers. We pose the problem using a density estimation formulation with an associated generative model. Based on this probability model, we first develop an iterative expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm and then derive its global solution. In addition, we develop two Bayesian methods based on variational Bayesian (VB) approximation, which are capable of automatic dimensionality selection. While the first method is based on an alternating optimization scheme for all unknowns, the second method makes use of recent results in VB matrix factorization leading to fast and effective estimation. Both methods are extended to handle sparse outliers for robustness and can handle missing values. Experimental results suggest that proposed methods are very effective in clustering and identifying outliers.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to group data points into low-dimensional subspaces when outliers are present. It formulates the task through density estimation and an associated generative model. This provides a probabilistic basis for estimating the underlying low-dimensional structure while addressing observations that do not fit it.

Starting from this model, the authors develop an iterative Expectation-Maximization algorithm and derive its global solution. They then introduce two variational Bayesian methods that can select dimensionality automatically. One alternates optimization over the unknown quantities; the other uses results from variational Bayesian matrix factorization to obtain fast and effective estimation.

Both Bayesian methods are extended to account for sparse outliers and can also handle missing values. These capabilities connect dimensionality selection, robustness, and incomplete observations within the proposed framework. Experiments suggest that the methods work very effectively for clustering and identifying outliers. The global-solution result belongs to the initial model development and should not be read as a blanket guarantee for every Bayesian extension.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic subspace-clustering framework supports automatic dimensionality selection, sparse outliers, and missing observations.

title: Probabilistic Low-Rank Subspace Clustering

abstract: Cross language text classiﬁcation is an important learning task in natural language processing. A critical challenge of cross language learning lies in that words of different languages are in disjoint feature spaces. In this paper, we propose a two-step representation learning method to bridge the feature spaces of different languages by exploiting a set of parallel bilingual documents. Speciﬁcally, we ﬁrst formulate a matrix completion problem to produce a complete parallel document-term matrix for all documents in two languages, and then induce a cross-lingual document representation by applying latent semantic indexing on the obtained matrix. We use a projected gradient descent algorithm to solve the formulated matrix completion problem with convergence guarantees. The proposed approach is evaluated by conducting a set of experiments with cross language sentiment classiﬁcation tasks on Amazon product reviews. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed learning approach outperforms a number of comparison cross language representation learning methods, especially when the number of parallel bilingual documents is small.

paragraphs: Text classifiers face a basic obstacle when transferring between languages: words in one language occupy a different feature space from words in another. This paper constructs a shared document representation using parallel bilingual documents. Those paired documents provide the connection needed to relate otherwise separate vocabularies.

The method has two stages. First, it formulates matrix completion to obtain a complete parallel document-term matrix covering all documents in both languages. This stage supplies the missing cross-language information in the representation. Second, latent semantic indexing extracts a shared representation from the completed matrix. The authors solve the completion problem with projected gradient descent and provide convergence guarantees for that optimization procedure.

The evaluation uses cross-language sentiment classification on Amazon product reviews. The proposed representation outperforms several comparison methods in those experiments, with particularly strong results when only a small number of bilingual document pairs are available. The findings suggest that completing the bilingual representation before extracting its shared semantic structure can make limited parallel data more useful for classification.
summary.tldr: Completing a bilingual document-term matrix before extracting shared semantic features improves cross-language sentiment classification, especially with few parallel documents.

title: A Novel Two-Step Method for Cross Language Representation Learning

abstract: This paper introduces the online probing" problem: In each round, the learner is able to purchase the values of a subset of feature values. After the learner uses this information to come up with a prediction for the given round, he then has the option of paying for seeing the loss that he is evaluated against. Either way, the learner pays for the imperfections of his predictions and whatever he chooses to observe, including the cost of observing the loss function for the given round and the cost of the observed features. We consider two variations of this problem, depending on whether the learner can observe the label for free or not. We provide algorithms and upper and lower bounds on the regret for both variants. We show that a positive cost for observing the label significantly increases the regret of the problem."

After the learner uses this information to come up with a prediction for the given round, he then has the option of paying for seeing the loss that he is evaluated against. Either way, the learner pays for the imperfections of his predictions and whatever he chooses to observe, including the cost of observing the loss function for the given round and the cost of the observed features. We consider two variations of this problem, depending on whether the learner can observe the label for free or not. We provide algorithms and upper and lower bounds on the regret for both variants. We show that a positive cost for observing the label significantly increases the regret of the problem."

paragraphs: The paper introduces online probing, a prediction problem in which information has a price. On each round, a learner chooses which feature values to buy and predicts using those observations. It then has the option to pay to observe the loss against which its prediction is evaluated.

The learner's total cost includes both prediction imperfections and purchased information. This creates linked decisions about what to observe before predicting and whether to acquire feedback afterward. Buying more information may help learning, but the purchase itself contributes to the objective the learner is trying to control.

The authors analyze two variants distinguished by whether labels are available for free. They provide algorithms and upper and lower regret bounds for each, and show that charging for labels significantly increases regret. The result makes the cost of feedback a central part of the learning problem: access to the information used to evaluate predictions can materially affect attainable performance, alongside the cost of observing features.
summary.tldr: Online probing jointly prices features, feedback, and prediction errors, and its regret bounds show a substantial penalty when labels also cost money.

title: Online Learning with Costly Features and Labels

abstract: Variational inference algorithms provide the most effective framework for large-scale training of Bayesian nonparametric models. Stochastic online approaches are promising, but are sensitive to the chosen learning rate and often converge to poor local optima. We present a new algorithm, memoized online variational inference, which scales to very large (yet finite) datasets while avoiding the complexities of stochastic gradient. Our algorithm maintains finite-dimensional sufficient statistics from batches of the full dataset, requiring some additional memory but still scaling to millions of examples. Exploiting nested families of variational bounds for infinite nonparametric models, we develop principled birth and merge moves allowing non-local optimization. Births adaptively add components to the model to escape local optima, while merges remove redundancy and improve speed. Using Dirichlet process mixture models for image clustering and denoising, we demonstrate major improvements in robustness and accuracy.

paragraphs: Training Bayesian nonparametric models on large datasets requires scalable inference, but stochastic online methods can depend strongly on learning-rate choices and settle into poor local solutions. This paper introduces memoized online variational inference to address those optimization difficulties for very large, finite datasets.

The algorithm retains finite-dimensional sufficient statistics from batches of the dataset. Keeping these summaries requires additional memory, but the method still scales to millions of examples and avoids the complexities of stochastic-gradient training. The authors also use nested families of variational bounds to develop principled operations that change the model's collection of components during optimization.

Birth operations introduce components adaptively to help escape local optima, while merge operations remove redundant components and improve speed. Together, these operations allow changes beyond small adjustments to the current model. Experiments using Dirichlet process mixtures for image clustering and denoising show major improvements in robustness and accuracy. The stated benefit combines scalable batch-summary storage with a more flexible optimization process, while explicitly accepting an additional memory cost.
summary.tldr: Memoized batch statistics and principled component births and merges improve large-scale variational inference for Dirichlet process mixtures.

title: Memoized Online Variational Inference for Dirichlet Process Mixture Models

abstract: We develop a sampling technique for Hierarchical Dirichlet process models. The parallel algorithm builds upon [Chang & Fisher 2013] by proposing large split and merge moves based on learned sub-clusters. The additional global split and merge moves drastically improve convergence in the experimental results. Furthermore, we discover that cross-validation techniques do not adequately determine convergence, and that previous sampling methods converge slower than were previously expected.
originalAbstract: We develop a sampling technique for Hierarchical Dirichlet process models. The parallel algorithm builds upon [Chang & Fisher 2013] by proposing large split and merge moves based on learned sub-clusters. The additional global split and merge moves drastically improve convergence in the experimental results. Furthermore, we discover that cross-validation techniques do not adequately determine convergence, and that previous sampling methods converge slower than were previously expected.

paragraphs: The paper develops a parallel sampling method for hierarchical Dirichlet process models. Its central focus is convergence: how effectively the sampler explores the model's possible configurations. The proposed method builds on an earlier sampling approach by using learned sub-clusters to construct large split and merge proposals.

These proposals let the sampler consider substantial changes to its clustering configuration, including additional global splits and merges. Learned sub-clusters guide those changes, providing structure for the proposed rearrangements. In the reported experiments, adding the global moves drastically improves convergence. This supports the use of broader, informed proposals as a way to improve sampling for these hierarchical models.

The paper also examines how convergence is assessed. The authors find that cross-validation techniques do not adequately determine convergence and that previous sampling methods converge more slowly than had been expected. These findings affect how the experimental improvements should be understood: evaluating a sampler requires attention to its convergence behavior, and cross-validation alone was insufficient for that purpose in their investigation.
summary.tldr: Parallel HDP sampling with learned split and merge proposals improves experimental convergence and exposes shortcomings in cross-validation-based convergence assessment.

title: Parallel Sampling of HDPs using Sub-Cluster Splits

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for probabilistic inference over functions. They have been applied to both regression and non-linear dimensionality reduction, and offer desirable properties such as uncertainty estimates, robustness to over-fitting, and principled ways for tuning hyper-parameters. However the scalability of these models to big datasets remains an active topic of research. We introduce a novel re-parametrisation of variational inference for sparse GP regression and latent variable models that allows for an efficient distributed algorithm. This is done by exploiting the decoupling of the data given the inducing points to re-formulate the evidence lower bound in a Map-Reduce setting. We show that the inference scales well with data and computational resources, while preserving a balanced distribution of the load among the nodes. We further demonstrate the utility in scaling Gaussian processes to big data. We show that GP performance improves with increasing amounts of data in regression (on flight data with 2 million records) and latent variable modelling (on MNIST). The results show that GPs perform better than many common models often used for big data.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer probabilistic models of functions, including uncertainty estimates and principled hyperparameter tuning. They are useful for regression and nonlinear dimensionality reduction, but applying them to large datasets raises computational challenges. This paper develops distributed inference for sparse Gaussian process regression and latent variable models.

The method reparameterizes variational inference by exploiting how data decouple when conditioned on inducing points. This lets the authors reformulate the evidence lower bound, the objective used for approximate inference, in a Map-Reduce setting. The resulting computation can be distributed across nodes, and the authors report good scaling with both data volume and computational resources while maintaining balanced workloads.

Experiments show that Gaussian process performance improves as more data are used, both for regression on two million flight records and for latent variable modeling on MNIST. The models also outperform many common approaches used for big data in the reported results. The contribution connects a reformulation of the inference objective to evidence that larger datasets can improve these probabilistic models.
summary.tldr: A variational reparameterization enables distributed sparse Gaussian process inference with balanced workloads and improved performance as data increase.

title: Distributed Variational Inference in Sparse Gaussian Process Regression and Latent Variable Models

abstract: Modeling the distribution of natural images is challenging, partly because of strong statistical dependencies which can extend over hundreds of pixels. Recurrent neural networks have been successful in capturing long-range dependencies in a number of problems but only recently have found their way into generative image models. We here introduce a recurrent image model based on multi-dimensional long short-term memory units which are particularly suited for image modeling due to their spatial structure. Our model scales to images of arbitrary size and its likelihood is computationally tractable. We find that it outperforms the state of the art in quantitative comparisons on several image datasets and produces promising results when used for texture synthesis and inpainting.

paragraphs: Natural images contain statistical relationships that can stretch across hundreds of pixels. Modeling an image distribution therefore requires accounting for more than nearby pixel relationships. This paper introduces a recurrent image model designed to capture those extended dependencies using multidimensional long short-term memory units, whose spatial organization suits image data.

The model combines this spatial recurrent structure with two useful properties: it can scale to images of arbitrary size, and its likelihood is computationally tractable. A tractable likelihood makes it possible to evaluate the probability the model assigns to an image. These properties connect the modeling of long-range relationships with a distribution that can be evaluated computationally.

The authors report better quantitative results than the state of the art on several image datasets. They also find promising results for texture synthesis and inpainting, which concern creating textures and filling missing image content. The quantitative comparisons support the model's distributional modeling ability in the evaluated settings, while the application results suggest its usefulness for generating and completing images.
summary.tldr: Spatial LSTMs model long-range image dependencies with tractable likelihoods and improve quantitative results on several image datasets.

title: Generative Image Modeling Using Spatial LSTMs

abstract: Mixture modeling is a general technique for making any simple model more expressive through weighted combination. This generality and simplicity in part explains the success of the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm, in which updates are easy to derive for a wide class of mixture models. However, the likelihood of a mixture model is non-convex, so EM has no known global convergence guarantees. Recently, method of moments approaches offer global guarantees for some mixture models, but they do not extend easily to the range of mixture models that exist. In this work, we present Polymom, an unifying framework based on method of moments in which estimation procedures are easily derivable, just as in EM. Polymom is applicable when the moments of a single mixture component are polynomials of the parameters. Our key observation is that the moments of the mixture model are a mixture of these polynomials, which allows us to cast estimation as a Generalized Moment Problem. We solve its relaxations using semidefinite optimization, and then extract parameters using ideas from computer algebra. This framework allows us to draw insights and apply tools from convex optimization, computer algebra and the theory of moments to study problems in statistical estimation. Simulations show good empirical performance on several models.

paragraphs: Mixture models combine simpler models with weights to represent richer distributions. Expectation maximization offers convenient updates for many such models, but their nonconvex likelihoods leave it without known global convergence guarantees. Moment-based methods provide global guarantees for some mixtures, yet deriving them across many model families has been difficult.

Polymom offers a unifying moment-based framework for models whose individual components have moments that are polynomial functions of their parameters. The key observation is that the full mixture's moments are weighted combinations of those same polynomials. This lets the authors express parameter estimation as a Generalized Moment Problem rather than deriving a separate procedure from scratch for each model.

Its contribution is a common route from a model's polynomial moments to an estimation procedure, linking statistical estimation with convex optimization and algebraic tools. Simulations show good empirical performance on several models; the stated applicability condition is the polynomial form of component moments.
summary.tldr: Polymom turns mixture estimation with polynomial component moments into a common framework using semidefinite optimization and algebraic parameter extraction.

title: Estimating Mixture Models via Mixtures of Polynomials

abstract: In this paper, we explore the inclusion of latent random variables into the hidden state of a recurrent neural network (RNN) by combining the elements of the variational autoencoder. We argue that through the use of high-level latent random variables, the variational RNN (VRNN) can model the kind of variability observed in highly structured sequential data such as natural speech. We empirically evaluate the proposed model against other related sequential models on four speech datasets and one handwriting dataset. Our results show the important roles that latent random variables can play in the RNN dynamics.

We argue that through the use of high-level latent random variables, the variational RNN (VRNN) can model the kind of variability observed in highly structured sequential data such as natural speech. We empirically evaluate the proposed model against other related sequential models on four speech datasets and one handwriting dataset. Our results show the important roles that latent random variables can play in the RNN dynamics.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a recurrent neural network can represent variability in structured sequences. An RNN carries a hidden state through a sequence, allowing its behavior to depend on earlier observations. The authors introduce latent random variables into this evolving state, combining recurrent modeling with elements of a variational autoencoder.

The resulting variational RNN, or VRNN, gives the model high-level random quantities alongside its recurrent dynamics. These variables provide a way to represent variation within sequences such as natural speech. The central argument is that this kind of variability deserves an explicit role in the model’s internal dynamics, rather than being handled only through the existing recurrent representation.

The authors compare the proposed model with related sequential models on four speech datasets and one handwriting dataset. They report that the results demonstrate important roles for latent random variables in RNN dynamics. The contribution is therefore both an architectural proposal and empirical support for incorporating structured randomness into models of sequential data.
summary.tldr: The VRNN combines recurrent neural networks with latent random variables to model variability in structured sequences.

title: A Recurrent Latent Variable Model for Sequential Data

abstract: Predicting the behavior of human participants in strategic settings is an important problem in many domains. Most existing work either assumes that participants are perfectly rational, or attempts to directly model each participant's cognitive processes based on insights from cognitive psychology and experimental economics. In this work, we present an alternative, a deep learning approach that automatically performs cognitive modeling without relying on such expert knowledge. We introduce a novel architecture that allows a single network to generalize across different input and output dimensions by using matrix units rather than scalar units, and show that its performance significantly outperforms that of the previous state of the art, which relies on expert-constructed features.
originalAbstract: Predicting the behavior of human participants in strategic settings is an important problem in many domains. Most existing work either assumes that participants are perfectly rational, or attempts to directly model each participant's cognitive processes based on insights from cognitive psychology and experimental economics. In this work, we present an alternative, a deep learning approach that automatically performs cognitive modeling without relying on such expert knowledge. We introduce a novel architecture that allows a single network to generalize across different input and output dimensions by using matrix units rather than scalar units, and show that its performance significantly outperforms that of the previous state of the art, which relies on expert-constructed features.

paragraphs: Predicting human decisions in strategic settings requires accounting for how people respond to choices involving other participants. Existing approaches commonly assume perfect rationality or build explicit cognitive models using expert knowledge. This paper explores learning those predictive patterns automatically with a deep neural network, reducing reliance on manually specified cognitive features.

Its architectural contribution addresses variation in the dimensions of the prediction problem. A single network must handle inputs and outputs of different sizes. The authors introduce matrix units in place of scalar units to allow this generalization. Accommodating changing dimensions is therefore part of the model design, rather than requiring a separately described fixed-size predictor for every setting.

The reported predictive performance significantly exceeds the previous state of the art, which uses expert-constructed features. This supports the usefulness of learning representations directly for the strategic-behavior prediction task studied. The contribution combines that empirical result with an architecture intended to share a predictive model across problems whose input and output dimensions differ.
summary.tldr: A neural architecture using matrix units predicts human strategic behavior across varying input and output sizes and outperforms the reported expert-feature baseline.

title: Deep Learning for Predicting Human Strategic Behavior

abstract: We propose a novel extension of the encoder-decoder framework, called a review network. The review network is generic and can enhance any existing encoder- decoder model: in this paper, we consider RNN decoders with both CNN and RNN encoders. The review network performs a number of review steps with attention mechanism on the encoder hidden states, and outputs a thought vector after each review step; the thought vectors are used as the input of the attention mechanism in the decoder. We show that conventional encoder-decoders are a special case of our framework. Empirically, we show that our framework improves over state-of- the-art encoder-decoder systems on the tasks of image captioning and source code captioning.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel extension of the encoder-decoder framework, called a review network. The review network is generic and can enhance any existing encoder- decoder model: in this paper, we consider RNN decoders with both CNN and RNN encoders. The review network performs a number of review steps with attention mechanism on the encoder hidden states, and outputs a thought vector after each review step; the thought vectors are used as the input of the attention mechanism in the decoder. We show that conventional encoder-decoders are a special case of our framework. Empirically, we show that our framework improves over state-of- the-art encoder-decoder systems on the tasks of image captioning and source code captioning.

paragraphs: An encoder-decoder model turns an input into internal representations and then generates an output sequence. This paper inserts a review stage between those operations. The review network revisits the encoder's hidden states through attention, producing a sequence of intermediate representations before the decoder uses them to generate a caption.

Each review step produces what the authors call a thought vector. The decoder's attention mechanism then operates on these vectors. This creates a way to process the encoded information further before generation, with several review steps supplying the representations on which the decoder focuses. The paper considers recurrent decoders paired with both convolutional and recurrent encoders.

The framework is presented as a general extension capable of enhancing existing encoder-decoder models, and conventional encoder-decoders are shown to be a special case. Empirically, review networks improve on state-of-the-art encoder-decoder systems for image captioning and source code captioning. The two applications support the usefulness of the review stage across different input types within the tested generation tasks.
summary.tldr: Review networks add attentive processing between encoding and decoding, improving image and source code captioning in experiments.

title: Review Networks for Caption Generation

abstract: Deep generative models have recently shown great promise in imitation learning for motor control. Given enough data, even supervised approaches can do one-shot imitation learning; however, they are vulnerable to cascading failures when the agent trajectory diverges from the demonstrations. Compared to purely supervised methods, Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) can learn more robust controllers from fewer demonstrations, but is inherently mode-seeking and more difficult to train. In this paper, we show how to combine the favourable aspects of these two approaches. The base of our model is a new type of variational autoencoder on demonstration trajectories that learns semantic policy embeddings. We show that these embeddings can be learned on a 9 DoF Jaco robot arm in reaching tasks, and then smoothly interpolated with a resulting smooth interpolation of reaching behavior. Leveraging these policy representations, we develop a new version of GAIL that (1) is much more robust than the purely-supervised controller, especially with few demonstrations, and (2) avoids mode collapse, capturing many diverse behaviors when GAIL on its own does not. We demonstrate our approach on learning diverse gaits from demonstration on a 2D biped and a 62 DoF 3D humanoid in the MuJoCo physics environment.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension in imitation learning for motor control. Supervised imitation can reproduce demonstrations but suffer cascading errors when its trajectory departs from them. Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning can learn more robust control from fewer demonstrations, yet may concentrate on a narrow subset of behaviors and be harder to train.

The authors begin with a new variational autoencoder over demonstration trajectories that learns semantic policy embeddings. On reaching tasks with a nine-degree-of-freedom Jaco arm, smooth interpolation between these embeddings produces smoothly changing reaching behavior. This demonstrates that the learned policy representation captures variation that can be used to generate intermediate behaviors.

They then use these representations in a modified GAIL approach. The resulting controller is substantially more robust than the purely supervised controller, especially with few demonstrations, and captures diverse behaviors while avoiding the mode collapse observed with GAIL alone. Demonstrations include learning varied gaits for a two-dimensional biped and a 62-degree-of-freedom three-dimensional humanoid in MuJoCo.
summary.tldr: Learned policy embeddings combined with adversarial imitation improve controller robustness while preserving diverse demonstrated behaviors.

title: Robust Imitation of Diverse Behaviors

abstract: Directed latent variable models that formulate the joint distribution as $p(x,z) = p(z) p(x \mid z)$ have the advantage of fast and exact sampling. However, these models have the weakness of needing to specify $p(z)$, often with a simple fixed prior that limits the expressiveness of the model. Undirected latent variable models discard the requirement that $p(z)$ be specified with a prior, yet sampling from them generally requires an iterative procedure such as blocked Gibbs-sampling that may require many steps to draw samples from the joint distribution $p(x, z)$. We propose a novel approach to learning the joint distribution between the data and a latent code which uses an adversarially learned iterative procedure to gradually refine the joint distribution, $p(x, z)$, to better match with the data distribution on each step. GibbsNet is the best of both worlds both in theory and in practice. Achieving the speed and simplicity of a directed latent variable model, it is guaranteed (assuming the adversarial game reaches the virtual training criteria global minimum) to produce samples from $p(x, z)$ with only a few sampling iterations. Achieving the expressiveness and flexibility of an undirected latent variable model, GibbsNet does away with the need for an explicit $p(z)$ and has the ability to do attribute prediction, class-conditional generation, and joint image-attribute modeling in a single model which is not trained for any of these specific tasks. We show empirically that GibbsNet is able to learn a more complex $p(z)$ and show that this leads to improved inpainting and iterative refinement of $p(x, z)$ for dozens of steps and stable generation without collapse for thousands of steps, despite being trained on only a few steps.

title: GibbsNet: Iterative Adversarial Inference for Deep Graphical Models

abstract: The dueling bandit is a learning framework where the feedback information in the learning process is restricted to noisy comparison between a pair of actions. In this paper, we address a dueling bandit problem based on a cost function over a continuous space. We propose a stochastic mirror descent algorithm and show that the algorithm achieves an $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$-regret bound under strong convexity and smoothness assumptions for the cost function. Then, we clarify the equivalence between regret minimization in dueling bandit and convex optimization for the cost function. Moreover, considering a lower bound in convex optimization, it is turned out that our algorithm achieves the optimal convergence rate in convex optimization and the optimal regret in dueling bandit except for a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: In a dueling-bandit problem, the learner receives noisy comparisons between two actions. This paper considers actions drawn from a continuous space, with their quality governed by a cost function. The challenge is to use these comparisons to make progressively better decisions while controlling the accumulated cost of learning.

The authors propose a stochastic mirror-descent algorithm and prove a regret bound of order √(T log T). The guarantee assumes that the cost function is strongly convex and smooth. Because this bound grows more slowly than the number of rounds T, the average regret decreases as learning proceeds within the studied setting.

The paper also establishes an equivalence between minimizing dueling-bandit regret and solving the associated convex optimization problem. This connection lets the authors use a convex-optimization lower bound to assess their algorithm. They conclude that it attains an optimal optimization convergence rate and optimal dueling-bandit regret apart from a logarithmic factor, providing a near-optimality result for comparison-based learning under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under strong convexity and smoothness, stochastic mirror descent achieves continuous dueling-bandit regret optimal up to a logarithmic factor.

title: Regret Analysis for Continuous Dueling Bandit

abstract: Representation learning has become an invaluable approach for learning from symbolic data such as text and graphs. However, state-of-the-art embedding methods typically do not account for latent hierarchical structures which are characteristic for many complex symbolic datasets. In this work, we introduce a new approach for learning hierarchical representations of symbolic data by embedding them into hyperbolic space -- or more precisely into an n-dimensional Poincaré ball. Due to the underlying hyperbolic geometry, this allows us to learn parsimonious representations of symbolic data by simultaneously capturing hierarchy and similarity. We present an efficient algorithm to learn the embeddings based on Riemannian optimization and show experimentally that Poincaré embeddings can outperform Euclidean embeddings significantly on data with latent hierarchies, both in terms of representation capacity and in terms of generalization ability.

paragraphs: Symbolic datasets such as text and graphs often contain hidden hierarchical structure. Embedding methods represent their elements numerically, but many approaches do not explicitly account for that hierarchy. This paper proposes placing symbolic data in hyperbolic space, specifically an n-dimensional Poincaré ball, to learn representations suited to this structure.

The choice of geometry allows the embeddings to capture both hierarchy and similarity in compact representations. These are complementary relationships: an embedding should convey how elements are related within a hierarchy as well as how similar they are. The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm based on Riemannian optimization, which accommodates the geometry of the embedding space.

Experiments show that Poincaré embeddings can substantially outperform Euclidean embeddings on data containing latent hierarchies. The reported advantages concern both representation capacity and generalization ability. The findings therefore support matching the geometry of the representation to hierarchical data, with the demonstrated gains specifically tied to datasets exhibiting that underlying structure.
summary.tldr: Poincaré embeddings use hyperbolic geometry to compactly capture hierarchy and similarity, with substantial gains on hierarchical data.

title: Poincaré Embeddings for Learning Hierarchical Representations

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful generative models, but suffer from training instability. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) makes progress toward stable training of GANs, but sometimes can still generate only poor samples or fail to converge. We find that these problems are often due to the use of weight clipping in WGAN to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can lead to undesired behavior. We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalize the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input. Our proposed method performs better than standard WGAN and enables stable training of a wide variety of GAN architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning, including 101-layer ResNets and language models with continuous generators. We also achieve high quality generations on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms.

paragraphs: Wasserstein GANs aim to improve the stability of adversarial training, yet they can still produce poor samples or fail to converge. This paper identifies weight clipping as a frequent source of those problems. Clipping is used to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, but the authors find that it can induce undesirable behavior.

Their alternative penalizes the norm of the critic's gradient with respect to its input. This changes how the critic is constrained: the training objective directly penalizes its input-gradient behavior instead of relying on clipped weights. The proposal targets a particular mechanism behind WGAN instability rather than changing the overall generator-and-critic setup.

The authors report better performance than standard WGAN and stable training across a broad range of architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning. Demonstrations include 101-layer residual networks and language models with continuous generators, alongside high-quality image generation on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms. These results provide empirical support for the gradient penalty as a broadly useful training modification.
summary.tldr: Replacing WGAN weight clipping with an input-gradient penalty improves reported training stability and generation quality across diverse architectures.

title: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs

abstract: The paper addresses the classical network tomography problem of inferring local traffic given origin-destination observations. Focussing on large complex public transportation systems, we build a scalable model that exploits input-output information to estimate the unobserved link/station loads and the users path preferences. Based on the reconstruction of the users' travel time distribution, the model is flexible enough to capture possible different path-choice strategies and correlations between users travelling on similar paths at similar times. The corresponding likelihood function is intractable for medium or large-scale networks and we propose two distinct strategies, namely the exact maximum-likelihood inference of an approximate but tractable model and the variational inference of the original intractable model. As an application of our approach, we consider the emblematic case of the London Underground network, where a tap-in/tap-out system tracks the start/exit time and location of all journeys in a day. A set of synthetic simulations and real data provided by Transport For London are used to validate and test the model on the predictions of observable and unobservable quantities.

paragraphs: Journey entry and exit records reveal where travel starts and ends, but leave intermediate routes and traffic loads unobserved. This paper develops a scalable network tomography model to estimate link and station loads alongside travelers' path preferences. It focuses on large public transportation networks, using the London Underground as its application.

The model reconstructs travel-time distributions and can represent different route-choice strategies. It also accommodates correlations among users traveling on similar paths at similar times. This flexibility matters because the same origin-destination observations can be associated with different patterns of travel through the network, which the model aims to infer.

For medium and large networks, the likelihood is computationally intractable. The authors therefore propose two inference strategies: exact maximum likelihood for a tractable approximation, and variational inference for the original model. They test and validate the approach using synthetic simulations and Transport for London data containing journey entry and exit times and locations. Evaluation addresses predictions of both observable and unobserved quantities.
summary.tldr: A scalable transport model infers hidden network loads and route preferences from journey entry and exit observations.

title: Tomography of the London Underground: a Scalable Model for Origin-Destination Data

abstract: Stochastic optimization of continuous objectives is at the heart of modern machine learning. However, many important problems are of discrete nature and often involve submodular objectives. We seek to unleash the power of stochastic continuous optimization, namely stochastic gradient descent and its variants, to such discrete problems. We first introduce the problem of stochastic submodular optimization, where one needs to optimize a submodular objective which is given as an expectation. Our model captures situations where the discrete objective arises as an empirical risk (e.g., in the case of exemplar-based clustering), or is given as an explicit stochastic model (e.g., in the case of influence maximization in social networks). By exploiting that common extensions act linearly on the class of submodular functions, we employ projected stochastic gradient ascent and its variants in the continuous domain, and perform rounding to obtain discrete solutions. We focus on the rich and widely used family of weighted coverage functions. We show that our approach yields solutions that are guaranteed to match the optimal approximation guarantees, while reducing the computational cost by several orders of magnitude, as we demonstrate empirically.

paragraphs: This paper brings stochastic continuous optimization to discrete submodular maximization. It considers objectives defined as expectations, which can arise either from empirical data or from an explicit random model. The abstract gives exemplar-based clustering and social-network influence maximization as examples of these two sources of stochastic objectives.

The approach moves the problem into a continuous domain, uses projected stochastic gradient ascent or related methods, and then rounds the result into a discrete solution. A key mathematical ingredient is that common extensions act linearly on submodular functions. The authors focus their guarantees on weighted coverage functions, a rich family within the broader submodular setting.

For that family, the method matches optimal approximation guarantees. This means it preserves the stated quality guarantee for an approximate solution, rather than claiming exact optimization. Experiments demonstrate computational-cost reductions of several orders of magnitude. The theoretical and empirical contributions complement each other: approximation quality is guaranteed, while the magnitude of the computational savings is established through the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Continuous stochastic optimization and rounding achieve optimal approximation guarantees for weighted coverage objectives with large empirical computational savings.

title: Stochastic Submodular Maximization: The Case of Coverage Functions

abstract: We present an algorithm to identify sparse dependence structure in continuous and non-Gaussian probability distributions, given a corresponding set of data. The conditional independence structure of an arbitrary distribution can be represented as an undirected graph (or Markov random field), but most algorithms for learning this structure are restricted to the discrete or Gaussian cases. Our new approach allows for more realistic and accurate descriptions of the distribution in question, and in turn better estimates of its sparse Markov structure. Sparsity in the graph is of interest as it can accelerate inference, improve sampling methods, and reveal important dependencies between variables. The algorithm relies on exploiting the connection between the sparsity of the graph and the sparsity of transport maps, which deterministically couple one probability measure to another.

The conditional independence structure of an arbitrary distribution can be represented as an undirected graph (or Markov random field), but most algorithms for learning this structure are restricted to the discrete or Gaussian cases. Our new approach allows for more realistic and accurate descriptions of the distribution in question, and in turn better estimates of its sparse Markov structure. Sparsity in the graph is of interest as it can accelerate inference, improve sampling methods, and reveal important dependencies between variables.
