paragraphs: A probabilistic graphical model represents conditional independence relationships among variables using a graph. Learning a sparse graph means identifying a relatively small set of dependencies that describes the distribution. This paper addresses that task for continuous, non-Gaussian data, extending beyond the discrete or Gaussian settings that restrict many existing structure-learning algorithms.

The method uses transport maps, which deterministically transform one probability measure into another. Its central mechanism is a connection between sparsity in these maps and sparsity in the distribution's graph. Exploiting that relationship provides a route from a representation of the probability distribution to an estimate of which variables remain conditionally dependent.

The approach matters because a more realistic description of a non-Gaussian distribution can support a better estimate of its dependence structure. Sparse graphs can also make inference faster, improve sampling methods, and reveal important relationships between variables. The contribution is an algorithm built around this transport-map connection, allowing sparse graphical modeling to address distributions beyond the usual Gaussian framework.
summary.tldr: The paper learns sparse dependence graphs for continuous non-Gaussian distributions by exploiting their connection to sparse transport maps.

title: Beyond normality: Learning sparse probabilistic graphical models in the non-Gaussian setting

abstract: We study finite-sum nonconvex optimization problems, where the objective function is an average of $n$ nonconvex functions. We propose a new stochastic gradient descent algorithm based on nested variance reduction. Compared with conventional stochastic variance reduced gradient (SVRG) algorithm that uses two reference points to construct a semi-stochastic gradient with diminishing variance in each iteration, our algorithm uses $K+1$ nested reference points to build a semi-stochastic gradient to further reduce its variance in each iteration. For smooth nonconvex functions, the proposed algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point (i.e., $\|\nabla F(\mathbf{x})\|_2\leq \epsilon$) within $\tilde O(n\land \epsilon^{-2}+\epsilon^{-3}\land n^{1/2}\epsilon^{-2})$\footnote{$\tilde O(\cdot)$ hides the logarithmic factors, and $a\land b$ means $\min(a,b)$.} number of stochastic gradient evaluations. This improves the best known gradient complexity of SVRG $O(n+n^{2/3}\epsilon^{-2})$ and that of SCSG $O(n\land \epsilon^{-2}+\epsilon^{-10/3}\land n^{2/3}\epsilon^{-2})$. For gradient dominated functions, our algorithm also achieves better gradient complexity than the state-of-the-art algorithms. Thorough experimental results on different nonconvex optimization problems back up our theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonconvex objectives formed by averaging n component functions. Stochastic gradient methods can reduce the work per update, but their gradient estimates vary. The proposed algorithm reduces that variance through nested reference points, extending the reference-point construction used by stochastic variance reduced gradient methods.

Conventional SVRG uses two reference points to construct its gradient estimate. This method uses K+1 nested reference points to reduce variance further. For smooth nonconvex functions, it reaches a point with gradient norm at most epsilon using a number of stochastic gradient evaluations bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by min(n, epsilon⁻²) + min(epsilon⁻³, sqrt(n)epsilon⁻²).

The stated bound improves the known gradient complexities of SVRG and SCSG. The authors also obtain better complexity for gradient-dominated functions, a separately identified class of objectives. Experiments on different nonconvex problems support the theory. The general smooth-case guarantee concerns reaching a small gradient, so its immediate meaning is efficient approximate first-order stationarity rather than guaranteed global minimization.
summary.tldr: Nested reference points reduce gradient-estimation variance and improve complexity bounds for nonconvex finite-sum optimization.

title: Stochastic Nested Variance Reduction for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Methods for learning from demonstration (LfD) have shown success in acquiring behavior policies by imitating a user. However, even for a single task, LfD may require numerous demonstrations. For versatile agents that must learn many tasks via demonstration, this process would substantially burden the user if each task were learned in isolation. To address this challenge, we introduce the novel problem of lifelong learning from demonstration, which allows the agent to continually build upon knowledge learned from previously demonstrated tasks to accelerate the learning of new tasks, reducing the amount of demonstrations required. As one solution to this problem, we propose the first lifelong learning approach to inverse reinforcement learning, which learns consecutive tasks via demonstration, continually transferring knowledge between tasks to improve performance.

However, even for a single task, LfD may require numerous demonstrations. For versatile agents that must learn many tasks via demonstration, this process would substantially burden the user if each task were learned in isolation. To address this challenge, we introduce the novel problem of lifelong learning from demonstration, which allows the agent to continually build upon knowledge learned from previously demonstrated tasks to accelerate the learning of new tasks, reducing the amount of demonstrations required. As one solution to this problem, we propose the first lifelong learning approach to inverse reinforcement learning, which learns consecutive tasks via demonstration, continually transferring knowledge between tasks to improve performance.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstration lets an agent acquire behavior by observing a user, but even one task may require many examples. For an agent expected to learn a broad collection of tasks, repeating that process independently can place a substantial burden on the person providing demonstrations. Previously learned tasks therefore represent potentially valuable knowledge for future learning.

The paper introduces lifelong learning from demonstration as a problem in which the agent continually builds on demonstrated tasks. Instead of treating every new task as a separate learning exercise, the agent transfers knowledge across a sequence of tasks. The intended benefit is faster learning of new behavior with fewer demonstrations from the user.

As a solution, the authors propose a lifelong approach to inverse reinforcement learning. It learns consecutive tasks through demonstration while continually transferring knowledge to improve performance. The contribution makes ongoing knowledge accumulation central to learning from a user: demonstrations serve both the current task and the agent's ability to learn subsequent tasks more efficiently.
summary.tldr: A lifelong inverse reinforcement learning approach transfers knowledge across demonstrated tasks to improve learning and reduce the user's demonstration burden.

title: Lifelong Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Bayes framework (McAllester, 1999) can incorporate knowledge about the learning algorithm and (data) distribution through the use of distribution-dependent priors, yielding tighter generalization bounds on data-dependent posteriors. Using this flexibility, however, is difficult, especially when the data distribution is presumed to be unknown. We show how a differentially private data-dependent prior yields a valid PAC-Bayes bound, and then show how non-private mechanisms for choosing priors can also yield generalization bounds. As an application of this result, we show that a Gaussian prior mean chosen via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD; Welling and Teh, 2011) leads to a valid PAC-Bayes bound due to control of the 2-Wasserstein distance to a differentially private stationary distribution. We study our data-dependent bounds empirically, and show that they can be nonvacuous even when other distribution-dependent bounds are vacuous.

Using this flexibility, however, is difficult, especially when the data distribution is presumed to be unknown. We show how a differentially private data-dependent prior yields a valid PAC-Bayes bound, and then show how non-private mechanisms for choosing priors can also yield generalization bounds. As an application of this result, we show that a Gaussian prior mean chosen via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD; Welling and Teh, 2011) leads to a valid PAC-Bayes bound due to control of the 2-Wasserstein distance to a differentially private stationary distribution. We study our data-dependent bounds empirically, and show that they can be nonvacuous even when other distribution-dependent bounds are vacuous.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayes analysis gives bounds on how a learned predictor generalizes beyond its training data. A well-chosen prior can incorporate knowledge about the learning procedure and data distribution, potentially tightening those bounds. Choosing such a prior is difficult when the underlying distribution is unknown and the available information comes from the training data itself.

This paper shows that a prior selected from data through a differentially private mechanism yields a valid PAC-Bayes bound. It also develops a route for certain non-private prior-selection mechanisms to produce generalization bounds. The contribution is therefore a way to justify informative data-dependent priors while accounting for how their selection uses the data.

As an application, the authors choose a Gaussian prior's mean using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. Validity follows from controlling its 2-Wasserstein distance to a differentially private stationary distribution. Empirical evaluations show that the resulting bounds can be nonvacuous when other distribution-dependent bounds are vacuous, meaning they can provide informative guarantees in those tested circumstances.
summary.tldr: Differential privacy provides a route to valid PAC-Bayes bounds with data-dependent priors, including some priors selected non-privately.

title: Data-dependent PAC-Bayes priors via differential privacy

abstract: Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have revolutionized the field of graph representation learning through effectively learned node embeddings, and achieved state-of-the-art results in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, current GNN methods are inherently flat and do not learn hierarchical representations of graphs---a limitation that is especially problematic for the task of graph classification, where the goal is to predict the label associated with an entire graph. Here we propose DiffPool, a differentiable graph pooling module that can generate hierarchical representations of graphs and can be combined with various graph neural network architectures in an end-to-end fashion. DiffPool learns a differentiable soft cluster assignment for nodes at each layer of a deep GNN, mapping nodes to a set of clusters, which then form the coarsened input for the next GNN layer. Our experimental results show that combining existing GNN methods with DiffPool yields an average improvement of 5-10% accuracy on graph classification benchmarks, compared to all existing pooling approaches, achieving a new state-of-the-art on four out of five benchmark datasets.

However, current GNN methods are inherently flat and do not learn hierarchical representations of graphs---a limitation that is especially problematic for the task of graph classification, where the goal is to predict the label associated with an entire graph. Here we propose DiffPool, a differentiable graph pooling module that can generate hierarchical representations of graphs and can be combined with various graph neural network architectures in an end-to-end fashion. DiffPool learns a differentiable soft cluster assignment for nodes at each layer of a deep GNN, mapping nodes to a set of clusters, which then form the coarsened input for the next GNN layer. Our experimental results show that combining existing GNN methods with DiffPool yields an average improvement of 5-10% accuracy on graph classification benchmarks, compared to all existing pooling approaches, achieving a new state-of-the-art on four out of five benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can learn useful representations of individual nodes, but predicting a label for an entire graph also calls for combining information across its structure. This paper identifies the flat organization of existing approaches as a limitation and introduces DiffPool, a module that learns hierarchical graph representations.

At each layer, DiffPool learns soft assignments of nodes to clusters. Those clusters form a smaller, coarser graph that becomes the input to the next graph neural network layer. Repeating this process creates successive levels of representation. Because the assignments are differentiable, the grouping process can be trained together with the rest of the network, and the module can work with different graph neural network architectures.

Experiments report an average accuracy improvement of 5–10% over the existing pooling approaches used for comparison, with state-of-the-art results on four of five graph classification datasets. These findings support learning the grouping structure as part of the classification model. They show that hierarchical aggregation can improve whole-graph predictions in the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: DiffPool learns differentiable node clusters to build graph hierarchies, improving accuracy on graph classification benchmarks.

title: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Differentiable Pooling

abstract: Boosting variational inference (BVI) approximates an intractable probability density by iteratively building up a mixture of simple component distributions one at a time, using techniques from sparse convex optimization to provide both computational scalability and approximation error guarantees. But the guarantees have strong conditions that do not often hold in practice, resulting in degenerate component optimization problems; and we show that the ad-hoc regularization used to prevent degeneracy in practice can cause BVI to fail in unintuitive ways. We thus develop universal boosting variational inference (UBVI), a BVI scheme that exploits the simple geometry of probability densities under the Hellinger metric to prevent the degeneracy of other gradient-based BVI methods, avoid difficult joint optimizations of both component and weight, and simplify fully-corrective weight optimizations. We show that for any target density and any mixture component family, the output of UBVI converges to the best possible approximation in the mixture family, even when the mixture family is misspecified. We develop a scalable implementation based on exponential family mixture components and standard stochastic optimization techniques. Finally, we discuss statistical benefits of the Hellinger distance as a variational objective through bounds on posterior probability, moment, and importance sampling errors. Experiments on multiple datasets and models show that UBVI provides reliable, accurate posterior approximations.
originalAbstract: Boosting variational inference (BVI) approximates an intractable probability density by iteratively building up a mixture of simple component distributions one at a time, using techniques from sparse convex optimization to provide both computational scalability and approximation error guarantees. But the guarantees have strong conditions that do not often hold in practice, resulting in degenerate component optimization problems; and we show that the ad-hoc regularization used to prevent degeneracy in practice can cause BVI to fail in unintuitive ways. We thus develop universal boosting variational inference (UBVI), a BVI scheme that exploits the simple geometry of probability densities under the Hellinger metric to prevent the degeneracy of other gradient-based BVI methods, avoid difficult joint optimizations of both component and weight, and simplify fully-corrective weight optimizations. We show that for any target density and any mixture component family, the output of UBVI converges to the best possible approximation in the mixture family, even when the mixture family is misspecified. We develop a scalable implementation based on exponential family mixture components and standard stochastic optimization techniques. Finally, we discuss statistical benefits of the Hellinger distance as a variational objective through bounds on posterior probability, moment, and importance sampling errors. Experiments on multiple datasets and models show that UBVI provides reliable, accurate posterior approximations.

Existing guarantees can require conditions that fail in practice, leading to degenerate component optimizations. This paper also shows that the ad hoc regularization used to prevent those problems can itself produce unexpected failures.

This prevents the degeneracy affecting other gradient-based approaches, avoids difficult joint optimization of a component and its weight, and simplifies reoptimizing mixture weights. The authors prove convergence to the best approximation available in the chosen mixture family for any target density and component family, including misspecified families.

A scalable implementation uses exponential-family components and standard stochastic optimization. The paper further connects Hellinger approximation error to errors in posterior probabilities, moments, and importance sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and models report reliable, accurate posterior approximations. The convergence guarantee concerns the best attainable mixture approximation, which need not equal the target when the family is misspecified.
summary.tldr: UBVI uses Hellinger geometry to avoid degenerate mixture optimization and converge to the best approximation in the chosen mixture family.

title: Universal Boosting Variational Inference

abstract: Finding local correspondences between images with different viewpoints requires local descriptors that are robust against geometric transformations. An approach for transformation invariance is to integrate out the transformations by pooling the features extracted from transformed versions of an image. However, the feature pooling may sacrifice the distinctiveness of the resulting descriptors. In this paper, we introduce a novel visual descriptor named Group Invariant Feature Transform (GIFT), which is both discriminative and robust to geometric transformations. The key idea is that the features extracted from the transformed versions of an image can be viewed as a function defined on the group of the transformations. Instead of feature pooling, we use group convolutions to exploit underlying structures of the extracted features on the group, resulting in descriptors that are both discriminative and provably invariant to the group of transformations. Extensive experiments show that GIFT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets and practically improves the performance of relative pose estimation.

paragraphs: Matching corresponding locations across images requires descriptors that remain useful when viewpoint changes alter local geometry. One way to obtain transformation invariance is to extract features from transformed images and pool them together. The paper identifies a tradeoff in that strategy: pooling may remove distinctions that help tell one image location from another.

GIFT treats features from different transformed versions as a function defined over a transformation group. It then applies group convolutions to exploit the relationships among those features, instead of immediately collapsing them through pooling. This gives the model a structured way to process transformation-dependent information while constructing the final descriptor. The resulting descriptors are discriminative and provably invariant to the transformation group being considered.

Experiments show improvements over leading methods on several benchmark datasets, as well as practical gains in relative pose estimation. The contribution connects a mathematical invariance property with usefulness for image correspondence. Its invariance guarantee applies to the specified group of transformations, while the experiments support the claim that the descriptors retain information needed for accurate matching.
summary.tldr: GIFT uses group convolutions to produce distinctive visual descriptors with provable invariance to the modeled transformation group.

title: GIFT: Learning Transformation-Invariant Dense Visual Descriptors via Group CNNs

abstract: Mixup~\cite{zhang2017mixup} is a recently proposed method for training deep neural networks where additional samples are generated during training by convexly combining random pairs of images and their associated labels. While simple to implement, it has shown to be a surprisingly effective method of data augmentation for image classification; DNNs trained with mixup show noticeable gains in classification performance on a number of image classification benchmarks. In this work, we discuss a hitherto untouched aspect of mixup training -- the calibration and predictive uncertainty of models trained with mixup. We find that DNNs trained with mixup are significantly better calibrated -- i.e the predicted softmax scores are much better indicators of the actual likelihood of a correct prediction -- than DNNs trained in the regular fashion. We conduct experiments on a number of image classification architectures and datasets -- including large-scale datasets like ImageNet -- and find this to be the case. Additionally, we find that merely mixing features does not result in the same calibration benefit and that the label smoothing in mixup training plays a significant role in improving calibration. Finally, we also observe that mixup-trained DNNs are less prone to over-confident predictions on out-of-distribution and random-noise data. We conclude that the typical overconfidence seen in neural networks, even on in-distribution data is likely a consequence of training with hard labels, suggesting that mixup training be employed for classification tasks where predictive uncertainty is a significant concern.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by blending pairs of images and their labels. This paper examines how that training procedure affects confidence estimates, extending attention beyond classification accuracy. A well-calibrated classifier gives confidence scores that reliably reflect how often its predictions are actually correct.

Across multiple image architectures and datasets, including ImageNet, the authors find that mixup produces substantially better calibration than ordinary training. Their investigation also finds that mixing features alone does not provide the same benefit. Blending the labels, which softens the training targets, plays a significant role in making confidence more informative.

The authors additionally observe less overconfidence on inputs outside the training distribution and on random noise. They interpret these results as suggesting that hard training labels are a likely source of neural-network overconfidence, even for familiar kinds of input. This is an empirical explanation and recommendation: mixup appears useful when trustworthy predictive uncertainty matters, without implying that every confidence score becomes reliable.
summary.tldr: Mixup empirically improves confidence calibration and reduces overconfidence, with softened labels playing a significant role.

title: On Mixup Training: Improved Calibration and Predictive Uncertainty for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we aim to understand the generalization properties of generative adversarial networks (GANs) from a new perspective of privacy protection. Theoretically, we prove that a differentially private learning algorithm used for training the GAN does not overfit to a certain degree, i.e., the generalization gap can be bounded. Moreover, some recent works, such as the Bayesian GAN, can be re-interpreted based on our theoretical insight from privacy protection. Quantitatively, to evaluate the information leakage of well-trained GAN models, we perform various membership attacks on these models. The results show that previous Lipschitz regularization techniques are effective in not only reducing the generalization gap but also alleviating the information leakage of the training dataset.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network should learn patterns that extend beyond its training examples. This paper examines that generalization problem through privacy protection, connecting dependence on training data with the risk of overfitting. The perspective also motivates measuring how much information a trained GAN exposes about its training set.

The theoretical result shows that using a differentially private learning algorithm to train a GAN bounds its generalization gap. This provides a qualified control on overfitting rather than a claim that overfitting disappears. The same privacy-based insight offers a way to reinterpret existing approaches, including Bayesian GANs.

To investigate leakage quantitatively, the authors perform membership attacks on trained models, testing whether training-set membership can be inferred. They find that existing Lipschitz regularization techniques both reduce the generalization gap and alleviate information leakage. The paper therefore combines a theoretical privacy-to-generalization connection with empirical evidence that a regularization approach can help on both fronts, without claiming that the measured leakage is eliminated.
summary.tldr: The paper links private GAN training to bounded generalization gaps and finds that Lipschitz regularization also reduces measured information leakage.

title: Generalization in Generative Adversarial Networks: A Novel Perspective from Privacy Protection

abstract: The success of lottery ticket initializations (Frankle and Carbin, 2019) suggests that small, sparsified networks can be trained so long as the network is initialized appropriately. Unfortunately, finding these "winning ticket'' initializations is computationally expensive. One potential solution is to reuse the same winning tickets across a variety of datasets and optimizers. However, the generality of winning ticket initializations remains unclear. Here, we attempt to answer this question by generating winning tickets for one training configuration (optimizer and dataset) and evaluating their performance on another configuration. Perhaps surprisingly, we found that, within the natural images domain, winning ticket initializations generalized across a variety of datasets, including Fashion MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and Places365, often achieving performance close to that of winning tickets generated on the same dataset. Moreover, winning tickets generated using larger datasets consistently transferred better than those generated using smaller datasets. We also found that winning ticket initializations generalize across optimizers with high performance. These results suggest that winning ticket initializations generated by sufficiently large datasets contain inductive biases generic to neural networks more broadly which improve training across many settings and provide hope for the development of better initialization methods.

This paper tests whether that effort can be reused by finding a winning ticket with one dataset and optimizer, then evaluating it under a different training configuration.

Within the natural-images domain, tickets transfer across a variety of datasets, including Fashion MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and Places365. Their performance is often close to that of tickets found specifically for the destination dataset. Tickets generated from larger datasets consistently transfer better than those from smaller datasets in the reported study. The authors also observe strong transfer across optimizers.

These findings suggest that some useful properties of a winning initialization extend beyond the configuration that produced it. The authors interpret tickets from sufficiently large datasets as potentially containing broadly useful inductive biases. That interpretation motivates better initialization methods, while the demonstrated transfer remains grounded in the datasets, optimizers, and natural-image domain studied.
summary.tldr: Winning sparse-network initializations transfer across natural-image datasets and optimizers, with tickets from larger datasets transferring better.

title: One ticket to win them all: generalizing lottery ticket initializations across datasets and optimizers

abstract: Self-supervised (SS) learning is a powerful approach for representation learning using unlabeled data. Recently, it has been applied to Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) training. Specifically, SS tasks were proposed to address the catastrophic forgetting issue in the GAN discriminator. In this work, we perform an in-depth analysis to understand how SS tasks interact with learning of generator. From the analysis, we identify issues of SS tasks which allow a severely mode-collapsed generator to excel the SS tasks. To address the issues, we propose new SS tasks based on a multi-class minimax game. The competition between our proposed SS tasks in the game encourages the generator to learn the data distribution and generate diverse samples. We provide both theoretical and empirical analysis to support that our proposed SS tasks have better convergence property. We conduct experiments to incorporate our proposed SS tasks into two different GAN baseline models. Our approach establishes state-of-the-art FID scores on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, CelebA, Imagenet $32\times32$ and Stacked-MNIST datasets, outperforming existing works by considerable margins in some cases. Our unconditional GAN model approaches performance of conditional GAN without using labeled data. Our code: \url{https://github.com/tntrung/msgan}

Our unconditional GAN model approaches performance of conditional GAN without using labeled data. Our code: \url{https://github.com/tntrung/msgan}

paragraphs: Self-supervised tasks had been added to generative adversarial networks to help prevent the discriminator from forgetting learned information. This paper examines how those tasks affect the generator. Its analysis identifies a problem: a generator can perform very well on the self-supervised tasks while suffering severe mode collapse and producing limited diversity.

The authors propose replacement self-supervised tasks organized as a multi-class minimax game. Competition among these tasks encourages the generator to learn the data distribution and produce diverse outputs. The paper provides theoretical and empirical analyses supporting better convergence properties, connecting the auxiliary training tasks more directly to the intended behavior of the generator.

The tasks are incorporated into two GAN baselines. Experiments report state-of-the-art FID scores on six datasets, with considerable improvements in some cases. The unconditional model also approaches conditional GAN performance without labeled data. These findings support designing self-supervision around its interaction with generation, since success on an auxiliary task alone can coexist with poor output diversity.
summary.tldr: A multi-class minimax formulation addresses self-supervised tasks that tolerate mode collapse and improves reported GAN convergence and generation quality.

title: Self-supervised GAN: Analysis and Improvement with Multi-class Minimax Game

abstract: Learning representations of sets of nodes in a graph is crucial for applications ranging from node-role discovery to link prediction and molecule classification. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved great success in graph representation learning. However, expressive power of GNNs is limited by the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test and thus GNNs generate identical representations for graph substructures that may in fact be very different. More powerful GNNs, proposed recently by mimicking higher-order-WL tests, only focus on representing entire graphs and they are computationally inefficient as they cannot utilize sparsity of the underlying graph. Here we propose and mathematically analyze a general class of structure-related features, termed Distance Encoding (DE). DE assists GNNs in representing any set of nodes, while providing strictly more expressive power than the 1-WL test. DE captures the distance between the node set whose representation is to be learned and each node in the graph. To capture the distance DE can apply various graph-distance measures such as shortest path distance or generalized PageRank scores. We propose two ways for GNNs to use DEs (1) as extra node features, and (2) as controllers of message aggregation in GNNs. Both approaches can utilize the sparse structure of the underlying graph, which leads to computational efficiency and scalability. We also prove that DE can distinguish node sets embedded in almost all regular graphs where traditional GNNs always fail. We evaluate DE on three tasks over six real networks: structural role prediction, link prediction, and triangle prediction. Results show that our models outperform GNNs without DE by up-to 15\% in accuracy and AUROC. Furthermore, our models also significantly outperform other state-of-the-art methods especially designed for the above tasks.

This paper addresses that limitation when representing a chosen set of nodes, which may be relevant to a node's role or a potential link. Its proposed Distance Encoding describes how every graph node relates by distance to the set being represented.

Distance can be measured through shortest paths or alternatives such as generalized PageRank scores. The encoding enters the network either as additional node features or as a controller of message aggregation. Both designs can exploit graph sparsity, supporting efficiency and scalability while adding information about the specific node set of interest.

The analysis establishes expressive power strictly beyond the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman test and proves a distinction result for node sets in almost all regular graphs where traditional GNNs fail. Experiments cover structural roles, links, and triangles across six real networks. The models improve accuracy and AUROC by up to 15% over GNNs without the encoding and outperform specialized methods on these tasks.
summary.tldr: Distance Encoding adds node-set-relative structure to graph neural networks, improving their provable expressiveness and empirical prediction performance.

title: Distance Encoding: Design Provably More Powerful Neural Networks for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Finding accurate solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) is a crucial task in all scientific and engineering disciplines. It has recently been shown that machine learning methods can improve the solution accuracy by correcting for effects not captured by the discretized PDE. We target the problem of reducing numerical errors of iterative PDE solvers and compare different learning approaches for finding complex correction functions. We find that previously used learning approaches are significantly outperformed by methods that integrate the solver into the training loop and thereby allow the model to interact with the PDE during training. This provides the model with realistic input distributions that take previous corrections into account, yielding improvements in accuracy with stable rollouts of several hundred recurrent evaluation steps and surpassing even tailored supervised variants. We highlight the performance of the differentiable physics networks for a wide variety of PDEs, from non-linear advection-diffusion systems to three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers approximate partial differential equations, and discretization can leave effects unresolved. Machine learning can help by predicting corrections, but those corrections also change the states encountered in later solver steps. This paper studies how to train correction functions for iterative solvers so that the learned model experiences the consequences of its own earlier corrections.

The proposed approach includes the solver inside the training loop through differentiable physics. The model interacts with the evolving simulation during training, receiving inputs that reflect previous corrections. This matters because learning a correction for one state is only part of the task: the correction must also work as the solver repeatedly produces new states.

The authors find that solver-integrated training significantly outperforms previously used approaches and even tailored supervised variants. They report improved accuracy with stable rollouts lasting several hundred recurrent evaluation steps. Evaluations cover equations ranging from nonlinear advection-diffusion systems to three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows, supporting the approach across the varied physical systems tested.
summary.tldr: Training correction models inside differentiable PDE solvers improves accuracy and supports stable multistep simulations in the evaluated systems.

title: Solver-in-the-Loop: Learning from Differentiable Physics to Interact with Iterative PDE-Solvers

abstract: The increased availability of massive point clouds coupled with their utility in a wide variety of applications such as robotics, shape synthesis, and self-driving cars has attracted increased attention from both industry and academia. Recently, deep neural networks operating on labeled point clouds have shown promising results on supervised learning tasks like classification and segmentation. However, supervised learning leads to the cumbersome task of annotating the point clouds. To combat this problem, we propose two novel self-supervised pre-training tasks that encode a hierarchical partitioning of the point clouds using a cover-tree, where point cloud subsets lie within balls of varying radii at each level of the cover-tree. Furthermore, our self-supervised learning network is restricted to pre-train on the support set (comprising of scarce training examples) used to train the downstream network in a few-shot learning (FSL) setting. Finally, the fully-trained self-supervised network's point embeddings are input to the downstream task's network. We present a comprehensive empirical evaluation of our method on both downstream classification and segmentation tasks and show that supervised methods pre-trained with our self-supervised learning method significantly improve the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, our method also outperforms previous unsupervised methods in downstream classification tasks.

This paper investigates self-supervised pretraining for few-shot classification and segmentation, where only scarce training examples are available. Its pretraining is restricted to the same support set used for the downstream task, so the method learns additional representations from that limited collection.

The authors introduce two pretraining tasks based on a cover-tree organization of each point cloud. This hierarchy groups subsets of points inside balls of different radii at successive levels. The tasks encode that hierarchical partitioning, providing training signals from the point clouds' own spatial structure. The trained network then supplies point embeddings as inputs to the downstream network.

In the reported evaluations, supervised methods using this pretraining significantly improve the accuracy of leading methods on classification and segmentation. The approach also outperforms previous unsupervised methods in downstream classification. These findings support using geometric organization to extract useful supervision from a small support set, making the available point clouds more informative before training the final task model.
summary.tldr: Cover-tree-based self-supervised tasks improve few-shot point-cloud classification and segmentation using only the available support set for pretraining.

title: Self-Supervised Few-Shot Learning on Point Clouds

abstract: The widespread adoption of deep learning is often attributed to its automatic feature construction with minimal inductive bias. However, in many real-world tasks, the learned function is intended to satisfy domain-specific constraints. We focus on monotonicity constraints, which are common and require that the function's output increases with increasing values of specific input features. We develop a counterexample-guided technique to provably enforce monotonicity constraints at prediction time. Additionally, we propose a technique to use monotonicity as an inductive bias for deep learning. It works by iteratively incorporating monotonicity counterexamples in the learning process. Contrary to prior work in monotonic learning, we target general ReLU neural networks and do not further restrict the hypothesis space. We have implemented these techniques in a tool called COMET. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results compared to existing monotonic learners, and can improve the model quality compared to those that were trained without taking monotonicity constraints into account.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks require an output to increase when particular input features increase. A neural network trained without this requirement may learn relationships that violate it. This paper develops methods for incorporating such monotonicity constraints while working with general ReLU networks, without further restricting the set of network functions considered.

The authors address the requirement in two ways. One technique uses counterexamples to provably enforce monotonicity at prediction time. Another repeatedly incorporates examples of monotonicity violations into learning, using the constraint as an inductive bias. These contributions distinguish guaranteed behavior during prediction from the use of domain knowledge to guide the training process.

The methods are implemented in COMET and evaluated on real-world datasets. The reported results reach state-of-the-art performance against existing monotonic learners and show that considering monotonicity can improve model quality relative to training without it. The significance is that a domain constraint can contribute to both dependable prediction behavior and useful learning, while retaining the expressive flexibility of general ReLU networks.
summary.tldr: COMET uses monotonicity counterexamples to guide neural-network learning and provably enforce monotonic predictions.

title: Counterexample-Guided Learning of Monotonic Neural Networks

abstract: While using invariant and equivariant maps, it is possible to apply deep learning to a range of primitive data structures, a formalism for dealing with hierarchy is lacking. This is a significant issue because many practical structures are hierarchies of simple building blocks; some examples include sequences of sets, graphs of graphs, or multiresolution images. Observing that the symmetry of a hierarchical structure is the ``wreath product'' of symmetries of the building blocks, we express the equivariant map for the hierarchy using an intuitive combination of the equivariant linear layers of the building blocks. More generally, we show that any equivariant map for the hierarchy has this form. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach to model design, we consider its application in the semantic segmentation of point-cloud data. By voxelizing the point cloud, we impose a hierarchy of translation and permutation symmetries on the data and report state-of-the-art on {semantic3d}, {s3dis}, and {vkitti}, that include some of the largest real-world point-cloud benchmarks.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach to model design, we consider its application in the semantic segmentation of point-cloud data. By voxelizing the point cloud, we impose a hierarchy of translation and permutation symmetries on the data and report state-of-the-art on {semantic3d}, {s3dis}, and {vkitti}, that include some of the largest real-world point-cloud benchmarks.

paragraphs: Many data structures contain other structures: a sequence may contain sets, or a graph may contain smaller graphs. Neural networks can respect the symmetries of individual building blocks, but combining those rules for a hierarchy requires a broader framework. This paper develops such a framework for constructing equivariant maps, whose outputs change consistently with transformations of their inputs.

The authors identify the symmetry of the hierarchy through a mathematical construction called the wreath product. They then express the hierarchical equivariant map as a combination of equivariant linear layers for the component structures. Their characterization shows that maps respecting the hierarchy's symmetry have this form, giving the construction a theoretical basis beyond an architectural recipe.

For an application, the authors voxelize point clouds, organizing the data into a hierarchy with translation and permutation symmetries. They use the resulting model for semantic segmentation and report state-of-the-art results on semantic3d, s3dis, and vkitti. These experiments connect the abstract symmetry framework to practical model design: the organization of the data determines how the network should share and transform information.
summary.tldr: A symmetry-based framework builds equivariant networks for hierarchical data and achieves reported state-of-the-art point-cloud segmentation results.

title: Equivariant Networks for Hierarchical Structures

abstract: We propose average Localisation-Recall-Precision (aLRP), a unified, bounded, balanced and ranking-based loss function for both classification and localisation tasks in object detection. aLRP extends the Localisation-Recall-Precision (LRP) performance metric (Oksuz et al., 2018) inspired from how Average Precision (AP) Loss extends precision to a ranking-based loss function for classification (Chen et al., 2020). aLRP has the following distinct advantages: (i) aLRP is the first ranking-based loss function for both classification and localisation tasks. (ii) Thanks to using ranking for both tasks, aLRP naturally enforces high-quality localisation for high-precision classification. (iii) aLRP provides provable balance between positives and negatives. (iv) Compared to on average ~6 hyperparameters in the loss functions of state-of-the-art detectors, aLRP Loss has only one hyperparameter, which we did not tune in practice. On the COCO dataset, aLRP Loss improves its ranking-based predecessor, AP Loss, up to around 5 AP points, achieves 48.9 AP without test time augmentation and outperforms all one-stage detectors. Code available at: https://github.com/kemaloksuz/aLRPLoss .

paragraphs: Object detection requires both recognizing objects and locating them accurately. The paper introduces average Localisation-Recall-Precision, or aLRP, as a single loss for training both capabilities. It develops a ranking-based objective from the LRP performance metric, extending an approach previously used by AP Loss for classification.

Using ranking for both tasks connects the ordering of predictions to their localization quality. The loss therefore encourages highly ranked, precise classifications to have accurate locations as well. The authors also prove balance between positive and negative examples. Its bounded, unified design uses one hyperparameter, which they leave untuned in practice, compared with roughly six on average in the detector losses discussed.

On COCO, aLRP improves over AP Loss by up to about five AP points and reaches 48.9 AP without test-time augmentation. The authors report outperforming all one-stage detectors in their comparison. These findings show how jointly structuring the two training objectives can improve reported detection performance while reducing the number of loss settings requiring attention.
summary.tldr: aLRP unifies classification and localization through a balanced ranking loss, improving reported detection results with one untuned hyperparameter.

title: A Ranking-based, Balanced Loss Function Unifying Classification and Localisation in Object Detection

abstract: Cortical networks are strongly recurrent, and neurons have intrinsic temporal dynamics. This sets them apart from deep feed-forward networks. Despite the tremendous progress in the application of deep feed-forward networks and their theoretical understanding, it remains unclear how the interplay of recurrence and non-linearities in recurrent cortical networks contributes to their function. The purpose of this work is to present a solvable recurrent network model that links to feed forward networks. By perturbative methods we transform the time-continuous, recurrent dynamics into an effective feed-forward structure of linear and non-linear temporal kernels. The resulting analytical expressions allow us to build optimal time-series classifiers from random reservoir networks. Firstly, this allows us to optimize not only the readout vectors, but also the input projection, demonstrating a strong potential performance gain. Secondly, the analysis exposes how the second order stimulus statistics is a crucial element that interacts with the non-linearity of the dynamics and boosts performance.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural systems combine feedback connections with dynamics that unfold over time. Understanding how that recurrence interacts with nonlinear responses is difficult. This paper introduces a solvable recurrent model that connects those dynamics to a feed-forward description, providing an analytical route to studying their contribution to time-series classification.

Using perturbative methods, the authors transform continuous-time recurrent dynamics into an effective structure of linear and nonlinear temporal kernels. These kernels describe the network's responses over time in a form suitable for analysis. The resulting expressions support construction of optimal time-series classifiers from random reservoir networks within the model studied.

The analysis enables optimization of both the readout vectors and the projection that brings inputs into the reservoir, revealing strong potential performance gains. It also identifies second-order stimulus statistics as a crucial contributor that interacts with nonlinear dynamics to improve performance. The work thus links a mathematical account of recurrence to concrete classifier design choices and to the temporal statistical information those classifiers exploit.
summary.tldr: An analytical feed-forward description of recurrent dynamics enables reservoir input and readout optimization and reveals the role of second-order stimulus statistics.

title: Unfolding recurrence by Green’s functions for optimized reservoir computing

abstract: For the gradient computation across the time domain in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) training, two different approaches have been independently studied. The first is to compute the gradients with respect to the change in spike activation (activation-based methods), and the second is to compute the gradients with respect to the change in spike timing (timing-based methods). In this work, we present a comparative study of the two methods and propose a new supervised learning method that combines them. The proposed method utilizes each individual spike more effectively by shifting spike timings as in the timing-based methods as well as generating and removing spikes as in the activation-based methods. Experimental results showed that the proposed method achieves higher performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency than the previous approaches.

paragraphs: Training spiking neural networks requires deciding how changes in spikes should influence the learning signal over time. Two approaches have been studied separately: activation-based methods differentiate with respect to changes in spike activation, while timing-based methods differentiate with respect to changes in when spikes occur. Each emphasizes a different way to modify network activity.

The paper compares these approaches and proposes a supervised learning method that combines them. It can shift the timing of individual spikes, as timing-based learning does, while also generating and removing spikes, as activation-based learning does. A spike can therefore contribute to learning through both its timing and its presence.

The authors report better accuracy and efficiency than previous approaches in their experiments. The significance lies in combining complementary kinds of adjustment within one training method, allowing individual spikes to be used more effectively. The findings support the combined approach in the evaluated settings, while the conceptual contribution is the unification of two previously separate ways to compute temporal learning signals.
summary.tldr: A combined spiking-network learning rule adjusts both spike timing and spike presence, improving accuracy and efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Unifying Activation- and Timing-based Learning Rules for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: We are interested in understanding how well Transformer language models (TLMs) can perform reasoning tasks when trained on knowledge encoded in the form of natural language. We investigate their systematic generalization abilities on a logical reasoning task in natural language, which involves reasoning over relationships between entities grounded in first-order logical proofs. Specifically, we perform soft theorem-proving by leveraging TLMs to generate natural language proofs. We test the generated proofs for logical consistency, along with the accuracy of the final inference. We observe length-generalization issues when evaluated on longer-than-trained sequences. However, we observe TLMs improve their generalization performance after being exposed to longer, exhaustive proofs. In addition, we discover that TLMs are able to generalize better using backward-chaining proofs compared to their forward-chaining counterparts, while they find it easier to generate forward chaining proofs. We observe that models that are not trained to generate proofs are better at generalizing to problems based on longer proofs. This suggests that Transformers have efficient internal reasoning strategies that are harder to interpret. These results highlight the systematic generalization behavior of TLMs in the context of logical reasoning, and we believe this work motivates deeper inspection of their underlying reasoning strategies.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether Transformer language models can generalize logical reasoning learned from natural-language knowledge. Models generate natural-language proofs about relationships between entities, grounded in first-order logic. Evaluation checks both the logical consistency of those proofs and the correctness of their final conclusions, making the reasoning sequence itself part of the assessment.

The authors observe difficulties when models encounter sequences longer than those seen during training. Exposure to longer, exhaustive proofs improves generalization. Proof direction also matters: backward-chaining proofs support better generalization than forward-chaining proofs, even though the models find forward-chaining proofs easier to generate.

Models trained without proof generation generalize better to problems requiring longer proofs. The authors interpret this as suggesting that Transformers may use efficient internal reasoning strategies that are harder to interpret. That interpretation remains a suggestion from the observed behavior. Overall, the study shows that generating an explicit proof, generating it easily, and generalizing to longer reasoning problems can behave differently within the same task setting.
summary.tldr: Transformer proof-generation experiments reveal length-generalization difficulties and show that proof format and proof-generation training affect generalization differently.

title: Measuring Systematic Generalization in Neural Proof Generation with Transformers

abstract: The standard problem setting in cooperative multi-agent settings is \emph{self-play} (SP), where the goal is to train a \emph{team} of agents that works well together. However, optimal SP policies commonly contain arbitrary conventions (``handshakes'') and are not compatible with other, independently trained agents or humans. This latter desiderata was recently formalized by \cite{Hu2020-OtherPlay} as the \emph{zero-shot coordination} (ZSC) setting and partially addressed with their \emph{Other-Play} (OP) algorithm, which showed improved ZSC and human-AI performance in the card game Hanabi. OP assumes access to the symmetries of the environment and prevents agents from breaking these in a mutually \emph{incompatible} way during training. However, as the authors point out, discovering symmetries for a given environment is a computationally hard problem. Instead, we show that through a simple adaption of k-level reasoning (KLR) \cite{Costa-Gomes2006-K-level}, synchronously training all levels, we can obtain competitive ZSC and ad-hoc teamplay performance in Hanabi, including when paired with a human-like proxy bot. We also introduce a new method, synchronous-k-level reasoning with a best response (SyKLRBR), which further improves performance on our synchronous KLR by co-training a best response.

paragraphs: Agents trained together through self-play can develop arbitrary conventions that their teammates understand but unfamiliar partners do not. Zero-shot coordination asks whether independently trained agents can cooperate without first learning such shared conventions together. This paper studies that challenge in Hanabi, where coordination also matters when an agent joins an unfamiliar team.

An earlier method, Other-Play, uses known environment symmetries to discourage incompatible conventions. Obtaining those symmetries can itself be computationally difficult. The authors investigate a different route based on k-level reasoning, adapting it so that all reasoning levels are trained synchronously. This changes the training organization used to prepare agents for coordination.

The resulting method achieves competitive zero-shot coordination and ad-hoc teamplay performance in Hanabi, including partnerships with a human-like proxy bot. The authors also introduce SyKLRBR, which co-trains a best response and improves further on their synchronous k-level method. The evidence supports this training approach for the tested coordination setting, with the proxy-bot result specifically addressing a human-like partner rather than establishing performance with human participants.
summary.tldr: Synchronously trained k-level reasoning enables competitive coordination with unfamiliar Hanabi partners, with further gains from co-training a best response.

title: K-level Reasoning for Zero-Shot Coordination in Hanabi

abstract: In video transformers, the time dimension is often treated in the same way as the two spatial dimensions. However, in a scene where objects or the camera may move, a physical point imaged at one location in frame $t$ may be entirely unrelated to what is found at that location in frame $t+k$. These temporal correspondences should be modeled to facilitate learning about dynamic scenes. To this end, we propose a new drop-in block for video transformers - trajectory attention - that aggregates information along implicitly determined motion paths. We additionally propose a new method to address the quadratic dependence of computation and memory on the input size, which is particularly important for high resolution or long videos. While these ideas are useful in a range of settings, we apply them to the specific task of video action recognition with a transformer model and obtain state-of-the-art results on the Kinetics, Something-Something V2, and Epic-Kitchens datasets.

paragraphs: A fixed location in successive video frames may show different physical content because objects or the camera move. Treating time like another spatial dimension can therefore overlook the correspondences needed to understand motion. This paper develops trajectory attention to incorporate those correspondences into video transformers.

Trajectory attention is a drop-in block that combines information along implicitly determined motion paths. Its organizing principle is to gather information according to how scene content moves through the video. The authors additionally propose a method addressing the quadratic growth of attention computation and memory with input size, a concern that becomes especially important for long videos or high-resolution frames.

The paper evaluates these ideas through transformer-based video action recognition, reporting state-of-the-art results on Kinetics, Something-Something V2, and Epic-Kitchens. These findings support the approach in the tested recognition setting. The contribution combines a motion-aware way of collecting temporal information with a computational method intended to make larger video inputs more manageable.
summary.tldr: Trajectory attention aggregates video information along implicit motion paths and achieves reported state-of-the-art action recognition results.

title: Keeping Your Eye on the Ball: Trajectory Attention in Video Transformers

abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) provide an elegant framework for density estimation, but they are notoriously difficult to train. Recent work has established links to generative adversarial networks, where the EBM is trained through a minimax game with a variational value function. We propose a bidirectional bound on the EBM log-likelihood, such that we maximize a lower bound and minimize an upper bound when solving the minimax game. We link one bound to a gradient penalty that stabilizes training, thereby provide grounding for best engineering practice. To evaluate the bounds we develop a new and efficient estimator of the Jacobi-determinant of the EBM generator. We demonstrate that these developments stabilize training and yield high-quality density estimation and sample generation.

paragraphs: Energy-based models offer a framework for estimating probability densities, but training them is difficult. This paper builds on a connection to generative adversarial networks, where learning is organized as a minimax game using a variational objective.

The authors introduce bounds on the model's log-likelihood from both directions. Their training procedure maximizes a lower bound while minimizing an upper bound. This gives the opposing parts of the game a shared statistical target, approached through quantities that constrain it from below and above.

One of these bounds is connected to a gradient penalty used to stabilize training. That connection gives a theoretical basis for an existing engineering practice. The paper also develops an efficient estimator of the generator's Jacobian determinant so that the proposed bounds can be evaluated.

The reported demonstrations show more stable training together with high-quality density estimates and generated samples. The contribution links a statistical training objective, a practical stabilization mechanism, and a computational tool needed to evaluate the objective within one approach.
summary.tldr: Training energy-based models with upper and lower likelihood bounds provides a principled route to more stable learning and high-quality generation.

title: Bounds all around: training energy-based models with bidirectional bounds

abstract: We consider stochastic optimization when one only has access to biased stochastic oracles of the objective, and obtaining stochastic gradients with low biases comes at high costs. This setting captures a variety of optimization paradigms widely used in machine learning, such as conditional stochastic optimization, bilevel optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. We examine a family of multi-level Monte Carlo (MLMC) gradient methods that exploit a delicate trade-off among the bias, the variance, and the oracle cost. We provide a systematic study of their convergences and total computation complexities for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex objectives, and demonstrate their superiority over the naive biased stochastic gradient method. Moreover, when applied to conditional stochastic optimization, the MLMC gradient methods significantly improve the best-known sample complexity in the literature.

This setting captures a variety of optimization paradigms widely used in machine learning, such as conditional stochastic optimization, bilevel optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. We examine a family of multi-level Monte Carlo (MLMC) gradient methods that exploit a delicate trade-off among the bias, the variance, and the oracle cost. We provide a systematic study of their convergences and total computation complexities for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex objectives, and demonstrate their superiority over the naive biased stochastic gradient method. Moreover, when applied to conditional stochastic optimization, the MLMC gradient methods significantly improve the best-known sample complexity in the literature.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization often relies on noisy estimates of a gradient. This paper considers a harder situation: those estimates are also biased, and reducing their bias increases their cost. Such a tradeoff appears in conditional stochastic optimization, bilevel optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. An accurate update can therefore be expensive even before considering how many updates learning requires.

The authors study a family of multi-level Monte Carlo gradient methods designed to balance bias, variance, and oracle cost. Bias concerns systematic error, variance concerns randomness, and oracle cost measures the effort needed to obtain the estimate. Considering all three together makes it possible to evaluate the total resources required to optimize an objective.

The paper provides convergence and total computational complexity analyses for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex objectives. It establishes advantages over a naive biased stochastic gradient method. For conditional stochastic optimization, the methods also substantially improve the best previously known sample complexity. The findings show why paying for lower bias at every step is not the only route to an efficient overall optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Multi-level Monte Carlo gradient methods balance bias, variance, and computation cost to improve stochastic optimization complexity.

title: On the Bias-Variance-Cost Tradeoff of Stochastic Optimization

abstract: The Transformer architecture has become a dominant choice in many domains, such as natural language processing and computer vision. Yet, it has not achieved competitive performance on popular leaderboards of graph-level prediction compared to mainstream GNN variants. Therefore, it remains a mystery how Transformers could perform well for graph representation learning. In this paper, we solve this mystery by presenting Graphormer, which is built upon the standard Transformer architecture, and could attain excellent results on a broad range of graph representation learning tasks, especially on the recent OGB Large-Scale Challenge. Our key insight to utilizing Transformer in the graph is the necessity of effectively encoding the structural information of a graph into the model. To this end, we propose several simple yet effective structural encoding methods to help Graphormer better model graph-structured data. Besides, we mathematically characterize the expressive power of Graphormer and exhibit that with our ways of encoding the structural information of graphs, many popular GNN variants could be covered as the special cases of Graphormer. The code and models of Graphormer will be made publicly available at \url{https://github.com/Microsoft/Graphormer}.

paragraphs: Transformers have been successful in language and vision, yet their performance on graph-level prediction had lagged behind established graph neural networks. This paper investigates whether the problem lies in how graph structure is supplied to the model. It introduces Graphormer, an architecture built on the standard Transformer with additional structural encodings.

The central idea is to encode the graph's structural information effectively so that the Transformer can use it during representation learning. The authors propose several simple encoding methods for this purpose. This makes graph organization an explicit part of the model's input representation, giving the architecture information needed to reason about graph-structured data.

The paper reports strong results across a broad collection of graph representation tasks, particularly the OGB Large-Scale Challenge. It also analyzes Graphormer's expressive power and shows that, with the proposed encodings, many popular graph neural network variants fall within it as special cases. The empirical and mathematical results together support structural encoding as a key ingredient in making Transformers effective for graphs.
summary.tldr: Graphormer equips a standard Transformer with structural encodings, yielding strong graph predictions and encompassing many GNN variants theoretically.

title: Do Transformers Really Perform Badly for Graph Representation?

abstract: The representations learned by large-scale NLP models such as BERT have been widely used in various tasks. However, the increasing model size of the pre-trained models also brings efficiency challenges, including inference speed and model size when deploying models on mobile devices. Specifically, most operations in BERT consist of matrix multiplications. These matrices are not low-rank and thus canonical matrix decomposition could not find an efficient approximation. In this paper, we observe that the learned representation of each layer lies in a low-dimensional space. Based on this observation, we propose DRONE (data-aware low-rank compression), a provably optimal low-rank decomposition of weight matrices, which has a simple closed form solution that can be efficiently computed. DRONE can be applied to both fully connected and self-attention layers appearing in the BERT model. In addition to compressing standard models, out method can also be used on distilled BERT models to further improve compression rate. Experimental results show that DRONE is able to improve both model size and inference speed with limited loss in accuracy. Specifically, DRONE alone achieves 1.92x speedup on the MRPC task with only 1.5% loss in accuracy, and when DRONE is combined with distillation, it further achieves over 12.3x speedup on various natural language inference tasks.

paragraphs: Large language-processing models face deployment costs from both storage and inference computation. In BERT, much of that computation consists of matrix multiplications. The paper observes that ordinary matrix decomposition struggles to compress the weight matrices efficiently because they are not low-rank, even though the representations produced at each layer occupy a low-dimensional space.

DRONE uses this representation structure to construct a data-aware low-rank decomposition of the weights. The authors provide a provably optimal formulation with an efficiently computable closed-form solution. These results support using the structure of actual layer representations to guide compression.
summary.tldr: DRONE compresses BERT using low-dimensional structure in layer representations, improving model size and inference speed with limited accuracy loss.

title: DRONE: Data-aware Low-rank Compression for Large NLP Models

abstract: Vision transformer (ViT) models exhibit substandard optimizability. In particular, they are sensitive to the choice of optimizer (AdamW vs. SGD), optimizer hyperparameters, and training schedule length. In comparison, modern convolutional neural networks are easier to optimize. Why is this the case? In this work, we conjecture that the issue lies with the patchify stem of ViT models, which is implemented by a stride-p p×p convolution (p = 16 by default) applied to the input image. This large-kernel plus large-stride convolution runs counter to typical design choices of convolutional layers in neural networks. To test whether this atypical design choice causes an issue, we analyze the optimization behavior of ViT models with their original patchify stem versus a simple counterpart where we replace the ViT stem by a small number of stacked stride-two 3×3 convolutions. While the vast majority of computation in the two ViT designs is identical, we find that this small change in early visual processing results in markedly different training behavior in terms of the sensitivity to optimization settings as well as the final model accuracy. Using a convolutional stem in ViT dramatically increases optimization stability and also improves peak performance (by ∼1-2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k), while maintaining flops and runtime. The improvement can be observed across the wide spectrum of model complexities (from 1G to 36G flops) and dataset scales (from ImageNet-1k to ImageNet-21k). These findings lead us to recommend using a standard, lightweight convolutional stem for ViT models in this regime as a more robust architectural choice compared to the original ViT model design.
originalAbstract: Vision transformer (ViT) models exhibit substandard optimizability. In particular, they are sensitive to the choice of optimizer (AdamW vs. SGD), optimizer hyperparameters, and training schedule length. In comparison, modern convolutional neural networks are easier to optimize. Why is this the case? In this work, we conjecture that the issue lies with the patchify stem of ViT models, which is implemented by a stride-p p×p convolution (p = 16 by default) applied to the input image. This large-kernel plus large-stride convolution runs counter to typical design choices of convolutional layers in neural networks. To test whether this atypical design choice causes an issue, we analyze the optimization behavior of ViT models with their original patchify stem versus a simple counterpart where we replace the ViT stem by a small number of stacked stride-two 3×3 convolutions. While the vast majority of computation in the two ViT designs is identical, we find that this small change in early visual processing results in markedly different training behavior in terms of the sensitivity to optimization settings as well as the final model accuracy. Using a convolutional stem in ViT dramatically increases optimization stability and also improves peak performance (by ∼1-2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k), while maintaining flops and runtime. The improvement can be observed across the wide spectrum of model complexities (from 1G to 36G flops) and dataset scales (from ImageNet-1k to ImageNet-21k). These findings lead us to recommend using a standard, lightweight convolutional stem for ViT models in this regime as a more robust architectural choice compared to the original ViT model design.

They replace that stem with a small stack of 3×3 convolutions using stride two. Most of the computation in the resulting transformer remains identical to the original design, allowing the study to focus on how early visual processing affects training. The comparison examines both sensitivity to optimization settings and final accuracy.

The convolutional stem substantially improves optimization stability and raises peak ImageNet-1k top-1 accuracy by about 1–2% while maintaining computational cost and runtime. Improvements appear across the tested model sizes and dataset scales, from ImageNet-1k to ImageNet-21k. These findings motivate the authors' recommendation to use a lightweight convolutional stem for vision transformers in the investigated regime.
summary.tldr: Replacing a vision transformer's patchify stem with small convolutions improves training stability and accuracy at comparable computation and runtime.

title: Early Convolutions Help Transformers See Better

abstract: We study linear regression from data distributed over a network of agents (with no master node) under high-dimensional scaling, which allows the ambient dimension to grow faster than the sample size. We propose a novel decentralization of the projected gradient algorithm whereby agents iteratively update their local estimates by a “double-mixing” mechanism, which suitably combines averages of iterates and gradients of neighbouring nodes. Under standard assumptions on the statistical model and network connectivity, the proposed method enjoys global linear convergence up to the statistical precision of the model. This improves on guarantees of (plain) DGD algorithms, whose iteration complexity grows undesirably with the ambient dimension. Our technical contribution is a novel convergence analysis that resembles (albeit different) algorithmic stability arguments extended to high-dimensions and distributed setting, which is of independent interest.
