paragraphs: DGD² addresses linear regression when data are spread across a network without a master node. It focuses on high-dimensional settings, where the number of variables may grow faster than the sample size. The challenge is to coordinate local estimates efficiently while accounting for the statistical precision that the available data can support.

The method decentralizes projected gradient updates using a double-mixing mechanism. Each agent combines averages of neighboring estimates with averages of neighboring gradients. These two kinds of information jointly guide the local update, allowing the network to coordinate both its current estimates and the directions in which those estimates should change.

Under standard assumptions about the statistical model and network connectivity, the algorithm converges globally at a linear rate until it reaches the model's statistical precision. This improves on plain decentralized gradient descent guarantees whose iteration complexity grows undesirably with ambient dimension. The proof uses a new analysis resembling algorithmic stability arguments, adapted to the combination of distributed computation and high-dimensional statistics.
summary.tldr: DGD² mixes neighboring estimates and gradients to achieve linear convergence to statistical precision in decentralized high-dimensional regression under stated assumptions.

title: DGD^2: A Linearly Convergent Distributed Algorithm For High-dimensional Statistical Recovery

abstract: How do we provably represent images succinctly so that their essential latent attributes are correctly captured by the representation to as high level of detail as possible? While today's deep networks (such as CNNs) produce image embeddings they do not have any provable properties and seem to work in mysterious non-interpretable ways. In this work we theoretically study synthetic images that are composed of a union or intersection of several mathematically specified shapes using thresholded polynomial functions (for e.g. ellipses, rectangles). We show how to produce a succinct sketch of such an image so that the sketch “smoothly” maps to the latent-coefficients producing the different shapes in the image. We prove several important properties such as: easy reconstruction of the image from the sketch, similarity preservation (similar shapes produce similar sketches), being able to index sketches so that other similar images and parts of other images can be retrieved, being able to store the sketches into a dictionary of concepts and shapes so parts of the same or different images that refer to the same shape can point to the same entry in this dictionary of common shape attributes.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a compact image representation can retain meaningful information about the shapes that generated an image. It studies a mathematical setting in which synthetic images are formed from unions or intersections of specified shapes. Thresholded polynomial functions describe those shapes, with ellipses and rectangles given as examples.

The authors construct a succinct sketch whose relationship to the underlying shape coefficients is smooth. That connection gives the representation an explicit relationship to latent image attributes. They prove that images can be reconstructed easily from their sketches and that similar shapes produce similar sketches, linking compactness to recoverable and similarity-preserving information.

The sketches also support indexing to retrieve similar images or image parts. A dictionary can store shared concepts and shape attributes, allowing matching parts within or across images to reference the same entry. These guarantees apply to the specified synthetic-image model. The contribution is a provable connection between a compact representation, its generating shapes, and operations such as reconstruction, retrieval, and attribute sharing.
summary.tldr: For synthetic images built from specified shapes, the paper constructs compact sketches with guarantees for reconstruction, similarity preservation, retrieval, and shared shape representations.

title: Sketching based Representations for Robust Image Classification with Provable Guarantees

abstract: Domain decomposition methods are widely used and effective in the approximation of solutions to partial differential equations. Yet the \textit{optimal} construction of these methods requires tedious analysis and is often available only in simplified, structured-grid settings, limiting their use for more complex problems. In this work, we generalize optimized Schwarz domain decomposition methods to unstructured-grid problems, using Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) and unsupervised learning to learn optimal modifications at subdomain interfaces. A key ingredient in our approach is an improved loss function, enabling effective training on relatively small problems, but robust performance on arbitrarily large problems, with computational cost linear in problem size. The performance of the learned linear solvers is compared with both classical and optimized domain decomposition algorithms, for both structured- and unstructured-grid problems.

paragraphs: Domain decomposition solves a partial differential equation by working with smaller subdomains. How those pieces communicate at their interfaces is crucial to constructing an effective solver. Optimizing that communication traditionally requires substantial analysis, and available constructions often depend on simplified settings with structured grids.

The paper extends optimized Schwarz domain decomposition to unstructured grids using graph convolutional neural networks. Through unsupervised learning, the networks learn modifications at subdomain interfaces. This places learning at the point where separate local calculations must interact, while retaining the domain decomposition approach to solving the overall equation.

An improved loss function is central to the method. The authors report that it enables training on relatively small problems while supporting robust performance on arbitrarily large ones, with computational cost linear in problem size. They compare the resulting linear solvers with classical and optimized domain decomposition algorithms on structured and unstructured grids. The contribution is a route to learning interface behavior that transfers across problem scales and extends solver construction beyond the structured settings where analytic optimization is more readily available.
summary.tldr: Graph networks learn domain decomposition interface conditions on small problems, supporting scalable solvers on unstructured grids.

title: Learning Interface Conditions in Domain Decomposition Solvers

abstract: We initiate a formal study of reproducibility in optimization. We define a quantitative measure of reproducibility of optimization procedures in the face of noisy or error-prone operations such as inexact or stochastic gradient computations or inexact initialization. We then analyze several convex optimization settings of interest such as smooth, non-smooth, and strongly-convex objective functions and establish tight bounds on the limits of reproducibility in each setting. Our analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off between computation and reproducibility: more computation is necessary (and sufficient) for better reproducibility.

paragraphs: Optimization procedures may produce different outcomes when their computations or starting points contain small errors or randomness. This paper makes reproducibility under such disturbances a formal object of study. It defines a quantitative measure that applies to sources of variation including approximate gradients, stochastic gradients, and inexact initialization.

The authors analyze several convex optimization settings, covering smooth, non-smooth, and strongly convex objective functions. For each setting, they establish tight bounds on achievable reproducibility. Tightness matters because it connects limitations on what an algorithm can accomplish with guarantees showing that those limits can be reached within the analysis.

The central result is a trade-off between computation and reproducibility: in the settings studied, better reproducibility requires more computation, and additional computation is sufficient to obtain it. This makes consistency across imperfect executions an explicit resource consideration in optimization. The framework gives a way to discuss that cost quantitatively, connecting the type of objective and the presence of computational errors to limits on reproducible outcomes.
summary.tldr: A formal analysis of convex optimization establishes tight reproducibility bounds and shows that better reproducibility requires, and can be achieved with, more computation.

title: Reproducibility in Optimization: Theoretical Framework and Limits

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) can be manipulated to perform specific behaviors when encountering a particular trigger pattern without affecting the performance on normal samples, which is referred to as backdoor attack. The backdoor attack is usually achieved by injecting a small proportion of poisoned samples into the training set, through which the victim trains a model embedded with the designated backdoor. In this work, we demonstrate that backdoor neurons are exposed by their pre-activation distributions, where populations from benign data and poisoned data show significantly different moments. This property is shown to be attack-invariant and allows us to efficiently locate backdoor neurons. On this basis, we make several proper assumptions on the neuron activation distributions, and propose two backdoor neuron detection strategies based on (1) the differential entropy of the neurons, and (2) the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the benign sample distribution and a poisoned statistics based hypothetical distribution. Experimental results show that our proposed defense strategies are both efficient and effective against various backdoor attacks.

paragraphs: A backdoored convolutional network can behave normally on ordinary inputs while responding to a trigger with an attacker-chosen behavior. Such backdoors can be introduced through a small proportion of poisoned training samples. This paper seeks to locate the neurons involved by examining their pre-activation distributions, meaning the values entering their activation functions.

The authors find that benign and poisoned inputs produce substantially different statistical moments for backdoor neurons. They show this distinguishing property to be attack-invariant. Based on assumptions about neuron activation distributions, they develop two detection strategies: one uses differential entropy, while the other uses Kullback-Leibler divergence between a benign distribution and a hypothetical distribution constructed from poisoned-data statistics.

The approach turns internal distributional behavior into evidence for identifying backdoor neurons. Its detection strategies rely on the stated distributional assumptions, rather than following from the moment differences alone. Experiments report that both defenses are computationally efficient and effective against various backdoor attacks. The findings support statistical inspection of pre-activations as a practical route to locating the internal components associated with trigger behavior.
summary.tldr: Differences in neuron pre-activation distributions motivate two efficient backdoor detection strategies supported by experiments across various attacks.

title: Pre-activation Distributions Expose Backdoor Neurons

abstract: Generative models (e.g., GANs, diffusion models) learn the underlying data distribution in an unsupervised manner. However, many applications of interest require sampling from a particular region of the output space or sampling evenly over a range of characteristics. For efficient sampling in these scenarios, we propose Generative Visual Prompt (PromptGen), a framework for distributional control over pre-trained generative models by incorporating knowledge of other off-the-shelf models. PromptGen defines control as energy-based models (EBMs) and samples images in a feed-forward manner by approximating the EBM with invertible neural networks, avoiding optimization at inference. Our experiments demonstrate how PromptGen can efficiently sample from several unconditional generative models (e.g., StyleGAN2, StyleNeRF, diffusion autoencoder, NVAE) in a controlled or/and de-biased manner using various off-the-shelf models: (1) with the CLIP model as control, PromptGen can sample images guided by text, (2) with image classifiers as control, PromptGen can de-bias generative models across a set of attributes or attribute combinations, and (3) with inverse graphics models as control, PromptGen can sample images of the same identity in different poses. (4) Finally, PromptGen reveals that the CLIP model shows a "reporting bias" when used as control, and PromptGen can further de-bias this controlled distribution in an iterative manner. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenWu98/Generative-Visual-Prompt.

paragraphs: A pretrained generator learns a broad output distribution, while an application may need a particular subset or a more balanced mix of attributes. PromptGen addresses this mismatch by using knowledge from other available models to control what an existing generator samples. Its focus is the distribution of generated outputs, including combinations of desired characteristics.

The framework represents the desired control with an energy-based model. It then approximates that model using invertible neural networks, enabling feed-forward image sampling without optimization at inference time. This makes the learned control usable through a direct sampling process.

Experiments demonstrate several forms of control across multiple unconditional generators. CLIP supplies text guidance, classifiers support balancing attributes or attribute combinations, and inverse graphics models support generating the same identity in different poses. The authors also identify reporting bias when CLIP provides the control signal and show that PromptGen can iteratively reduce bias in the resulting distribution. The findings illustrate both the flexibility of borrowing control signals from existing models and the need to account for biases those signals introduce.
summary.tldr: PromptGen learns efficient sampling controls for pretrained generators using existing models for text guidance, attribute balancing, and pose control.

title: Generative Visual Prompt: Unifying Distributional Control of Pre-Trained Generative Models

abstract: Traditional machine learning follows a close-set assumption that the training and test set share the same label space. While in many practical scenarios, it is inevitable that some test samples belong to unknown classes (open-set). To fix this issue, Open-Set Recognition (OSR), whose goal is to make correct predictions on both close-set samples and open-set samples, has attracted rising attention. In this direction, the vast majority of literature focuses on the pattern of open-set samples. However, how to evaluate model performance in this challenging task is still unsolved. In this paper, a systematic analysis reveals that most existing metrics are essentially inconsistent with the aforementioned goal of OSR: (1) For metrics extended from close-set classification, such as Open-set F-score, Youden's index, and Normalized Accuracy, a poor open-set prediction can escape from a low performance score with a superior close-set prediction. (2) Novelty detection AUC, which measures the ranking performance between close-set and open-set samples, ignores the close-set performance. To fix these issues, we propose a novel metric named OpenAUC. Compared with existing metrics, OpenAUC enjoys a concise pairwise formulation that evaluates open-set performance and close-set performance in a coupling manner. Further analysis shows that OpenAUC is free from the aforementioned inconsistency properties. Finally, an end-to-end learning method is proposed to minimize the OpenAUC risk, and the experimental results on popular benchmark datasets speak to its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Open-set recognition requires handling both familiar classes and examples from classes absent during training. Evaluating that combined goal is difficult. This paper analyzes existing metrics and finds that some can give favorable scores when strong familiar-class predictions conceal poor unknown-class handling, while novelty-detection AUC ignores familiar-class classification performance.

The authors propose OpenAUC, a metric with a pairwise formulation that couples the evaluation of known-class and unknown-class performance. This makes the relationship between the two responsibilities part of the evaluation itself. Their analysis shows that OpenAUC avoids the specific inconsistency properties identified in the existing metrics.

The paper also introduces an end-to-end learning method that minimizes OpenAUC risk. Experiments on established benchmark datasets support its effectiveness. The contribution therefore spans both measuring the task and training for that measurement: it aims to align the score and learning objective with the requirement to classify familiar inputs correctly while also dealing successfully with unfamiliar classes.
summary.tldr: OpenAUC jointly evaluates known-class classification and unknown-class handling, avoiding specific inconsistencies in existing open-set recognition metrics.

title: OpenAUC: Towards AUC-Oriented Open-Set Recognition

abstract: Learning With Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA) (Foerster et al. [2018a]) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that typically learns reciprocity-based cooperation in partially competitive environments. However, LOLA often fails to learn such behaviour on more complex policy spaces parameterized by neural networks, partly because the update rule is sensitive to the policy parameterization. This problem is especially pronounced in the opponent modeling setting, where the opponent's policy is unknown and must be inferred from observations; in such settings, LOLA is ill-specified because behaviorally equivalent opponent policies can result in non-equivalent updates. To address this shortcoming, we reinterpret LOLA as approximating a proximal operator, and then derive a new algorithm, proximal LOLA (POLA), which uses the proximal formulation directly. Unlike LOLA, the POLA updates are parameterization invariant, in the sense that when the proximal objective has a unique optimum, behaviorally equivalent policies result in behaviorally equivalent updates. We then present practical approximations to the ideal POLA update, which we evaluate in several partially competitive environments with function approximation and opponent modeling. This empirically demonstrates that POLA achieves reciprocity-based cooperation more reliably than LOLA.

paragraphs: Learning With Opponent-Learning Awareness, or LOLA, can learn cooperation based on reciprocity in environments where agents have partly competing interests. However, it often struggles with more complex neural-network policies. One cause is that its update depends on how a policy is parameterized, even when different parameterizations produce the same behavior.

This becomes especially problematic when an agent must infer an opponent’s policy from observations. Two opponent models that behave identically can still lead LOLA to different updates. The authors reinterpret LOLA as an approximation to a proximal operator and derive proximal LOLA, or POLA, by using the proximal formulation directly. When its proximal objective has a unique optimum, equivalent policy behaviors produce equivalent updated behaviors.

The paper also develops practical approximations to the ideal POLA update and tests them in several partially competitive environments with function approximation and opponent modeling. POLA learns reciprocity-based cooperation more reliably than LOLA in these experiments. The conditional invariance result explains the mathematical motivation, while the experiments support the practical value of the approximate updates.
summary.tldr: POLA reformulates opponent-aware learning to provide conditional parameterization invariance and empirically learn reciprocal cooperation more reliably than LOLA.

title: Proximal Learning With Opponent-Learning Awareness

abstract: Structured representations such as keypoints are widely used in pose transfer, conditional image generation, animation, and 3D reconstruction. However, their supervised learning requires expensive annotation for each target domain. We propose a self-supervised method that learns to disentangle object structure from the appearance with a graph of 2D keypoints linked by straight edges. Both the keypoint location and their pairwise edge weights are learned, given only a collection of images depicting the same object class. The resulting graph is interpretable, for example, AutoLink recovers the human skeleton topology when applied to images showing people. Our key ingredients are i) an encoder that predicts keypoint locations in an input image, ii) a shared graph as a latent variable that links the same pairs of keypoints in every image, iii) an intermediate edge map that combines the latent graph edge weights and keypoint locations in a soft, differentiable manner, and iv) an inpainting objective on randomly masked images. Although simpler, AutoLink outperforms existing self-supervised methods on the established keypoint and pose estimation benchmarks and paves the way for structure-conditioned generative models on more diverse datasets. Project website: https://xingzhehe.github.io/autolink/.

paragraphs: Keypoints can describe an object's structure for tasks such as animation and image generation, but manually labeling them for each object domain is expensive. AutoLink learns a structural representation from a collection of images of the same object class. Its representation is a graph of two-dimensional points connected by straight edges.

An encoder predicts point locations separately for each image, while a shared latent graph connects the same pairs of points throughout the collection. Both the locations and connection weights are learned. A differentiable edge map combines them, allowing the model to learn through an image-inpainting objective that asks it to reconstruct randomly masked image regions.

The shared connections provide a consistent structure while allowing point positions to change between images. The resulting graphs can be interpretable: on images of people, AutoLink recovers human skeleton topology. The authors report better results than existing self-supervised methods on established keypoint and pose-estimation benchmarks. They also identify the approach as a step toward structure-conditioned generation on more diverse datasets.
summary.tldr: AutoLink learns interpretable keypoint graphs from unlabeled images by combining shared connections with an image-inpainting objective.

title: AutoLink: Self-supervised Learning of Human Skeletons and Object Outlines by Linking Keypoints

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) as an effective paradigm of representation learning has achieved tremendous success on various curated datasets in diverse scenarios. Nevertheless, when facing the long-tailed distribution in real-world applications, it is still hard for existing methods to capture transferable and robust representation. The attribution is that the vanilla SSL methods that pursue the sample-level uniformity easily leads to representation learning disparity, where head classes with the huge sample number dominate the feature regime but tail classes with the small sample number passively collapse. To address this problem, we propose a novel Geometric Harmonization (GH) method to encourage the category-level uniformity in representation learning, which is more benign to the minority and almost does not hurt the majority under long-tailed distribution. Specially, GH measures the population statistics of the embedding space on top of self-supervised learning, and then infer an fine-grained instance-wise calibration to constrain the space expansion of head classes and avoid the passive collapse of tail classes. Our proposal does not alter the setting of SSL and can be easily integrated into existing methods in a low-cost manner. Extensive results on a range of benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of \methodspace with high tolerance to the distribution skewness.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can struggle when a dataset contains many examples of a few categories and few examples of many others. The paper attributes part of this problem to objectives that spread individual samples uniformly through the representation space. With uneven category frequencies, common categories can dominate that space while rare categories become poorly distinguished.

Geometric Harmonization changes the emphasis toward uniformity at the category level. It measures population statistics in the learned embedding space and derives adjustments for individual examples. These adjustments constrain the expansion of common categories and aim to prevent rare categories from collapsing. The approach retains the self-supervised setting and is designed to integrate into existing methods at low cost.

The intended benefit is better treatment of minority categories with almost no harm to majority categories. Results across benchmark datasets support the method’s effectiveness and tolerance of strongly skewed distributions. The broader implication is that how representation space is distributed matters: spreading samples evenly can still leave categories unevenly represented when their sample counts differ.
summary.tldr: Geometric Harmonization adjusts self-supervised representations to reduce domination by frequent categories and collapse among rare ones.

title: Combating Representation Learning Disparity with Geometric Harmonization

abstract: The core components of many modern neural network architectures, such as transformers, convolutional, or graph neural networks, can be expressed as linear layers with *weight-sharing*. Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC), a second-order optimisation method, has shown promise to speed up neural network training and thereby reduce computational costs. However, there is currently no framework to apply it to generic architectures, specifically ones with linear weight-sharing layers. In this work, we identify two different settings of linear weight-sharing layers which motivate two flavours of K-FAC -- *expand* and *reduce*. We show that they are exact for deep linear networks with weight-sharing in their respective setting. Notably, K-FAC-reduce is generally faster than K-FAC-expand, which we leverage to speed up automatic hyperparameter selection via optimising the marginal likelihood for a Wide ResNet. Finally, we observe little difference between these two K-FAC variations when using them to train both a graph neural network and a vision transformer. However, both variations are able to reach a fixed validation metric target in $50$-$75$\% of the number of steps of a first-order reference run, which translates into a comparable improvement in wall-clock time. This highlights the potential of applying K-FAC to modern neural network architectures.

title: Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature for Modern Neural Network Architectures

abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a powerful method for tackling expensive black-box optimization problems. As a sequential model-based optimization strategy, BO iteratively explores promising solutions until a predetermined budget, either iterations or time, is exhausted. The decision on when to terminate BO significantly influences both the quality of solutions and its computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose a simple, yet theoretically grounded, two-step method for automatically terminating BO. Our core concept is to proactively identify if the search is within a convex region by examining previously observed samples. BO is halted once the local regret within this convex region falls below a predetermined threshold. To enhance numerical stability, we propose an approximation method for calculating the termination indicator by solving a bilevel optimization problem. We conduct extensive empirical studies on diverse benchmark problems, including synthetic functions, reinforcement learning, and hyperparameter optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method saves up to $\approx 80\%$ computational budget yet is with an order of magnitude smaller performance degradation, comparing against the other peer methods. In addition, our proposed termination method is robust in terms of the setting of its termination criterion.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization often continues until a fixed time or iteration budget runs out, even though deciding when to stop directly affects cost and solution quality. This paper proposes an automatic termination rule that examines already observed samples to assess whether further local search is worthwhile.

The method first attempts to identify whether the search is within a convex region. It then stops when local regret in that region falls below a predetermined threshold. To make the termination indicator more numerically stable, the authors introduce an approximation computed through a bilevel optimization problem. The stopping decision is therefore tied to a local region and an explicit tolerance.

The authors report savings of up to approximately 80% of the computational budget, with performance degradation an order of magnitude smaller than that of comparison methods. They also find robustness to the termination criterion’s setting. These results support using past observations to guide stopping while keeping the rule’s assessment focused on local regret.
summary.tldr: A two-step stopping rule uses observed samples and local regret to terminate Bayesian optimization early with limited empirical performance loss.

title: “Why Not Looking backward?” A Robust Two-Step Method to Automatically Terminate Bayesian Optimization

abstract: One of the goals of causal inference is to generalize from past experiments and observational data to novel conditions. While it is in principle possible to eventually learn a mapping from a novel experimental condition to an outcome of interest, provided a sufficient variety of experiments is available in the training data, coping with a large combinatorial space of possible interventions is hard. Under a typical sparse experimental design, this mapping is ill-posed without relying on heavy regularization or prior distributions. Such assumptions may or may not be reliable, and can be hard to defend or test. In this paper, we take a close look at how to warrant a leap from past experiments to novel conditions based on minimal assumptions about the factorization of the distribution of the manipulated system, communicated in the well-understood language of factor graph models. A postulated interventional factor model (IFM) may not always be informative, but it conveniently abstracts away a need for explicitly modeling unmeasured confounding and feedback mechanisms, leading to directly testable claims. Given an IFM and datasets from a collection of experimental regimes, we derive conditions for identifiability of the expected outcomes of new regimes never observed in these training data. We implement our framework using several efficient algorithms, and apply them on a range of semi-synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting an untried intervention is difficult when experiments cover only a small fraction of possible conditions. Many different outcome mappings may fit the available evidence. This paper asks when predictions about new experimental regimes can be justified through assumptions about how the manipulated system's probability distribution factors into smaller pieces.

The authors express those assumptions using an interventional factor model. This representation avoids requiring an explicit account of unmeasured confounding and feedback mechanisms, while producing claims that can be tested. A proposed factor model may still be uninformative; its usefulness depends on what structure it asserts and which experimental regimes have been observed.

Given a factor model and data from multiple regimes, the paper derives conditions under which expected outcomes in previously unseen regimes are identifiable. That means the available information can determine those expectations under the model's assumptions. The authors implement efficient algorithms and apply them to semi-synthetic experiments, connecting the identification framework to concrete computational procedures.
summary.tldr: Interventional factor models provide testable structural assumptions for identifying expected outcomes under previously unseen experimental regimes.

title: Intervention Generalization: A View from Factor Graph Models

abstract: In this work, we study two-player zero-sum stochastic games and develop a variant of the smoothed best-response learning dynamics that combines independent learning dynamics for matrix games with the minimax value iteration for stochastic games. The resulting learning dynamics are payoff-based, convergent, rational, and symmetric between the two players. Our theoretical results present to the best of our knowledge the first last-iterate finite-sample analysis of such independent learning dynamics. To establish the results, we develop a coupled Lyapunov drift approach to capture the evolution of multiple sets of coupled and stochastic iterates, which might be of independent interest.

The resulting learning dynamics are payoff-based, convergent, rational, and symmetric between the two players. Our theoretical results present to the best of our knowledge the first last-iterate finite-sample analysis of such independent learning dynamics. To establish the results, we develop a coupled Lyapunov drift approach to capture the evolution of multiple sets of coupled and stochastic iterates, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in two-player zero-sum stochastic games, where the players have opposing objectives and their decisions unfold across changing states. It focuses on independent, payoff-based learning: each player learns through the outcomes of play. The challenge is to establish convergence while both players' learning processes interact with one another.

The proposed method combines two ingredients. It uses independent learning dynamics for matrix games together with minimax value iteration for stochastic games. A variant of smoothed best-response dynamics connects these pieces. The resulting procedure is described as convergent, rational, and symmetric between the players, so its construction does not give the two players fundamentally different learning roles.

The main theoretical contribution is a finite-sample analysis of the last iterate, addressing the learning process's current output rather than only its eventual behavior. The authors identify this as the first such analysis for these dynamics, to their knowledge. Their proof develops a coupled Lyapunov drift approach to track several interacting stochastic updates, a technique they suggest could also be useful independently.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a finite-sample convergence analysis for the current output of independent, payoff-based learning in two-player zero-sum stochastic games.

title: A Finite-Sample Analysis of Payoff-Based Independent Learning in Zero-Sum Stochastic Games

abstract: Test-time prompt tuning, which learns prompts online with unlabelled test samples during the inference stage, has demonstrated great potential by learning effective prompts on-the-fly without requiring any task-specific annotations. However, its performance often degrades clearly along the tuning process when the prompts are continuously updated with the test data flow, and the degradation becomes more severe when the domain of test samples changes continuously. We propose HisTPT, a Historical Test-time Prompt Tuning technique that memorizes the useful knowledge of the learnt test samples and enables robust test-time prompt tuning with the memorized knowledge. HisTPT introduces three types of knowledge banks, namely, local knowledge bank, hard-sample knowledge bank, and global knowledge bank, each of which works with different mechanisms for effective knowledge memorization and test-time prompt optimization. In addition, HisTPT features an adaptive knowledge retrieval mechanism that regularizes the prediction of each test sample by adaptively retrieving the memorized knowledge. Extensive experiments show that HisTPT achieves superior prompt tuning performance consistently while handling different visual recognition tasks (e.g., image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection) and test samples from continuously changing domains.

paragraphs: Test-time prompt tuning adapts a vision model's prompts using unlabeled samples encountered during inference. This offers adaptation without task-specific annotations, but continued updates can degrade performance. The paper highlights that the problem becomes more severe when incoming samples repeatedly shift between domains.

HisTPT addresses this by retaining useful knowledge from previously processed samples. It introduces three stores: a local knowledge bank, a hard-sample knowledge bank, and a global knowledge bank. Each uses a different mechanism to support memory and prompt optimization. The aim is to make ongoing adaptation benefit from what has already been learned.

An adaptive retrieval mechanism chooses stored knowledge to regularize the prediction for each new sample. This connects historical information to current decisions instead of relying on continued prompt updates alone. Experiments report consistently stronger prompt tuning across image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, including streams with continuously changing domains. The findings support memory and selective retrieval as useful components of sustained adaptation without labeled test data.
summary.tldr: HisTPT uses historical knowledge banks and adaptive retrieval to stabilize prompt tuning as unlabeled test data changes.

title: Historical Test-time Prompt Tuning for Vision Foundation Models

abstract: Data selection has emerged as a core issue for large-scale visual-language model pretaining (e.g., CLIP), particularly with noisy web-curated datasets. Three main data selection approaches are: (1) leveraging external non-CLIP models to aid data selection, (2) training new CLIP-style embedding models that are more effective at selecting high-quality data than the original OpenAI CLIP model, and (3) designing better metrics or strategies universally applicable to any CLIP embedding without requiring specific model properties (e.g., CLIPScore is one popular metric). While the first two approaches have been extensively studied, the third remains under-explored. In this paper, we advance the third approach by proposing two new methods. Firstly, instead of classical CLIP scores that only consider the alignment between two modalities from a single sample, we introduce $\textbf{negCLIPLoss}$, a method inspired by CLIP training loss that adds the alignment between one sample and its contrastive pairs as an extra normalization term to CLIPScore for better quality measurement. Secondly, when downstream tasks are known, we propose a new norm-based metric, $\textbf{NormSim}$, to measure the similarity between pretraining data and target data. We test our methods on the data selection benchmark, DataComp [Gadre et al., 2023]. Compared to the best baseline using only OpenAI's CLIP-L/14, our methods achieve a 5.3\% improvement on ImageNet-1k and a 2.8\% improvement on 38 downstream evaluation tasks. Moreover, both $\textbf{negCLIPLoss}$ and $\textbf{NormSim}$ are compatible with existing techniques. By combining our methods with the current best methods DFN [Fang et al., 2023] and HYPE [Kim et al., 2024], we can boost average performance on downstream tasks by 0.9\%, achieving a new state-of-the-art on the DataComp-medium benchmark.

Its focus is improving the selection metric applied to CLIP embeddings, rather than requiring a specialized new embedding model. Better selection can make the same pool of candidate training data more useful for downstream tasks.

The results show that selection rules themselves offer gains beyond changing the model that supplies embeddings.
summary.tldr: negCLIPLoss and NormSim improve image-text data selection by considering contrastive comparisons and, when available, similarity to target-task data.

title: CLIPLoss and Norm-Based Data Selection Methods for Multimodal Contrastive Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on massive corpora have shown remarkable success in knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet, most of them rely on pre-stored knowledge. Inducing new general knowledge from a specific environment andperforming reasoning with the acquired knowledge—situated inductive reasoning, is crucial and challenging for machine intelligence. In this paper, we design Mars, an interactive environment devised for situated inductive reasoning. It introduces counter-commonsense game mechanisms by modifying terrain, survival setting and task dependency while adhering to certain principles. In Mars, agents need to actively interact with their surroundings, derive useful rules and perform decision-making tasks in specific contexts. We conduct experiments on various RL-based and LLM-based methods, finding that they all struggle on this challenging situated inductive reasoning benchmark. Furthermore, we explore Induction from Reflection, where we instruct agents to perform inductive reasoning from history trajectory. The superior performance underscores the importance of inductive reasoning in Mars. Through Mars, we aim to galvanize advancements in situated inductive reasoning and set the stage for developing the next generation of AI systems that can reason in an adaptive and context-sensitive way.

paragraphs: A model can answer knowledge-intensive questions using information acquired during training without learning new rules from its current surroundings. Mars targets the latter ability: interacting with an environment, inducing general knowledge from experience, and using that knowledge to make decisions. The paper calls this situated inductive reasoning.

Mars is an interactive environment whose terrain, survival conditions, and task dependencies are modified to introduce mechanisms that conflict with ordinary expectations. Agents must investigate the environment and discover useful rules for its particular context. This design makes the acquisition of local knowledge central to successful behavior, creating a test of adaptation through interaction.

Experiments show that the evaluated reinforcement-learning and language-model methods all struggle on the benchmark. The authors also explore Induction from Reflection, which prompts agents to infer rules from their past trajectories. Its superior performance supports the importance of explicitly reasoning over experience in Mars. The findings establish a challenging benchmark and a promising improvement, while leaving the broader goal of reliable situated reasoning open.
summary.tldr: Mars tests whether agents can discover unfamiliar environmental rules through interaction, with reflection-based induction improving performance on the challenging benchmark.

title: Mars: Situated Inductive Reasoning in an Open-World Environment

abstract: We propose a novel neural networks based approach to efficiently answer arbitrary Most Probable Explanation (MPE) queries—a well-known NP-hard task—in large probabilistic models such as Bayesian and Markov networks, probabilistic circuits, and neural auto-regressive models. By arbitrary MPE queries, we mean that there is no predefined partition of variables into evidence and non-evidence variables. The key idea is to distill all MPE queries over a given probabilistic model into a neural network and then use the latter for answering queries, eliminating the need for time-consuming inference algorithms that operate directly on the probabilistic model. We improve upon this idea by incorporating inference-time optimization with self-supervised loss to iteratively improve the solutions and employ a teacher-student framework that provides a better initial network, which in turn, helps reduce the number of inference-time optimization steps. The teacher network utilizes a self-supervised loss function optimized for getting the exact MPE solution, while the student network learns from the teacher's near-optimal outputs through supervised loss. We demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of our approach on various datasets and a broad class of probabilistic models, showcasing its practical effectiveness.

paragraphs: A Most Probable Explanation query asks a probabilistic model for the most likely assignment of unknown variables given observed ones. Answering such queries is computationally difficult. This paper addresses the flexible version of the problem, where any variables can serve as observations rather than being assigned that role in advance.

The authors train a neural network to answer queries for a particular probabilistic model, transferring work away from repeatedly running inference on the original model. They also refine answers at inference time using a self-supervised objective. A teacher-student setup improves the starting point: the teacher pursues an objective targeting exact MPE solutions, while the student learns from the teacher’s near-optimal answers.

A better starting network reduces the number of refinement steps needed. Experiments across several datasets and types of probabilistic models demonstrate practical effectiveness and scalability. The contribution is a learned route to answering many different queries efficiently, supported by iterative improvement; the teacher’s exact-solution objective should not be confused with a guarantee that every returned answer is exact.
summary.tldr: A teacher-student neural approach learns to answer flexible probabilistic explanation queries and refines its answers during inference.

title: A Neural Network Approach for Efficiently Answering Most Probable Explanation Queries in Probabilistic Models

abstract: In this work, we present MotionBooth, an innovative framework designed for animating customized subjects with precise control over both object and camera movements. By leveraging a few images of a specific object, we efficiently fine-tune a text-to-video model to capture the object's shape and attributes accurately. Our approach presents subject region loss and video preservation loss to enhance the subject's learning performance, along with a subject token cross-attention loss to integrate the customized subject with motion control signals. Additionally, we propose training-free techniques for managing subject and camera motions during inference. In particular, we utilize cross-attention map manipulation to govern subject motion and introduce a novel latent shift module for camera movement control as well. MotionBooth excels in preserving the appearance of subjects while simultaneously controlling the motions in generated videos. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate the superiority and effectiveness of our method. Models and codes will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Creating a video of a particular subject requires preserving its appearance while also controlling how it and the camera move. MotionBooth addresses these requirements together. Given a few images of a specific object, it fine-tunes a text-to-video model to learn the object's shape and attributes for customized video generation.

The training procedure combines several losses with distinct roles. Subject-region and video-preservation losses improve learning of the customized subject, while a subject-token cross-attention loss connects that subject with motion-control signals. This links appearance customization to the model components used for controlling movement, helping the generated subject remain identifiable while participating in the requested motion.

At inference, MotionBooth controls subject motion by manipulating cross-attention maps and controls camera motion through a latent-shift module. These motion-control techniques require no additional training during inference. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report effective motion control alongside strong preservation of subject appearance, with superior results in the evaluated comparisons. The contribution is a framework that integrates subject customization, object movement, and camera movement within the same video-generation process.
summary.tldr: MotionBooth customizes a video model from a few subject images and controls both subject and camera motion during generation.

title: MotionBooth: Motion-Aware Customized Text-to-Video Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have acquired the ability to solve general tasks by utilizing instruction finetuning (IFT). However, IFT still relies heavily on instance training of extensive task data, which greatly limits the adaptability of LLMs to real-world scenarios where labeled task instances are scarce and broader task generalization becomes paramount. Contrary to LLMs, humans acquire skills and complete tasks not merely through repeated practice but also by understanding and following instructional guidelines. This paper is dedicated to simulating human learning to address the shortcomings of instance training, focusing on instruction learning to enhance cross-task generalization. Within this context, we introduce Task Adapters Generation from Instructions (TAGI), which automatically constructs the task-specific model in a parameter generation manner based on the given task instructions without retraining for unseen tasks. Specifically, we utilize knowledge distillation to enhance the consistency between TAGI developed through Learning with Instruction and task-specific models developed through Training with Instance, by aligning the labels, output logits, and adapter parameters between them. TAGI is endowed with cross-task generalization capabilities through a two-stage training process that includes hypernetwork pretraining and finetuning. We evaluate TAGI on the Super-Natural Instructions and P3 datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that TAGI can match or even outperform traditional meta-trained models and other hypernetwork models, while significantly reducing computational requirements. Our code will be available at https://github.com/Xnhyacinth/TAGI.

paragraphs: Task Adapters Generation from Instructions, or TAGI, targets situations where a language model must handle new tasks with few labeled examples available. Standard instruction fine-tuning still depends heavily on training instances. TAGI instead learns to use a task's instructions to generate task-specific adapter parameters, allowing it to construct an adapted model for an unseen task without retraining on that task.

The framework learns this capability through hypernetwork pretraining followed by fine-tuning. Knowledge distillation connects instruction-based generation with models trained on task examples. Specifically, training aligns labels, output logits, and adapter parameters, so the instruction-generated model is encouraged to behave consistently with a model developed through instance training.

Evaluations on Super-Natural Instructions and P3 show that TAGI can match or exceed traditional meta-trained models and other hypernetwork approaches while substantially reducing computational requirements. The result supports learning a reusable mapping from task descriptions to model parameters. Its cross-task capability comes from the two-stage training process, which prepares the system to generate adapters when new instructions arrive.
summary.tldr: TAGI learns to generate task-specific adapters from instructions, supporting unseen tasks without task-specific retraining.

title: From Instance Training to Instruction Learning: Task Adapters Generation from Instructions

abstract: Identifying causal effects is a key problem of interest across many disciplines. The two long-standing approaches to estimate causal effects are observational and experimental (randomized) studies. Observational studies can suffer from unmeasured confounding, which may render the causal effects unidentifiable. On the other hand, direct experiments on the target variable may be too costly or even infeasible to conduct. A middle ground between these two approaches is to estimate the causal effect of interest through proxy experiments, which are conducted on variables with a lower cost to intervene on compared to the main target. In an earlier work, we studied this setting and demonstrated that the problem of designing the optimal (minimum-cost) experiment for causal effect identification is NP-complete and provided a naive algorithm that may require solving exponentially many NP-hard problems as a sub-routine in the worst case. In this work, we provide a few reformulations of the problem that allow for designing significantly more efficient algorithms to solve it as witnessed by our extensive simulations. Additionally, we study the closely-related problem of designing experiments that enable us to identify a given effect through valid adjustments sets.

Direct experiments may resolve that difficulty, but intervening on the variable of interest can be expensive or infeasible. Proxy experiments offer another route: intervene on cheaper variables that still allow the desired causal effect to be identified.

The paper studies how to choose such experiments at minimum cost. Earlier work established that this design problem is NP-complete and supplied an algorithm that could require exponentially many difficult subproblems in the worst case. The new contribution is a set of reformulations that make substantially more efficient solution algorithms possible.

Extensive simulations provide evidence for the improved computational efficiency. The paper also examines experiment design for identifying effects through valid adjustment sets, connecting intervention choices with another route to causal identification. The practical significance is better computational handling of a difficult design problem: finding affordable experiments that supply the information needed to identify a particular effect.
summary.tldr: New reformulations make it faster to design low-cost proxy experiments that identify a desired causal effect.

title: Fast Proxy Experiment Design for Causal Effect Identification

abstract: Autonomous trucking is a promising technology that can greatly impact modern logistics and the environment. Ensuring its safety on public roads is one of the main duties that requires an accurate perception of the environment. To achieve this, machine learning methods rely on large datasets, but to this day, no such datasets are available for autonomous trucks. In this work, we present MAN TruckScenes, the first multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking. MAN TruckScenes allows the research community to come into contact with truck-specific challenges, such as trailer occlusions, novel sensor perspectives, and terminal environments for the first time. It comprises more than 740 scenes of 20 s each within a multitude of different environmental conditions. The sensor set includes 4 cameras, 6 lidar, 6 radar sensors, 2 IMUs, and a high-precision GNSS. The dataset's 3D bounding boxes were manually annotated and carefully reviewed to achieve a high quality standard. Bounding boxes are available for 27 object classes, 15 attributes, and a range of more than 230 m. The scenes are tagged according to 34 distinct scene tags, and all objects are tracked throughout the scene to promote a wide range of applications. Additionally, MAN TruckScenes is the first dataset to provide 4D radar data with 360° coverage and is thereby the largest radar dataset with annotated 3D bounding boxes. Finally, we provide extensive dataset analysis and baseline results. The dataset, development kit, and more will be available online.

Its contribution is a truck-focused evaluation and training resource for perception research relevant to road safety.
summary.tldr: MAN TruckScenes supplies annotated, multimodal truck recordings that expose truck-specific perception challenges across diverse conditions.

title: MAN TruckScenes: A multimodal dataset for autonomous trucking in diverse conditions

abstract: Detecting and handling misspecified objectives, such as reward functions, has been widely recognized as one of the central challenges within the domain of Artificial Intelligence (AI) safety research. However, even with the recognition of the importance of this problem, we are unaware of any works that attempt to provide a clear definition for what constitutes (a) misspecified objectives and (b) successfully resolving such misspecifications. In this work, we use the theory of mind, i.e., the human user's beliefs about the AI agent, as a basis to develop a formal explanatory framework, called Expectation Alignment (EAL), to understand the objective misspecification and its causes.Our EAL framework not only acts as an explanatory framework for existing works but also provides us with concrete insights into the limitations of existing methods to handle reward misspecification and novel solution strategies. We use these insights to propose a new interactive algorithm that uses the specified reward to infer potential user expectations about the system behavior. We show how one can efficiently implement this algorithm by mapping the inference problem into linear programs. We evaluate our method on a set of standard Markov Decision Process (MDP) benchmarks.

paragraphs: A reward function can direct an AI system toward behavior that differs from what its user intended. This paper argues that understanding such misspecification requires examining the user’s beliefs about the agent. It introduces Expectation Alignment, a formal framework that uses those beliefs to explain what it means for an objective to be misspecified and for the mismatch to be resolved.

The framework treats expectations about system behavior as part of the problem, rather than interpreting the supplied reward in isolation. The authors use this perspective to explain existing approaches, identify limitations in how they handle reward misspecification, and derive possible new strategies for addressing it.

They then propose an interactive algorithm that works backward from the specified reward to infer potential user expectations. The inference can be expressed as linear programs, providing an efficient implementation route. The method is evaluated on standard Markov Decision Process benchmarks. The contribution joins a formal account of expectation mismatch with a concrete algorithm for investigating and addressing it.
summary.tldr: Expectation Alignment formalizes reward misspecification through users’ beliefs about an agent and derives an interactive method for inferring their expectations.

title: Expectation Alignment: Handling Reward Misspecification in the Presence of Expectation Mismatch

abstract: Although current large language models are complex, the most basic specifications of the underlying language generation problem itself are simple to state: given a finite set of training samples from an unknown language, produce valid new strings from the language that don't already appear in the training data. Here we ask what we can conclude about language generation using only this specification, without further assumptions. In particular, suppose that an adversary enumerates the strings of an unknown target language L that is known only to come from one of a possibly infinite list of candidates. A computational agent is trying to learn to generate from this language; we say that the agent generates from $L$ in the limit if after some finite point in the enumeration of $L$, the agent is able to produce new elements that come exclusively from $L$ and that have not yet been presented by the adversary. Our main result is that there is an agent that is able to generate in the limit for every countable list of candidate languages. This contrasts dramatically with negative results due to Gold and Angluin in a well-studied model of language learning where the goal is to identify an unknown language from samples; the difference between these results suggests that identifying a language is a fundamentally different problem than generating from it.

paragraphs: This paper asks a basic theoretical question: can an agent learn to produce valid new strings from an unknown language without identifying the language itself? The setup gives the agent examples revealed by an adversary. The target language is known only to belong to a candidate list, which may be infinite.

Success is defined as generation in the limit. After some finite point in the sequence of revealed examples, the agent must produce strings that belong to the target language and have not yet appeared. The main result establishes that an agent with this property exists for every countable list of candidate languages. The guarantee concerns eventual generation after that finite point, rather than correctness from the first example.

This result contrasts with established impossibility results for identifying an unknown language from examples. The distinction matters because generation asks for valid unseen members, whereas identification asks which language is being observed. The paper shows that these goals have fundamentally different possibilities in its formal setting, providing a theoretical separation between learning to generate and learning to identify.
summary.tldr: For every countable candidate-language list, an agent can eventually generate valid unseen strings even though identifying the target language can be impossible.

title: Language Generation in the Limit

abstract: Although 3D point cloud recognition has achieved substantial progress on standard benchmarks, the typical models are vulnerable to point cloud corruptions, leading to security threats in real-world applications. To improve the corruption robustness, various data augmentation methods have been studied, but they are mainly limited to the spatial domain. As the point cloud has low information density and significant spatial redundancy, it is challenging to analyze the effects of corruptions. In this paper, we focus on the frequency domain to observe the underlying structure of point clouds and their corruptions. Through graph Fourier transform (GFT), we observe a correlation between the corruption robustness of point cloud recognition models and their sensitivity to different frequency bands, which is measured by the GFT spectrum of the model’s Jacobian matrix. To reduce the sensitivity and improve the corruption robustness, we propose Frequency Adversarial Training (FAT) that adopts frequency-domain adversarial examples as data augmentation to train robust point cloud recognition models against corruptions. Theoretically, we provide a guarantee of FAT on its out-of-distribution generalization performance. Empirically, we conduct extensive experiments with various network architectures to validate the effectiveness of FAT, which achieves the new state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Point cloud recognition models can perform well on standard benchmarks while remaining vulnerable to corrupted inputs. Most augmentation methods address this in spatial coordinates. The paper instead studies frequency structure, motivated by the difficulty of understanding corruption in point clouds with sparse information and substantial spatial redundancy. A graph Fourier transform provides the basis for this analysis.

The authors observe a correlation between corruption robustness and model sensitivity to different frequency bands. They measure this sensitivity using the graph Fourier spectrum of the model's Jacobian, which describes how model outputs respond to input changes. This connects robustness to the kinds of frequency variation that particularly affect a model's predictions.

The goal is to reduce sensitivity and improve resistance to corruptions. The findings support frequency-domain analysis as a useful guide for designing robustness training.
summary.tldr: Frequency Adversarial Training uses graph Fourier analysis to target sensitivities associated with corruption vulnerability in point cloud recognition.

title: Improving Robustness of 3D Point Cloud Recognition from a Fourier Perspective

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities, demystifying their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly vital. Neuron attribution, which attributes LLM outputs to specific neurons to reveal the semantic properties they learn, has emerged as a key interpretability approach. However, while neuron attribution has made significant progress in deciphering text-only LLMs, its application to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains less explored. To address this gap, we propose a novel Neuron Attribution method tailored for MLLMs, termed NAM. Specifically, NAM not only reveals the modality-specific semantic knowledge learned by neurons within MLLMs, but also highlights several intriguing properties of neurons, such as cross-modal invariance and semantic sensitivity. These properties collectively elucidate the inner workings mechanism of MLLMs, providing a deeper understanding of how MLLMs process and generate multi-modal content. Through theoretical analysis and empirical validation, we demonstrate the efficacy of NAM and the valuable insights it offers. Furthermore, leveraging NAM, we introduce a multi-modal knowledge editing paradigm, underscoring the practical significance of our approach for downstream applications of MLLMs.

paragraphs: Neuron attribution connects a model's outputs to individual neurons to investigate the semantic information they encode. Although this approach has progressed in text-only language models, its use in multimodal models is less developed. NAM is an attribution method designed specifically to examine how neurons participate in processing and generating content across modalities.

The method reveals modality-specific semantic knowledge and highlights properties described as cross-modal invariance and semantic sensitivity. These properties concern how neuronal behavior relates to meaning across different modalities and how it responds to semantic content. Together, they offer a more detailed view of internal representations than simply observing the model's final output.

The authors support NAM with theoretical analysis and empirical validation. They also use it to introduce a multimodal knowledge-editing paradigm, connecting interpretability with a downstream application. The contribution therefore includes both a way to inspect learned semantic structure and a proposed way to use that understanding when editing knowledge in a multimodal language model.
summary.tldr: NAM attributes multimodal language-model outputs to neurons, revealing semantic properties and supporting a knowledge-editing approach.

title: Towards Neuron Attributions in Multi-Modal Large Language Models

abstract: Protecting the copyright of large language models (LLMs) has become crucial due to their resource-intensive training and accompanying carefully designed licenses. However, identifying the original base model of an LLM is challenging due to potential parameter alterations. In thisstudy, we introduce HuRef, a human-readable fingerprint for LLMs that uniquely identifies the base model without interfering with training or exposing model parameters to the public.We first observe that the vector direction of LLM parameters remains stable after the model has converged during pretraining, with negligible perturbations through subsequent training steps, including continued pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF, which makes it a sufficient conditionto identify the base model.The necessity is validated by continuing to train an LLM with an extra term to drive away the model parameters' direction and the model becomes damaged. However, this direction is vulnerable to simple attacks like dimension permutation or matrix rotation, which significantly change it without affecting performance. To address this, leveraging the Transformer structure, we systematically analyze potential attacks and define three invariant terms that identify an LLM's base model. Due to the potential risk of information leakage, we cannot publish invariant terms directly. Instead, we map them to a Gaussian vector using an encoder, then convert it into a natural image using StyleGAN2, and finally publish the image. In our black-box setting, all fingerprinting steps are internally conducted by the LLMs owners. To ensure the published fingerprints are honestly generated, we introduced Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP).Experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/LUMIA-Group/HuRef.

paragraphs: HuRef aims to identify a language model's original base model through a human-readable fingerprint without publishing its parameters. The authors observe that parameter-vector directions remain stable after pretraining convergence through continued pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF. They present this stability as a sufficient identification condition and report damage when extra training deliberately pushes directions away.

Direction alone is vulnerable to parameter permutations and matrix rotations that preserve performance. To address these transformations, the authors analyze Transformer structure and define three invariant quantities for base-model identification. Because publishing those quantities could expose information, an encoder maps them to a Gaussian vector, which StyleGAN2 then converts into an image for publication.

In the proposed black-box arrangement, model owners perform the fingerprinting steps internally. Zero-knowledge proofs are introduced to verify honest fingerprint generation without making the underlying quantities public. Experiments across several language models support the method's effectiveness. The resulting design combines structural identification, a viewable image, and a verification mechanism for fingerprints generated by the owners themselves.
summary.tldr: HuRef converts model-identifying invariant quantities into image fingerprints and uses zero-knowledge proofs to verify their generation.

title: HuRef: HUman-REadable Fingerprint for Large Language Models

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to help deep neural networks to learn new knowledge while retaining what has been learned. Owing to their powerful generalizability, pre-trained vision-language models such as Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) have lately gained traction as practical CL candidates. However, the domain mismatch between the pre-training and the downstream CL tasks calls for finetuning of the CLIP on the latter. The deterministic nature of the existing finetuning methods makes them overlook the many possible interactions across the modalities and deems them unsafe for high-risk tasks requiring reliable uncertainty estimation. To address these, our work proposes **C**ontinual **L**e**A**rning with **P**robabilistic finetuning (CLAP) - a probabilistic modeling framework over visual-guided text features per task, thus providing more calibrated CL finetuning. Unlike recent data-hungry anti-forgetting CL techniques, CLAP alleviates forgetting by exploiting the rich pre-trained knowledge of CLIP for weight initialization and distribution regularization of task-specific parameters. Cooperating with the diverse range of existing prompting methods, CLAP can surpass the predominant deterministic finetuning approaches for CL with CLIP. We conclude with out-of-the-box applications of superior uncertainty estimation abilities of CLAP including novel data detection and exemplar selection within the existing CL setups. Our code is available at https://github.com/srvCodes/clap4clip.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new knowledge while retaining earlier capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models such as CLIP are promising starting points, but differences between pretraining and downstream tasks motivate further adaptation. The paper argues that deterministic finetuning overlooks possible interactions between visual and textual information and provides inadequate treatment of uncertainty.

CLAP introduces probabilistic modeling of text features guided by visual information for each task. This gives finetuning a way to represent uncertainty rather than relying only on a single deterministic representation. To reduce forgetting, it uses CLIP's pretrained knowledge both to initialize task-specific parameters and to regularize their distributions, making existing knowledge part of the adaptation process.

The framework works with a range of prompting methods and can outperform predominant deterministic approaches to continual learning with CLIP. The paper also demonstrates uses of its improved uncertainty estimation, including detecting novel data and choosing exemplars within continual learning setups. These applications connect uncertainty modeling to concrete decisions about unfamiliar inputs and which examples to retain.
summary.tldr: CLAP adds probabilistic task adaptation to CLIP, improving uncertainty estimation while using pretrained knowledge to alleviate forgetting.

title: CLAP4CLIP: Continual Learning with Probabilistic Finetuning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Adapting to dynamic data distributions is a practical yet challenging task. One effective strategy is to use a model ensemble, which leverages the diverse expertise of different models to transfer knowledge to evolving data distributions. However, this approach faces difficulties when the dynamic test distribution is available only in small batches and without access to the original source data. To address the challenge of adapting to dynamic distributions in such practical settings, we propose continual multi-source adaptation to dynamic distributions (CONTRAST), a novel method that optimally combines multiple source models to adapt to the dynamic test data. CONTRAST has two distinguishing features. First, it efficiently computes the optimal combination weights to combine the source models to adapt to the test data distribution continuously as a function of time. Second, it identifies which of the source model parameters to update so that only the model which is most correlated to the target data is adapted, leaving the less correlated ones untouched; this mitigates the issue of ``forgetting" the source model parameters by focusing only on the source model that exhibits the strongest correlation with the test batch distribution. Through theoretical analysis we show that the proposed method is able to optimally combine the source models and prioritize updates to the model least prone to forgetting. Experimental analysis on diverse datasets demonstrates that the combination of multiple source models does at least as well as the best source (with hindsight knowledge), and performance does not degrade as the test data distribution changes over time (robust to forgetting).

paragraphs: CONTRAST addresses adaptation when incoming data changes over time, arrives only in small batches, and the original training data is unavailable. It starts with several source models whose different expertise may be useful under different conditions. The challenge is to combine that expertise while avoiding updates that erase useful knowledge.

The method continually computes combination weights for the source models as the test distribution evolves. It also chooses which model to update: only the source model most strongly correlated with the current target batch is adapted. The less correlated models retain their parameters, preserving knowledge that could otherwise be lost through repeated adaptation.

The theoretical analysis supports optimal combination of the source models and prioritization of the model least prone to forgetting. In experiments across diverse datasets, the ensemble performs at least as well as the best source selected with hindsight, and its performance does not degrade as the test distribution changes. These results connect selective updating with sustained adaptation in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: CONTRAST continually reweights source models and selectively updates the best-matched one to adapt to changing data while mitigating forgetting.

title: CONTRAST: Continual Multi-source Adaptation to Dynamic Distributions

abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables a model's ability to refuse, with minimal effect on other capabilities. This interpretable rank-one weight edit results in an effective jailbreak technique that is simpler and more efficient than fine-tuning. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size.
