Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables a model's ability to refuse, with minimal effect on other capabilities. This interpretable rank-one weight edit results in an effective jailbreak technique that is simpler and more efficient than fine-tuning. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

paragraphs: Chat models are trained to follow benign instructions while refusing harmful requests, but the internal mechanism behind refusal is less clear. This paper investigates that mechanism across 13 open-source chat models with sizes up to 72 billion parameters.

For each model, the authors identify a single direction in its residual-stream activations that mediates refusal. Removing that direction prevents refusal of harmful instructions, while adding it produces refusal even for harmless ones. These interventions provide evidence that the identified component has a functional role in refusal behavior, beyond simply being associated with examples where refusal occurs.

The authors use this finding to develop an interpretable rank-one weight edit that disables refusal with minimal effects on other capabilities, reporting a simpler and more efficient jailbreak than fine-tuning. They also analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the same refusal-related direction. The findings expose brittleness in the safety fine-tuning of the studied models and demonstrate how understanding internal representations can enable direct control over behavior.
summary.tldr: Across 13 studied chat models, a single internal direction mediates refusal, revealing a vulnerability in their safety fine-tuning.

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction

abstract: The transformer architecture by Vaswani et al. (2017) is now ubiquitous across application domains, from natural language processing to speech processing and image understanding. We propose DenseFormer, a simple modification to the standard architecture that improves the perplexity of the model without increasing its size---adding a few thousand parameters for large-scale models in the 100B parameters range. Our approach relies on an additional averaging step after each transformer block, which computes a weighted average of current and past representations---we refer to this operation as Depth-Weighted-Average (DWA). The learned DWA weights exhibit coherent patterns of information flow, revealing the strong and structured reuse of activations from distant layers. Experiments demonstrate that DenseFormer is more data efficient, reaching the same perplexity of much deeper transformer models, and that for the same perplexity, these new models outperform transformer baselines in terms of memory efficiency and inference time.

paragraphs: DenseFormer changes how information moves through a transformer. After each transformer block, it adds a learned weighted average of the current representation and representations from earlier blocks. The operation, called Depth-Weighted-Average, gives later processing stages an explicit way to reuse information produced at multiple depths.

The modification adds very few parameters relative to the models discussed: only a few thousand for models around the hundred-billion-parameter scale. The learned averaging weights also reveal structured patterns, including substantial reuse of activations from distant layers. This matters because the additional connections are used in a coherent way, providing evidence that the model benefits from access to earlier representations.

Experiments report improved perplexity and greater data efficiency, with DenseFormer reaching the perplexity of substantially deeper transformers. When models are compared at the same perplexity, DenseFormer also improves memory efficiency and inference time over transformer baselines. The findings suggest that changing information flow across depth can improve predictive performance and computational efficiency without a substantial increase in parameter count.
summary.tldr: DenseFormer learns weighted combinations of representations across transformer layers, improving perplexity and efficiency with very few additional parameters.

title: DenseFormer: Enhancing Information Flow in Transformers via Depth Weighted Averaging

abstract: Transformers have emerged as a competitive alternative to convnets in vision tasks, yet they lack the architectural inductive bias of convnets, which may hinder their potential performance. Specifically, Vision Transformers (ViTs) are not translation‑invariant and are more sensitive to minor image translations than standard convnets. Previous studies have shown, however, that convnets are also not perfectly shift‑invariant, due to aliasing in downsampling and nonlinear layers. Consequently, anti‑aliasing approaches have been proposed to certify convnets translation robustness. Building on this line of work, we propose an Alias‑Free ViT, which combines two main components. First, it uses alias-free downsampling and nonlinearities. Second, it uses linear cross‑covariance attention that is shift‑equivariant to both integer and fractional translations, enabling a shift-invariant global representation. Our model maintains competitive performance in image classification and outperforms similar‑sized models in terms of robustness to adversarial translations.

paragraphs: Small translations of an image can change a vision transformer's output even when its content remains the same. Convolutional networks also have imperfect shift invariance because downsampling and nonlinear operations can introduce aliasing. This paper builds on approaches that address those sources of instability and brings that reasoning into the design of a vision transformer.

Alias-Free ViT combines alias-free downsampling and nonlinearities with linear cross-covariance attention. The attention mechanism is shift-equivariant for both whole-pixel and fractional translations: its representation follows the image's movement in a consistent way. This supports a global representation that remains invariant to those shifts, connecting the behavior of internal features to the desired stability of the final representation.

The reported experiments show competitive image classification performance and better robustness to adversarial translations than similarly sized models. The contribution therefore concerns both architectural behavior and measured robustness. It shows how addressing translation sensitivity within the model's operations can preserve classification capability while making deliberately chosen image shifts less disruptive in the evaluated comparisons.
summary.tldr: Alias-Free ViT combines alias-free operations with shift-equivariant attention to improve robustness to image translations while maintaining competitive classification performance.

title: Alias-Free ViT: Fractional Shift Invariance via Linear Attention

abstract: Deep learning has emerged as a pivotal tool for accelerating research in the life sciences, with the low-level processing of biomedical images (e.g., registration, fusion, restoration, super-resolution) being one of its most critical applications. Platforms such as ImageJ (Fiji) and napari have enabled the development of customized plugins for various models. However, these plugins are typically based on models that are limited to specific tasks and datasets, making them less practical for biologists. To address this challenge, we introduce **Orochi**, the first application-oriented, efficient, and versatile image processor designed to overcome these limitations. Orochi is pre-trained on patches/volumes extracted from the raw data of over 100 publicly available studies using our Random Multi-scale Sampling strategy. We further propose Task-related Joint-embedding Pre-Training (TJP), which employs biomedical task-related degradation for self-supervision rather than relying on Masked Image Modelling (MIM), which performs poorly in downstream tasks such as registration. To ensure computational efficiency, we leverage Mamba's linear computational complexity and construct Multi-head Hierarchy Mamba. Additionally, we provide a three-tier fine-tuning framework (Full, Normal, and Light) and demonstrate that Orochi achieves comparable or superior performance to current state-of-the-art specialist models, even with lightweight parameter-efficient options. We hope that our study contributes to the development of an all-in-one workflow, thereby relieving biologists from the overwhelming task of selecting among numerous models. Our pre-trained weights and code will be released.

Orochi aims to provide a broadly adaptable processor that can support these different kinds of low-level image work.

Its pre-training data consist of patches and volumes sampled at multiple scales from more than 100 public studies. The proposed Task-related Joint-embedding Pre-Training uses degradations connected to biomedical processing tasks as its self-supervised signal. The authors motivate this choice by the poor downstream performance of masked image modeling on tasks such as registration.

Full, Normal, and Light fine-tuning options provide different adaptation levels. The reported evaluations show comparable or superior performance to specialist state-of-the-art models, including with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation. These results support the possibility of a more unified processing workflow built around broad pre-training and task-relevant supervision.
summary.tldr: Orochi combines broad biomedical pre-training, task-related self-supervision, and efficient adaptation to support multiple image-processing tasks.

title: Orochi: Versatile Biomedical Image Processor

abstract: Standard training metrics like loss fail to explain the emergence of complex capabilities in large language models. We take a spectral approach to investigate the geometry of learned representations across pretraining and post-training, measuring effective rank (RankMe) and eigenspectrum decay (αReQ). With OLMo (1B-7B) and Pythia (160M-12B) models, we uncover a consistent non-monotonic sequence of three geometric phases during autoregressive pretraining. The initial “warmup” phase exhibits rapid representational collapse. This is followed by an “entropy-seeking” phase, where the manifold’s dimensionality expands substantially, coinciding with peak n-gram memorization. Subsequently, a “compression-seeking” phase imposes anisotropic consolidation, selectively preserving variance along dominant eigendirections while contracting others, a transition marked with significant improvement in downstream task performance. We show these phases can emerge from a fundamental interplay of cross-entropy optimization under skewed token frequencies and representational bottlenecks (d ≪ |V|). Post-training further transforms geometry: SFT and DPO drive “entropy-seeking” dynamics to integrate specific instructional or preferential data, improving in-distribution performance while degrading out-of-distribution robustness. Conversely, RLVR induces “compression-seeking” , enhancing reward alignment but reducing generation diversity.

paragraphs: Training loss does not fully describe how language-model capabilities emerge. This paper examines the geometry of internal representations using effective rank and eigenspectrum decay. Across OLMo and Pythia models, it identifies three recurring phases during pretraining, revealing changes in how representations use their available dimensions.

An initial warmup phase rapidly collapses representations. An entropy-seeking phase then expands dimensionality and coincides with peak n-gram memorization. Finally, a compression-seeking phase concentrates variation along dominant directions while shrinking others, alongside substantial downstream performance improvement. The authors show that these phases can arise from cross-entropy optimization with uneven token frequencies and representation dimensions much smaller than the vocabulary.

Post-training produces related but distinct changes. In the study, supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization expand representations, improving in-distribution performance while weakening out-of-distribution robustness. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards instead encourages compression, improving reward alignment while reducing generation diversity. These findings connect training choices to representation geometry and behavioral tradeoffs, providing a view of model development beyond the loss curve.
summary.tldr: Representation geometry reveals three pretraining phases and distinct post-training tradeoffs involving performance, robustness, reward alignment, and diversity.

title: Tracing the Representation Geometry of Language Models from Pretraining to Post-training

abstract: We present Q-chunking, a simple yet effective recipe for improving reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks. Our recipe is designed for the offline-to-online RL setting, where the goal is to leverage an offline prior dataset to maximize the sample-efficiency of online learning. Effective exploration and sample-efficient learning remain central challenges in this setting, as it is not obvious how the offline data should be utilized to acquire a good exploratory policy. Our key insight is that action chunking, a technique popularized in imitation learning where sequences of future actions are predicted rather than a single action at each timestep, can be applied to temporal difference (TD)-based RL methods to mitigate the exploration challenge. Q-chunking adopts action chunking by directly running RL in a *chunked* action space, enabling the agent to (1) leverage temporally consistent behaviors from offline data for more effective online exploration and (2) use unbiased $n$-step backups for more stable and efficient TD learning. Our experimental results demonstrate that Q-chunking exhibits strong offline performance and online sample efficiency, outperforming prior best offline-to-online methods on a range of long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Long tasks with infrequent rewards make it difficult for reinforcement learning agents to discover useful behavior. Q-chunking addresses this in offline-to-online learning, where an agent first has access to an existing dataset and then learns through additional interaction. The challenge is to turn that dataset into effective exploration and efficient subsequent learning.

The method treats a sequence of future actions as one action chunk and runs temporal-difference reinforcement learning directly in this chunked action space. This allows the agent to draw on temporally consistent behaviors in the offline data. It also enables unbiased multi-step backups, which the authors use to support more stable and efficient value learning.

Across a range of long-horizon manipulation tasks with sparse rewards, Q-chunking shows strong offline performance and online sample efficiency, outperforming the prior best offline-to-online methods in the reported experiments. Its contribution is a simple recipe for bringing action chunking, already used in imitation learning, into value-based learning in a way that addresses both exploration and training updates.
summary.tldr: Q-chunking learns over action sequences to improve exploration and sample efficiency in offline-to-online reinforcement learning.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Action Chunking

abstract: Recent advances in video generation have enabled the synthesis of high-quality and visually realistic clips using diffusion transformer models. However, most existing approaches operate purely in the 2D pixel space and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling 3D structures, often resulting in temporally inconsistent geometries, implausible motions, and structural artifacts. In this work, we introduce geometric regularization losses into video generation by augmenting latent diffusion models with per-frame depth prediction. We adopted depth as the geometric representation because of the great progress in depth prediction and its compatibility with image-based latent encoders. Specifically, to enforce structural consistency over time, we propose a multi-view geometric loss that aligns the predicted depth maps across frames within a shared 3D coordinate system. Our method bridges the gap between appearance generation and 3D structure modeling, leading to improved spatio-temporal coherence, shape consistency, and physical plausibility. Experiments across multiple datasets show that our approach produces significantly more stable and geometrically consistent results than existing baselines.

paragraphs: A generated video can look convincing frame by frame while its underlying shapes shift inconsistently over time. GeoVideo addresses this gap by adding explicit geometric supervision to latent diffusion video generation. The motivation is that producing realistic two-dimensional appearances alone does not provide a direct mechanism for maintaining coherent three-dimensional structure.

The method augments the generator with depth prediction for each frame. Depth is chosen because of progress in depth estimation and its compatibility with image-based latent encoders. A multi-view geometric loss then aligns the predicted depth maps in a shared three-dimensional coordinate system. This gives the model a training signal that connects structure across frames, alongside its appearance-generation task.

Across multiple datasets, experiments show more stable and geometrically consistent videos than the compared baselines. The reported benefits include better shape consistency, coherence across space and time, and physical plausibility. The contribution is the connection between generated appearance and an explicit depth-based structural constraint, allowing consistency to be encouraged through geometry rather than inferred solely from the visual quality of individual frames.
summary.tldr: GeoVideo adds depth prediction and cross-frame geometric alignment to improve the structural consistency of generated videos.

title: GeoVideo: Introducing Geometric Regularization into Video Generation Model

abstract: Causal representation learning in the anti-causal setting—labels cause features rather than the reverse—presents unique challenges requiring specialized approaches. We propose Anti-Causal Invariant Abstractions (ACIA), a novel measure-theoretic framework for anti-causal representation learning. ACIA employs a two-level design: low-level representations capture how labels generate observations, while high-level representations learn stable causal patterns across environment-specific variations. ACIA addresses key limitations of existing approaches by: (1) accommodating prefect and imperfect interventions through interventional kernels, (2) eliminating dependency on explicit causal structures, (3) handling high-dimensional data effectively, and (4) providing theoretical guarantees for out-of-distribution generalization. Experiments on synthetic and real-world medical datasets demonstrate that ACIA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and invariance metrics. Furthermore, our theoretical results establish tight bounds on performance gaps between training and unseen environments, confirming the efficacy of our approach for robust anti-causal learning. {{Code is available at \url{https://github.com/ArmanBehnam/ACIA}}}.

paragraphs: The paper studies representation learning in an anti-causal setting, where labels cause observed features. Its goal is to learn representations that remain useful when the environment changes. Anti-Causal Invariant Abstractions, or ACIA, provides a measure-theoretic framework for separating how observations are generated from the stable patterns that support predictions across environments.

ACIA uses two representation levels. The lower level captures how labels generate observations, while the higher level captures causal patterns that persist through environment-specific variation. Interventional kernels allow the framework to accommodate both perfect and imperfect interventions. The approach also avoids requiring an explicit causal structure and is designed to handle high-dimensional data.

The theoretical results provide guarantees for out-of-distribution generalization and tight bounds on performance differences between training and unseen environments. Experiments on synthetic data and real-world medical datasets report better accuracy and invariance than state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the two-level design within the anti-causal setting studied, connecting stable representations with both formal analysis and empirical performance.
summary.tldr: ACIA learns two levels of anti-causal representations to capture observation generation and stable patterns across changing environments.

title: Measure-Theoretic Anti-Causal Representation Learning

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental problem that has been extensively studied over past few decades, with most research focusing on point-based clustering such as $k$-means, $k$-median, and $k$-center. However, numerous real-world applications, such as motion analysis, computer vision, and missing data analysis, require clustering over structured data, including lines, time series and affine subspaces (flats), where traditional point-based clustering algorithms often fall short. In this paper, we study the $k$-means of lines problem, where the input is a set $L$ of lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ centers $C$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the sum of squared distances from each line in $L$ to its nearest center in $C$ is minimized. The local search algorithm is a well-established strategy for point-based $k$-means clustering, known for its efficiency and provable approximation guarantees. However, extending local search algorithm to the $k$-means of lines problem is nontrivial, as the capture relation used in point-based clustering does not generalize to the line setting. This is because that the point-to-line distance function lack the triangle inequality property that supports geometric analysis in point-based clustering. Moreover, since lines extend infinitely in space, it is difficult to identify effective swap points that can significantly reduce the clustering cost. To overcome above obstacles, we introduce a *proportional capture relation* that links optimal and current centers based the assignment proportions of lines, enabling a refined analysis that bypasses the triangle inequality barrier. We also introduce a *CrossLine* structure, which provides a principled discretization of the geometric space around line pairs, and ensures coverage of high-quality swap points essential for local search, thereby enabling effective execution of the local search process. Consequently, based on the proposed components, we develop the first single-swap local search algorithm for the $k$-means of lines problem, achieving a $(500+\varepsilon)$-approximation in polynomial time for low-dimensional Euclidean space.

The aim is to choose k centers that minimize the total squared distance from each line to its nearest center. This setting matters for applications involving structured geometric information, where methods developed for collections of points do not transfer straightforwardly.

The authors adapt local search, which improves a solution by replacing a center. Two obstacles make this difficult: point-to-line distances lack the triangle inequality needed by familiar analyses, and infinitely extending lines make useful replacement locations hard to identify. Their proportional capture relation connects current and optimal centers through line-assignment proportions. A second construction, CrossLine, discretizes space around pairs of lines while retaining high-quality replacement candidates.

Together, these components yield what the authors identify as the first single-swap local search algorithm for this problem. In low-dimensional Euclidean space, it runs in polynomial time and provides a 500-plus-epsilon approximation guarantee. That is a theoretical bound on solution quality relative to the optimum, rather than a reported typical error or empirical accuracy.
summary.tldr: A new geometric analysis enables polynomial-time single-swap local search with a 500-plus-epsilon approximation guarantee for clustering lines in low dimensions.

title: A Single-Swap Local Search Algorithm for k-Means of Lines

abstract: In many scientific experiments, the data annotating cost constraints the pace for testing novel hypotheses. Yet, modern machine learning pipelines offer a promising solution—provided their predictions yield correct conclusions. We focus on Prediction-Powered Causal Inferences (PPCI), i.e., estimating the treatment effect in an unlabeled target experiment, relying on training data with the same outcome annotated but potentially different treatment or effect modifiers. We first show that conditional calibration guarantees valid PPCI at population level. Then, we introduce a sufficient representation constraint transferring validity across experiments, which we propose to enforce in practice in Deconfounded Empirical Risk Minimization, our new model-agnostic training objective. We validate our method on synthetic and real-world scientific data, solving impossible problem instances for Empirical Risk Minimization even with standard invariance constraints. In particular, for the first time, we achieve valid causal inference on a scientific experiment with complex recording and no human annotations, fine-tuning a foundational model on our similar annotated experiment.

paragraphs: Scientific experiments can be slowed by the cost of labeling outcomes. This paper asks when predictions from a model trained on an annotated experiment can support valid treatment-effect estimates in another experiment whose outcomes are unlabeled. The outcome is shared across experiments, but treatments or factors that modify their effects may differ.

The authors first show that conditional calibration is sufficient for valid prediction-powered causal inference at the population level. They then introduce a sufficient constraint on learned representations that allows validity to transfer across experiments. Their proposed training objective, Deconfounded Empirical Risk Minimization, is model-agnostic and aims to enforce that constraint in practice.

Tests on synthetic and real scientific data address instances that ordinary empirical risk minimization cannot solve, even with standard invariance constraints. The authors also report valid causal inference for an experiment involving complex recordings without human annotations in that target experiment, using a foundation model fine-tuned on a similar annotated experiment. The result illustrates how a carefully trained predictor can support causal conclusions, beyond simply producing plausible outcome estimates.
summary.tldr: A calibration-based theory and deconfounded training objective support treatment-effect estimation in an unlabeled experiment using a related labeled experiment.

title: Prediction-Powered Causal Inferences

abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) marry modality-specific vision or audio encoders with a shared text decoder. While the encoder is compute- intensive but memory-light, the decoder is the opposite, yet state-of-the-art serving stacks still time-multiplex these complementary kernels, idling SMs or HBM in turn. We introduce SpaceServe, a serving system that space-multiplexes MLLMs: it decouples all modality encoders from the decoder, and co-locates them on the same GPU using fine-grained SM partitioning available in modern runtimes. abstract: Video reasoning, the task of enabling machines to infer from dynamic visual content through multi-step logic, is crucial for advanced AI. While the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) mechanism has enhanced reasoning in text-based tasks, its application to video understanding remains underexplored. This paper presents a systematic analysis revealing that CoT often degrades performance in video reasoning, generating verbose but misleading internal monologues, and leading to hallucinated visual details and overridden correct intuitions—a phenomenon we term "visual thinking drift." We explain this drift through a Bayesian lens, positing that CoT traces often diverge from actual visual evidence, instead amplifying internal biases or language priors, causing models to storytell rather than engage in grounded reasoning. To counteract this, we introduce Visual Evidence Reward (VER), a novel reinforcement learning framework that explicitly rewards the generation of reasoning traces that are verifiably grounded in visual evidence. Comprehensive evaluation across 10 diverse video understanding benchmarks demonstrates that our Video-VER model consistently achieves top performance. Our work sheds light on the distinct challenges of video-centric reasoning and encourages the development of AI that robustly grounds its inferences in visual evidence---for large multimodal models that not only "think before answering", but also "see while thinking".

Under this account, an increasingly elaborate explanation may reflect a plausible story rather than what happened on screen. This is presented as an explanation of the observed drift, not a claim that every reasoning trace has this problem.

To counter it, Visual Evidence Reward uses reinforcement learning to reward reasoning traces that can be verified against visual evidence. The resulting Video-VER model consistently achieves top performance across ten video-understanding benchmarks in the reported evaluation. The findings support training the evidential quality of intermediate reasoning, so that additional reasoning remains connected to the video instead of merely becoming more fluent or detailed.
summary.tldr: Video-VER rewards visually grounded reasoning to counter the misleading chain-of-thought drift observed in video-understanding models.

title: When Thinking Drifts: Evidential Grounding for Robust Video Reasoning

abstract: Probabilistic reasoning is a key aspect of both human and artificial intelligence that allows for handling uncertainty and ambiguity in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a new numerical reasoning task under uncertainty for large language models, focusing on estimating the privacy risk of user-generated documents containing privacy-sensitive information. We propose BRANCH, a new LLM methodology that estimates the $k$-privacy value of a text—the size of the population matching the given information. BRANCH factorizes a joint probability distribution of personal information as random variables. The probability of each factor in a population is estimated separately using a Bayesian network and combined to compute the final $k$-value. Our experiments show that this method successfully estimates the $k$-value 73% of the time, a 13% increase compared to o3-mini with chain-of-thought reasoning. We also find that LLM uncertainty is a good indicator for accuracy, as high variance predictions are 37.47% less accurate on average.

paragraphs: A document can disclose several pieces of personal information whose combination narrows the population it describes. This paper frames privacy-risk estimation as a numerical reasoning task under uncertainty. Its target is a text's k-privacy value: the number of people in a population who match the information given.

BRANCH estimates this value by treating personal attributes as random variables and factorizing their joint probability distribution. A Bayesian network structures the separate probability estimates, which are then combined to calculate the final k-value. The approach breaks the overall estimation problem into connected probabilistic parts, making the relationships among disclosed attributes part of the calculation.

In the reported experiments, BRANCH successfully estimates the k-value 73% of the time, described as a 13% increase over o3-mini using chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors also find that high-variance predictions are 37.47% less accurate on average. This observed relationship suggests that model uncertainty can help indicate estimation reliability. Together, the findings support structured probabilistic reasoning for this privacy task and show that prediction variability contains useful information about accuracy.
summary.tldr: BRANCH uses Bayesian probability decomposition to estimate how many people match sensitive text, with prediction variance providing an empirical signal of accuracy.

title: Probabilistic Reasoning with LLMs for Privacy Risk Estimation

abstract: Variational quantum algorithms hold the promise to address meaningful quantum problems already on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. In spite of the promise, they face the challenge of designing quantum circuits that both solve the target problem and comply with device limitations. Quantum architecture search (QAS) automates the design process of quantum circuits, with reinforcement learning (RL) emerging as a promising approach. Yet, RL-based QAS methods encounter significant scalability issues, as computational and training costs grow rapidly with the number of qubits, circuit depth, and hardware noise. To address these challenges, we introduce $\textit{TensorRL-QAS}$, {an improved} framework that combines tensor network methods with RL for QAS. By warm-starting the QAS with a matrix product state approximation of the target solution, TensorRL-QAS effectively narrows the search space to physically meaningful circuits and accelerates the convergence to the desired solution. Tested on several quantum chemistry problems of up to 12-qubit, TensorRL-QAS achieves up to a 10-fold reduction in CNOT count and circuit depth compared to baseline methods, while maintaining or surpassing chemical accuracy. It reduces classical optimizer function evaluation by up to 100-fold, accelerates training episodes by up to 98\%, and can achieve 50\% success probability for 10-qubit systems, far exceeding the $<$1\% rates of baseline. Robustness and versatility are demonstrated both in the noiseless and noisy scenarios, where we report a simulation of an 8-qubit system. Furthermore, TensorRL-QAS demonstrates effectiveness on systems on 20-qubit quantum systems, positioning it as a state-of-the-art quantum circuit discovery framework for near-term hardware and beyond.

title: TensorRL-QAS: Reinforcement learning with tensor networks for improved quantum architecture search

abstract: A critical bottleneck in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is sample inefficiency, as training high-performance agents often demands extensive environmental interactions. Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) mitigates this by building world models that simulate environmental dynamics and generate synthetic experience, improving sample efficiency. However, conventional world models process observations holistically, failing to decouple dynamic objects and temporal features from static backgrounds. This approach is computationally inefficient, especially for visual tasks where dynamic objects significantly influence rewards and decision-making performance. To address this, we introduce DyMoDreamer, a novel MBRL algorithm that incorporates a dynamic modulation mechanism to improve the extraction of dynamic features and enrich the temporal information. DyMoDreamer employs differential observations derived from a novel inter-frame differencing mask, explicitly encoding object-level motion cues and temporal dynamics. Dynamic modulation is modeled as stochastic categorical distributions and integrated into a recurrent state-space model (RSSM), enhancing the model's focus on reward-relevant dynamics. Experiments demonstrate that DyMoDreamer sets a new state-of-the-art on the Atari $100$k benchmark with a $156.6$\% mean human-normalized score, establishes a new record of $832$ on the DeepMind Visual Control Suite, and gains a $9.5$\% performance improvement after $1$M steps on the Crafter benchmark.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning reduces the need for real environmental interactions by learning a world model that generates simulated experience. In visual environments, however, processing the whole observation together can obscure the moving objects and temporal changes that matter for rewards. DyMoDreamer introduces a mechanism intended to make these dynamics more explicit within the learned model.

The method constructs differential observations using a mask derived from differences between frames. These observations encode object motion and temporal information. Dynamic modulation is represented through stochastic categorical distributions and incorporated into a recurrent state-space model. This connects the motion-focused representation with the model's evolving internal description of the environment.

On Crafter, performance improves by 9.5% after one million steps. These findings support the value of explicitly extracting changing visual features when building world models for decision-making.
summary.tldr: DyMoDreamer improves visual reinforcement learning by incorporating explicit motion cues into its world model.

title: DyMoDreamer: World Modeling with Dynamic Modulation

abstract: Speech Foundation Models encounter significant performance degradation when deployed in real-world scenarios involving acoustic domain shifts, such as background noise and speaker accents. Test-time adaptation (TTA) has recently emerged as a viable strategy to address such domain shifts at inference time without requiring access to source data or labels. However, existing TTA approaches, particularly those relying on backpropagation, are memory-intensive, limiting their applicability in speech tasks and resource-constrained settings. Although backpropagation-free methods offer improved efficiency, existing ones exhibit poor accuracy. This is because they are predominantly developed for vision tasks, which fundamentally differ from speech task formulations, noise characteristics, and model architecture, posing unique transferability challenges. In this paper, we introduce E-BAT, first Efficient BAckpropagation-free TTA framework designed explicitly for speech foundation models. E-BAT achieves a balance between adaptation effectiveness and memory efficiency through three key components: (i) lightweight prompt adaptation for a forward-pass-based feature alignment, (ii) a multi-scale loss to capture both global (utterance-level) and local distribution shifts (token-level) and (iii) a test-time exponential moving average mechanism for stable adaptation across utterances. Experiments conducted on four noisy speech datasets spanning sixteen acoustic conditions demonstrate consistent improvements, with 4.1\%--13.5% accuracy gains over backpropogation-free baselines and 2.0$\times$–6.4$\times$ GPU memory savings compared to backpropogation-based methods. By enabling scalable and robust adaptation under acoustic variability, this work paves the way for developing more efficient adaptation approaches for practical speech processing systems in real-world environments.

summary.tldr: E-BAT adapts speech models without backpropagation, improving accuracy over forward-only baselines while using less memory than backpropagation-based methods.

title: E-BATS: Efficient Backpropagation-Free Test-Time Adaptation for Speech Foundation Models

abstract: Event cameras provide asynchronous, low-latency, and high-dynamic-range visual signals, making them ideal for real-time perception tasks such as object detection. However, effectively modeling the temporal dynamics of event streams remains a core challenge. Most existing methods follow frame-based detection paradigms, applying temporal modules only at high-level features, which limits early-stage temporal modeling. Transformer-based approaches introduce global attention to capture long-range dependencies, but often add unnecessary complexity and overlook fine-grained temporal cues. In this paper, we propose a CNN-RNN hybrid framework that rethinks temporal modeling for event-based object detection. Our approach is based on two key insights: (1) introducing recurrent modules at lower spatial scales to preserve detailed temporal information where events are most dense, and (2) utilizing Decoupled Deformable-enhanced Recurrent Layers specifically designed according to the inherent motion characteristics of event cameras to extract multiple spatiotemporal features, and performing independent downsampling at multiple spatiotemporal scales to enable flexible, scale-aware representation learning. These multi-scale features are then fused via a feature pyramid network to produce robust detection outputs. Experiments on Gen1, 1 Mpx and eTram dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves superior accuracy over recent transformer-based models, highlighting the importance of precise temporal feature extraction in early stages. This work offers a new perspective on designing architectures for event-driven vision beyond attention-centric paradigms. Code: https://github.com/BIT-Vision/SATE.

paragraphs: Event cameras produce asynchronous visual signals with low latency and high dynamic range. Detecting objects from these streams requires careful treatment of timing. This paper argues that methods inherited from frame-based detection often introduce temporal processing too late, while global attention can add complexity without capturing the fine temporal cues that matter.

The proposed framework combines convolutional and recurrent networks. It introduces recurrent processing early enough to preserve detailed temporal information in event-dense features. Decoupled Deformable-enhanced Recurrent Layers extract multiple spatiotemporal features using a design informed by event-camera motion characteristics. Independent downsampling across multiple scales supports flexible representations, which a feature pyramid network combines into detection outputs.

Experiments on Gen1, 1 Mpx, and eTram show higher accuracy than recent transformer-based models. These results support the paper's central architectural argument: the placement and design of temporal feature extraction can matter greatly for event-based detection. The approach demonstrates the effectiveness of recurrent, scale-aware processing in the evaluated datasets, offering a direction beyond relying primarily on global attention.
summary.tldr: An early, scale-aware CNN–RNN temporal encoder improves event-camera object detection over recent transformer-based models on three datasets.

title: Rethinking Scale-Aware Temporal Encoding for Event-based Object Detection

abstract: We propose *feature perturbation*, a simple yet effective exploration strategy for contextual bandits that injects randomness directly into feature inputs, instead of randomizing unknown parameters or adding noise to rewards. Remarkably, this algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ worst-case regret bound for generalized linear contextual bandits, while avoiding the $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{3/2}\sqrt{T})$ regret typical of existing randomized bandit algorithms. Because our algorithm eschews parameter sampling, it is both computationally efficient and naturally extends to non-parametric or neural network models. We verify these advantages through empirical evaluations, demonstrating that feature perturbation not only surpasses existing methods but also unifies strong practical performance with the near-optimal regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit methods must explore possible choices while using the information already available to make rewarding decisions. This paper introduces feature perturbation, which creates exploratory behavior by adding randomness directly to input features. The method moves the source of randomness away from unknown model parameters or observed rewards.

For generalized linear contextual bandits, the authors prove a worst-case regret bound of roughly d times the square root of T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, d represents feature dimension and T the number of rounds. This improves the dimension dependence over the roughly d to the three-halves times square root of T bound typical of existing randomized bandit algorithms.

Because the algorithm avoids parameter sampling, the authors describe it as computationally efficient and naturally extendable to nonparametric and neural models. Empirical evaluations report stronger performance than existing methods. The theoretical guarantee is stated for generalized linear bandits, while the broader modeling flexibility concerns the exploration mechanism. Together, these results support perturbing inputs as a simple route to effective exploration with strong regret guarantees.
summary.tldr: Randomizing input features provides efficient bandit exploration with improved dimension dependence in generalized linear regret guarantees.

title: Exploration via Feature Perturbation in Contextual Bandits

abstract: Monitoring AIs at runtime can help us detect and stop harmful actions. In this paper, we study how to efficiently combine multiple runtime monitors into a single monitoring protocol. The protocol's objective is to maximize the probability of applying a safety intervention on misaligned outputs (i.e., maximize recall). Since running monitors and applying safety interventions are costly, the protocol also needs to adhere to an average-case budget constraint. Taking the monitors' performance and cost as given, we develop an algorithm to find the best protocol. The algorithm exhaustively searches over when and which monitors to call, and allocates safety interventions based on the Neyman-Pearson lemma. By focusing on likelihood ratios and strategically trading off spending on monitors against spending on interventions, we more than double our recall rate compared to a naive baseline in a code review setting. We also show that combining two monitors can Pareto dominate using either monitor alone. Our framework provides a principled methodology for combining existing monitors to detect undesirable behavior in cost-sensitive settings.

paragraphs: Runtime monitors examine AI outputs so that a system can intervene when it detects undesirable behavior. Using more monitors may improve detection, but both running checks and taking protective action have costs. This paper studies how to combine existing monitors while keeping average spending within a budget and maximizing the probability of intervening on misaligned outputs.

Taking each monitor's performance and cost as given, the authors develop an algorithm that searches exhaustively over which monitors to call and when. It allocates interventions using the Neyman-Pearson lemma, a statistical rule based on likelihood ratios. The resulting protocol balances spending on gathering evidence against spending on action once that evidence is available.

In a code review setting, the approach more than doubles recall relative to a naive baseline. The authors also show that combining two monitors can achieve a cost-and-detection trade-off that dominates either alone. These findings support treating monitor selection and intervention decisions as one optimization problem, with the strongest protocol depending on the supplied performance estimates and budget.
summary.tldr: Jointly optimizing monitor calls and safety interventions can improve detection while respecting an average cost budget.

title: Combining Cost Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety

abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) problems, central to decision-making scenarios like logistics and manufacturing, are traditionally solved using problem-specific algorithms requiring significant domain expertise. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating CO problem solving, existing approaches rely on intermediate steps such as code generation or solver invocation, limiting their generality and accessibility. This paper introduces a novel framework that empowers LLMs to serve as end-to-end CO solvers by directly mapping natural language problem descriptions to solutions. We propose a two-stage training strategy: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) imparts LLMs with solution construction patterns from domain-specific solvers, while a feasibility-and-optimality-aware reinforcement learning (FOARL) process explicitly mitigates constraint violations and refines solution quality. Evaluation across seven NP-hard CO problems shows that our method achieves a high feasibility rate and reduces the average optimality gap to 1.03–8.20% by tuning a 7B-parameter LLM, surpassing both general-purpose LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o), reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1), and domain-specific heuristics. Our method establishes a unified language-based pipeline for CO without extensive code execution or manual architectural adjustments for different problems, offering a general and language-driven alternative to traditional solver design while maintaining relative feasibility guarantees.

Our method establishes a unified language-based pipeline for CO without extensive code execution or manual architectural adjustments for different problems, offering a general and language-driven alternative to traditional solver design while maintaining relative feasibility guarantees.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization requires selecting a good solution while satisfying a problem’s constraints. This paper trains language models to produce solutions directly from natural-language problem descriptions. It targets the dependence of existing language-model approaches on intermediate code generation or external solver calls, aiming for a unified process across different optimization problems.

Training has two stages. Supervised fine-tuning teaches solution-construction patterns obtained from domain-specific solvers. A subsequent reinforcement learning stage explicitly considers feasibility and optimality, discouraging constraint violations while improving solution quality. This separates learning how to construct candidate solutions from further training them to meet constraints and achieve better objectives.

Across seven NP-hard problems, the tuned 7-billion-parameter model achieves high feasibility and reported average optimality gaps of 1.03–8.20%. It outperforms evaluated general-purpose language models, reasoning models, and domain-specific heuristics. These results support direct language-based optimization as an alternative to problem-specific pipelines, without requiring extensive code execution or manual architectural changes for each problem. High feasibility and small gaps describe the reported performance; they do not imply every output is feasible or exactly optimal.
summary.tldr: Two-stage training enables a 7B language model to directly solve seven combinatorial optimization problems with high feasibility and small reported optimality gaps.

title: Large Language Models as End-to-end Combinatorial Optimization Solvers

abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) seeks to render photorealistic, 3D‑consistent images of a scene from unseen camera poses given only a sparse set of posed views. Existing deterministic networks render observed regions quickly but blur unobserved areas, whereas stochastic diffusion‑based methods hallucinate plausible content yet incur heavy training‑ and inference‑time costs. In this paper, we propose a hybrid framework that unifies the strengths of both paradigms. A bidirectional transformer encodes multi‑view image tokens and Plücker‑ray embeddings, producing a shared latent representation. Two lightweight heads then act on this representation: (i) a feed‑forward regression head that renders pixels where geometry is well constrained, and (ii) a masked autoregressive diffusion head that completes occluded or unseen regions. The entire model is trained end‑to‑end with joint photometric and diffusion losses, without handcrafted 3D inductive biases, enabling scalability across diverse scenes. Experiments demonstrate that our method attains state‑of‑the‑art image quality while reducing rendering time by an order of magnitude compared with fully generative baselines.

paragraphs: Novel view synthesis creates images from camera positions absent from a sparse collection of observed views. Visible parts of a scene can support direct rendering, while hidden regions require plausible completion. UMAMI combines these capabilities to address the blur associated with deterministic rendering and the high computational cost of fully generative approaches.

A bidirectional transformer encodes image tokens from multiple views together with ray representations describing their viewing geometry. Two lightweight heads use the shared representation. A feed-forward regression head renders pixels where geometry is well constrained, while a masked autoregressive diffusion head completes occluded or unseen content. The model is trained jointly with photometric and diffusion losses, without handcrafted three-dimensional inductive biases.

Experiments report state-of-the-art image quality and an order-of-magnitude reduction in rendering time compared with fully generative baselines. The architectural division makes the reason for the efficiency gain clear: direct prediction and generative completion serve different parts of the rendering problem. A shared representation lets the model coordinate those functions within a single end-to-end training framework.
summary.tldr: UMAMI combines direct rendering with generative completion, achieving strong view-synthesis quality and an order-of-magnitude rendering speedup over fully generative baselines.

title: UMAMI: Unifying Masked Autoregressive Models and Deterministic Rendering for View Synthesis

abstract: Unsupervised learning of graphical models is an important task in many domains. Although maximum likelihood learning is computationally hard, there do exist consistent learning algorithms (e.g., psuedo-likelihood and its variants). However, inference in the learned models is still hard, and thus they are not directly usable. In other words, given a probabilistic query they are not guaranteed to provide an answer that is close to the true one. In the current paper, we provide a learning algorithm that is guaranteed to provide approximately correct probabilistic inference. We focus on a particular class of models, namely high girth graphs in the correlation decay regime. It is well known that approximate inference (e.g, using loopy BP) in such models yields marginals that are close to the true ones. Motivated by this, we propose an algorithm that always returns models of this type, and hence in the models it returns inference is approximately correct. We derive finite sample results guaranteeing that beyond a certain sample size, the resulting models will answer probabilistic queries with a high level of accuracy. Results on synthetic data show that the models we learn indeed outperform those obtained by other algorithms, which do not return high girth graphs.

paragraphs: Learning a probabilistic graphical model does not automatically make it useful for answering probabilistic questions. Even when a learning algorithm is statistically consistent, inference in its output can remain computationally difficult. This paper builds the requirements of approximate inference into the learning procedure itself.

The method always returns models with high-girth graphs in the correlation decay regime. High girth means the graphs lack short cycles, while correlation decay limits the persistence of dependence across distance. For this class, approximate inference methods such as loopy belief propagation are known to produce marginal probabilities close to the model’s true marginals.

The paper also derives finite-sample guarantees: beyond a specified sample-size threshold, learned models answer probabilistic queries with high accuracy. This connects the tractability of inference within the returned model to the statistical quality of the learned answers. Synthetic-data experiments show advantages over algorithms that do not return high-girth graphs. The guarantees depend on the restricted model class that makes reliable approximate inference possible.
summary.tldr: Learning high-girth graphical models in the correlation decay regime enables approximate inference guarantees and finite-sample guarantees for accurate probabilistic answers.

title: Inferning with High Girth Graphical Models

abstract: The cover tree data structure speeds up exact nearest neighbor queries over arbitrary metric spaces. This paper makes cover trees even faster. In particular, we provide (1) a simpler definition of the cover tree that reduces the number of nodes from O(n) to exactly n, (2) an additional invariant that makes queries faster in practice, (3) algorithms for constructing and querying the tree in parallel on multiprocessor systems, and (4) a more cache efficient memory layout. On standard benchmark datasets, we reduce the number of distance computations by 10–50%. On a large-scale bioinformatics dataset, we reduce the number of distance computations by 71%. On a large-scale image dataset, our parallel algorithm with 16 cores reduces tree construction time from 3.5 hours to 12 minutes.

paragraphs: Cover trees organize data to accelerate exact nearest-neighbor searches in arbitrary metric spaces. This paper improves their structure and implementation while retaining that exact-search purpose. The contribution combines a simpler tree definition, a new structural invariant, parallel algorithms, and a memory layout designed to use the cache more efficiently.

The revised definition gives a tree with exactly one node per data point, replacing an earlier linear-order node count with an exact count of n. The additional invariant helps queries run faster in practice. Parallel construction and querying exploit multiprocessor systems, while the memory-layout change addresses the cost of accessing the tree during computation.

The reported benchmarks show 10–50% fewer distance computations on standard datasets and 71% fewer on a large bioinformatics dataset. On a large image dataset, construction using 16 cores takes 12 minutes instead of 3.5 hours. These results demonstrate gains in both search work and construction time, with each numerical improvement tied to its stated evaluation setting.
summary.tldr: Structural, parallel, and memory-layout improvements make cover trees faster to construct and query while preserving exact nearest-neighbor search.

title: Faster cover trees

abstract: We describe a method for removing the effect of confounders in order to reconstruct a latent quantity of interest. The method, referred to as half-sibling regression , is inspired by recent work in causal inference using additive noise models. We provide a theoretical justification and illustrate the potential of the method in a challenging astronomy application.
originalAbstract: We describe a method for removing the effect of confounders in order to reconstruct a latent quantity of interest. The method, referred to as half-sibling regression , is inspired by recent work in causal inference using additive noise models. We provide a theoretical justification and illustrate the potential of the method in a challenging astronomy application.

paragraphs: Measurements can reflect both a quantity of scientific interest and the influence of confounding factors. This paper addresses the task of removing those confounding effects so that the underlying, unobserved quantity can be reconstructed. Its astronomy application concerns systematic errors in the search for exoplanets, where separating the desired signal from other influences is the motivating problem.

The proposed method is called half-sibling regression. It is inspired by causal inference research using additive noise models. This places the reconstruction problem in a causal framework: the method is concerned with the effects of confounders on observations and with recovering the latent quantity after accounting for those effects.

The authors provide a theoretical justification for the method and illustrate its potential through a challenging astronomy application. These are complementary contributions: the theory supports the proposed reconstruction approach, while the application shows its relevance to a scientific measurement problem. The stated finding is an illustration of potential, so the contribution should be understood as a justified method with a motivating demonstration rather than a claim of universal confounder removal.
summary.tldr: Half-sibling regression uses a causally motivated approach to remove confounding effects and reconstruct a latent scientific signal.

title: Removing systematic errors for exoplanet search via latent causes

abstract: An active learner is given a model class $\Theta$, a large sample of unlabeled data drawn from an underlying distribution and access to a labeling oracle that can provide a label for any of the unlabeled instances. The goal of the learner is to find a model $\theta \in \Theta$ that fits the data to a given accuracy while making as few label queries to the oracle as possible. In this work, we consider a theoretical analysis of the label requirement of active learning for regression under a heteroscedastic noise model, where the noise depends on the instance. We provide bounds on the convergence rates of active and passive learning for heteroscedastic regression. Our results illustrate that just like in binary classification, some partial knowledge of the nature of the noise can lead to significant gains in the label requirement of active learning.

The goal of the learner is to find a model $\theta \in \Theta$ that fits the data to a given accuracy while making as few label queries to the oracle as possible. paragraphs: Active regression asks which examples should receive labels when obtaining those labels is costly. The learner starts with many unlabeled examples, a collection of candidate models, and access to an oracle that supplies requested labels. Its aim is to reach a specified prediction accuracy while requesting as few labels as possible.

This paper studies that problem when noise varies across examples, a setting called heteroscedastic regression. Rather than treating every observation as equally noisy, the analysis allows the uncertainty in a label to depend on its input. The authors establish convergence-rate bounds for both active learning and passive learning, providing a theoretical basis for comparing their label requirements.

The central finding is that partial knowledge about the noise can substantially improve the label efficiency of active learning. This is a conditional opportunity: the benefit comes from having some information about how noise behaves. The results connect selective labeling in regression to similar gains already recognized in binary classification.
summary.tldr: Partial knowledge of input-dependent noise can substantially reduce the labels needed for active regression.

title: Active Heteroscedastic Regression

abstract: This paper focuses on convex constrained optimization problems, where the solution is subject to a convex inequality constraint. In particular, we aim at challenging problems for which both projection into the constrained domain and a linear optimization under the inequality constraint are time-consuming, which render both projected gradient methods and conditional gradient methods (a.k.a. the Frank-Wolfe algorithm) expensive. In this paper, we develop projection reduced optimization algorithms for both smooth and non-smooth optimization with improved convergence rates under a certain regularity condition of the constraint function. We first present a general theory of optimization with only one projection. Its application to smooth optimization with only one projection yields $O(1/\epsilon)$ iteration complexity, which improves over the $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ iteration complexity established before for non-smooth optimization and can be further reduced under strong convexity. Then we introduce a local error bound condition and develop faster algorithms for non-strongly convex optimization at the price of a logarithmic number of projections. In particular, we achieve an iteration complexity of $\widetilde O(1/\epsilon^{2(1-\theta)})$ for non-smooth optimization and $\widetilde O(1/\epsilon^{1-\theta})$ for smooth optimization, where $\theta\in(0,1]$ appearing the local error bound condition characterizes the functional local growth rate around the optimal solutions. Novel applications in solving the constrained $\ell_1$ minimization problem and a positive semi-definite constrained distance metric learning problem demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve significant speed-up compared with previous algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies convex optimization when enforcing the constraint is itself expensive. Projected gradient methods repeatedly move their estimates back into the permitted region, while conditional gradient methods solve related linear optimization problems. The authors target settings where both operations take substantial time, making the number of constraint-handling operations an important computational concern.

Under a regularity condition on the constraint function, they develop methods that require fewer projections. Their general framework permits optimization with just one projection. For smooth objectives, it achieves an iteration complexity of O(1/epsilon), with further improvements available under strong convexity. This distinguishes the cost of improving the objective from the cost of enforcing feasibility.

They also obtain faster rates for objectives without strong convexity by assuming a local error bound and allowing a logarithmic number of projections. The rates depend on smoothness and growth near optimal solutions. Applications to constrained l1 minimization and distance metric learning demonstrate substantial speed improvements over earlier algorithms.
summary.tldr: Under stated regularity and growth conditions, fewer projections can make constrained convex optimization faster.

title: A Richer Theory of Convex Constrained Optimization with Reduced Projections and Improved Rates

abstract: We analyze the performance of the greedy algorithm, and also a discrete semi-gradient based algorithm, for maximizing the sum of a suBmodular and suPermodular (BP) function (both of which are non-negative monotone non-decreasing) under two types of constraints, either a cardinality constraint or $p\geq 1$ matroid independence constraints. These problems occur naturally in several real-world applications in data science, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. The problems are ordinarily inapproximable to any factor. Using the curvature $\curv_f$ of the submodular term, and introducing $\curv^g$ for the supermodular term (a natural dual curvature for supermodular functions), however, both of which are computable in linear time, we show that BP maximization can be efficiently approximated by both the greedy and the semi-gradient based algorithm. The algorithms yield multiplicative guarantees of $\frac{1}{\curv_f}\left[1-e^{-(1-\curv^g)\curv_f}\right]$ and $\frac{1-\curv^g}{(1-\curv^g)\curv_f + p}$ for the two types of constraints respectively. For pure monotone supermodular constrained maximization, these yield $1-\curvg$ and $(1-\curvg)/p$ for the two types of constraints respectively. We also analyze the hardness of BP maximization and show that our guarantees match hardness by a constant factor and by $O(\ln(p))$ respectively. Computational experiments are also provided supporting our analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximization of a sum containing both a submodular term and a supermodular term. These capture diminishing and increasing returns, respectively, and both terms are assumed nonnegative and monotone. Feasible selections obey either a size limit or p matroid independence constraints. Without additional structure, these problems admit no general approximation factor.

The authors analyze a greedy algorithm and a discrete semi-gradient algorithm using curvature measures for the two terms. They introduce a dual curvature for the supermodular component, and both measures can be computed in linear time. The resulting multiplicative guarantees depend on these curvatures and on the constraint type, identifying when efficient approximation is possible.

For a purely supermodular objective, the guarantees simplify to one minus its curvature under a size constraint, and that quantity divided by p under matroid constraints. The authors also compare their guarantees with hardness results, matching them within a constant factor and an O(log p) factor, respectively. Computational experiments support the analysis, linking practical algorithms to measurable properties of the objective.
summary.tldr: Curvature-dependent guarantees show when greedy and semi-gradient methods can approximate constrained sums of monotone submodular and supermodular functions.

title: Greed is Still Good: Maximizing Monotone Submodular+Supermodular (BP) Functions

abstract: We present a mechanism to compute a sketch (succinct summary) of how a complex modular deep network processes its inputs. The sketch summarizes essential information about the inputs and outputs of the network and can be used to quickly identify key components and summary statistics of the inputs. Furthermore, the sketch is recursive and can be unrolled to identify sub-components of these components and so forth, capturing a potentially complicated DAG structure. These sketches erase gracefully; even if we erase a fraction of the sketch at random, the remainder still retains the “high-weight” information present in the original sketch. The sketches can also be organized in a repository to implicitly form a “knowledge graph”; it is possible to quickly retrieve sketches in the repository that are related to a sketch of interest; arranged in this fashion, the sketches can also be used to learn emerging concepts by looking for new clusters in sketch space. Finally, in the scenario where we want to learn a ground truth deep network, we show that augmenting input/output pairs with these sketches can theoretically make it easier to do so.

paragraphs: A complex modular network can process inputs through many interacting components. This paper proposes compact summaries, called sketches, that retain essential information about that processing and the network's inputs and outputs. The sketches support quick identification of important components and input summary statistics without requiring the full description to be inspected at once.

Their recursive structure allows a component's sketch to be unpacked into subcomponents, capturing potentially complicated directed acyclic graph relationships. They also retain high-weight information when a fraction of the sketch is erased at random. This graceful degradation makes the summary useful even when only part of its original content remains.

Collections of sketches can serve as an implicit knowledge graph, supporting retrieval of related sketches and discovery of emerging concepts through new clusters in sketch space. Finally, for the task of learning a ground-truth deep network, the authors show that adding sketches to input–output examples can theoretically make learning easier. The proposal thus connects compact representation, structured retrieval, and learning support.
summary.tldr: Recursive sketches compactly summarize modular network processing, support related-content retrieval, and can theoretically aid learning a ground-truth network.

title: Recursive Sketches for Modular Deep Learning

abstract: We quantify the separation between the numbers of labeled examples required to learn in two settings: Settings with and without the knowledge of the distribution of the unlabeled data. More specifically, we prove a separation by $\Theta(\log n)$ multiplicative factor for the class of projections over the Boolean hypercube of dimension $n$. We prove that there is no separation for the class of all functions on domain of any size. Learning with the knowledge of the distribution (a.k.a. fixed-distribution learning) can be viewed as an idealized scenario of semi-supervised learning where the number of unlabeled data points is so great that the unlabeled distribution is known exactly. For this reason, we call the separation the value of unlabeled data.
originalAbstract: We quantify the separation between the numbers of labeled examples required to learn in two settings: Settings with and without the knowledge of the distribution of the unlabeled data. More specifically, we prove a separation by $\Theta(\log n)$ multiplicative factor for the class of projections over the Boolean hypercube of dimension $n$. We prove that there is no separation for the class of all functions on domain of any size. Learning with the knowledge of the distribution (a.k.a. fixed-distribution learning) can be viewed as an idealized scenario of semi-supervised learning where the number of unlabeled data points is so great that the unlabeled distribution is known exactly. For this reason, we call the separation the value of unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Unlabeled data reveal how inputs are distributed without directly providing their desired outputs. This paper asks how much that knowledge can reduce the number of labeled examples needed for learning. It compares learning with and without exact knowledge of the input distribution, isolating the informational value of knowing where data come from.

For the class of projections on an n-dimensional Boolean hypercube, the authors prove a multiplicative separation of order log n in labeled sample requirements. For the class containing all functions on a domain of any size, they prove that there is no separation. These contrasting results show that the value of distribution knowledge depends on the class being learned.

Exact distribution knowledge is an idealized version of semi-supervised learning in which unlabeled data are sufficiently plentiful to reveal the distribution completely. The results therefore quantify the value of unlabeled information in that ideal setting. They establish that even this strong knowledge can help for one function class while providing no separation for another.
summary.tldr: Exact input-distribution knowledge yields a logarithmic labeled-sample separation for Boolean projections but none for the class of all functions.

title: The information-theoretic value of unlabeled data in semi-supervised learning

abstract: This work proposes the first set of simple, practically useful, and provable algorithms for two inter-related problems. (i) The first is low-rank matrix recovery from magnitude-only (phaseless) linear projections of each of its columns. This finds important applications in phaseless dynamic imaging, e.g., Fourier Ptychographic imaging of live biological specimens. Our guarantee shows that, in the regime of small ranks, the sample complexity required is only a little larger than the order-optimal one, and much smaller than what standard (unstructured) phase retrieval methods need. %Moreover our algorithm is fast and memory-efficient if only the minimum required number of measurements is used (ii) The second problem we study is a dynamic extension of the above: it allows the low-dimensional subspace from which each image/signal (each column of the low-rank matrix) is generated to change with time. We introduce a simple algorithm that is provably correct as long as the subspace changes are piecewise constant.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of a low-rank matrix when each column is observed only through magnitudes of linear projections. The missing phase information makes these measurements incomplete in a particular way. The low-rank structure supplies a relationship among columns that the proposed algorithms can use, with applications including dynamic imaging of live biological specimens.

For this recovery problem, the authors provide simple algorithms with theoretical guarantees. In the small-rank regime, the required sample complexity is only slightly above the order-optimal amount and substantially below the requirements of standard phase-retrieval methods that do not exploit the shared structure. The gain comes from treating the columns as a related low-rank collection.

The paper also considers a dynamic version in which the low-dimensional subspace generating the signals can change over time. It introduces an algorithm with a correctness guarantee when those changes are piecewise constant. This extends the recovery framework to changing signal collections while making the temporal assumption behind the guarantee explicit.
summary.tldr: Provable algorithms exploit low-rank structure to recover signals from magnitude-only measurements, including piecewise-constant subspace changes.

title: Phaseless PCA: Low-Rank Matrix Recovery from Column-wise Phaseless Measurements

abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. The literature is rich with algorithms that can easily craft successful adversarial examples. In contrast, the performance of defense techniques still lags behind. This paper proposes ME-Net, a defense method that leverages matrix estimation (ME). In ME-Net, images are preprocessed using two steps: first pixels are randomly dropped from the image; then, the image is reconstructed using ME. We show that this process destroys the adversarial structure of the noise, while re-enforcing the global structure in the original image. Since humans typically rely on such global structures in classifying images, the process makes the network mode compatible with human perception. We conduct comprehensive experiments on prevailing benchmarks such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and Tiny-ImageNet. Comparing ME-Net with state-of-the-art defense mechanisms shows that ME-Net consistently outperforms prior techniques, improving robustness against both black-box and white-box attacks.
