The preprocessing has two stages. It first removes randomly chosen pixels and then reconstructs the image using matrix estimation. The authors show that this process destroys the adversarial structure of the noise while reinforcing global structure in the original image. They connect that emphasis on global structure to human image classification, arguing that it makes the network's behavior more compatible with human perception.

The method is evaluated on MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and Tiny-ImageNet. Across the reported comparisons, ME-Net consistently improves on prior defenses against both black-box and white-box attacks. These findings provide empirical support for random pixel removal followed by structured reconstruction as an adversarial defense. The reported robustness improvements concern the evaluated attacks and benchmarks.
summary.tldr: ME-Net randomly removes pixels and reconstructs images with matrix estimation, improving adversarial robustness in the reported benchmark comparisons.

title: ME-Net: Towards Effective Adversarial Robustness with Matrix Estimation

abstract: This paper presents a new Graph Neural Network (GNN) type using feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). Many standard GNN variants propagate information along the edges of a graph by computing messages based only on the representation of the source of each edge. In GNN-FiLM, the representation of the target node of an edge is used to compute a transformation that can be applied to all incoming messages, allowing feature-wise modulation of the passed information. Different GNN architectures are compared in extensive experiments on three tasks from the literature, using re-implementations of many baseline methods. Hyperparameters for all methods were found using extensive search, yielding somewhat surprising results: differences between state of the art models are much smaller than reported in the literature and well-known simple baselines that are often not compared to perform better than recently proposed GNN variants. Nonetheless, GNN-FiLM outperforms these methods on a regression task on molecular graphs and performs competitively on other tasks.

GNN-FiLM adds a role for the receiving node: its representation determines a transformation applied to incoming messages, allowing the receiver to modulate individual features of the information it receives.

The paper also makes a substantial effort to compare architectures consistently. The authors reimplement many baseline methods and conduct extensive hyperparameter searches across three established tasks. Under this evaluation, differences among leading models are much smaller than earlier reports suggested. Familiar simple baselines, which are often omitted from comparisons, also outperform some more recently proposed GNN variants.

Against these carefully evaluated alternatives, GNN-FiLM performs best on a molecular graph regression task and remains competitive on the other tasks. The results support feature-wise modulation as a useful architectural choice without establishing that it wins everywhere. They also show why broad baseline coverage and thorough tuning matter when judging whether an architectural change provides a meaningful improvement.
summary.tldr: GNN-FiLM lets receiving nodes modulate incoming features and performs strongly in comparisons that also reveal the competitiveness of simple baselines.

title: GNN-FiLM: Graph Neural Networks with Feature-wise Linear Modulation

abstract: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference in discrete-valued Markov random fields is a fundamental problem in machine learning that involves identifying the most likely configuration of random variables given a distribution. Due to the difficulty of this combinatorial problem, linear programming (LP) relaxations are commonly used to derive specialized message passing algorithms that are often interpreted as coordinate descent on the dual LP. To achieve more desirable computational properties, a number of methods regularize the LP with an entropy term, leading to a class of smooth message passing algorithms with convergence guarantees. In this paper, we present randomized methods for accelerating these algorithms by leveraging techniques that underlie classical accelerated gradient methods. The proposed algorithms incorporate the familiar steps of standard smooth message passing algorithms, which can be viewed as coordinate minimization steps. We show that these accelerated variants achieve faster rates for finding $\epsilon$-optimal points of the unregularized problem, and, when the LP is tight, we prove that the proposed algorithms recover the true MAP solution in fewer iterations than standard message passing algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the most likely assignment of discrete variables in a Markov random field. This task, called MAP inference, is a difficult combinatorial optimization problem. A common approach replaces it with a linear programming relaxation and solves that easier problem through message passing. Adding entropy regularization produces smoother versions of these algorithms with convergence guarantees.

The authors develop randomized methods that accelerate this smooth message passing. Their approach draws on techniques behind classical accelerated gradient methods while retaining familiar message passing updates. These updates can be understood as minimizing over selected coordinates, so the contribution builds acceleration around operations already used by existing algorithms.

The theoretical results establish faster rates for reaching a specified accuracy on the original, unregularized optimization problem. They also establish faster recovery of the actual MAP assignment when the linear programming relaxation is tight. That condition matters: the guarantee of recovering the true discrete solution applies when the relaxation faithfully captures it.
summary.tldr: Randomized acceleration speeds up entropy-regularized message passing, with faster true MAP recovery when the linear programming relaxation is tight.

title: Accelerated Message Passing for Entropy-Regularized MAP Inference

abstract: Subsampling a signal of interest can reduce costly data transfer, battery drain, radiation exposure and acquisition time in a wide range of problems. The recently proposed Deep Probabilistic Subsampling (DPS) method effectively integrates subsampling in an end-to-end deep learning model, but learns a static pattern for all datapoints. We generalize DPS to a sequential method that actively picks the next sample based on the information acquired so far; dubbed Active-DPS (A-DPS). We validate that A-DPS improves over DPS for MNIST classification at high subsampling rates. Moreover, we demonstrate strong performance in active acquisition Magnetic Resonance Image (MRI) reconstruction, outperforming DPS and other deep learning methods.

paragraphs: Collecting only part of a signal can reduce acquisition time, data transfer, battery use, or radiation exposure, depending on the application. Deep Probabilistic Subsampling integrates the choice of measurements into a model trained from input to output. Its restriction is that the learned sampling pattern stays the same for every data point.

Active-DPS changes this into a sequential process. After obtaining some measurements, the method uses the information already collected to choose the next sample. This lets acquisition respond to the particular signal being examined. The contribution is an adaptive extension of the existing learned subsampling approach, linking successive measurement choices to what the model has observed.

The authors report improvements over the static method on MNIST classification at high subsampling rates. They also demonstrate strong results for actively acquiring measurements for MRI reconstruction, outperforming DPS and other deep learning methods in their evaluation. These findings support adapting acquisition to each example when only a subset of the signal is collected.
summary.tldr: Active-DPS chooses each new measurement using previously acquired information, improving reported classification and MRI reconstruction results over static subsampling.

title: Active Deep Probabilistic Subsampling

abstract: Maximizing a monotone submodular function is a fundamental task in machine learning. In this paper we study the deletion robust version of the problem under the classic matroids constraint. Here the goal is to extract a small size summary of the dataset that contains a high value independent set even after an adversary deleted some elements. We present constant-factor approximation algorithms, whose space complexity depends on the rank $k$ of the matroid and the number $d$ of deleted elements. In the centralized setting we present a $(3.582+O(\varepsilon))$-approximation algorithm with summary size $O(k + \frac{d}{\eps^2}\log \frac{k}{\eps})$. In the streaming setting we provide a $(5.582+O(\varepsilon))$-approximation algorithm with summary size and memory $O(k + \frac{d}{\eps^2}\log \frac{k}{\eps})$. We complement our theoretical results with an in-depth experimental analysis showing the effectiveness of our algorithms on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to retain a useful small summary when some of its elements may later be deleted by an adversary. Usefulness is measured by a monotone submodular objective, which captures increasing value with diminishing returns. A matroid constraint specifies which selected subsets are feasible. The summary must still contain a high-value feasible selection after deletions.

The authors give constant-factor approximation algorithms for centralized and streaming settings. Their storage requirements depend on the matroid rank k and the deletion budget d. Both use summary size O(k + (d/ε²) log(k/ε)); the streaming algorithm also has this memory bound. This makes the retained information explicitly responsive to both selection capacity and the number of losses it must withstand.

The centralized approximation factor is 3.582 + O(ε), while the streaming factor is 5.582 + O(ε). These are bounded-quality guarantees rather than promises of exact optimization after deletion. Experiments on real-world datasets also demonstrate effectiveness, complementing the theoretical tradeoff between compact storage and resilience.
summary.tldr: Compact summaries preserve provably good submodular selections under adversarial deletions, in both centralized and streaming settings.

title: Deletion Robust Submodular Maximization over Matroids

abstract: Data-driven model predictive control has two key advantages over model-free methods: a potential for improved sample efficiency through model learning, and better performance as computational budget for planning increases. However, it is both costly to plan over long horizons and challenging to obtain an accurate model of the environment. In this work, we combine the strengths of model-free and model-based methods. We use a learned task-oriented latent dynamics model for local trajectory optimization over a short horizon, and use a learned terminal value function to estimate long-term return, both of which are learned jointly by temporal difference learning. Our method, TD-MPC, achieves superior sample efficiency and asymptotic performance over prior work on both state and image-based continuous control tasks from DMControl and Meta-World. Code and videos are available at https://nicklashansen.github.io/td-mpc.

paragraphs: Model predictive control can use a learned environment model to plan actions, offering potential advantages in sample efficiency and benefits from additional planning computation. However, long planning horizons are costly, and accurate environment models are difficult to learn. TD-MPC combines short-horizon model-based planning with a learned estimate of longer-term value.

The method learns a task-oriented dynamics model in a latent representation and uses it for local trajectory optimization over a short horizon. At the end of that horizon, a terminal value function estimates the return that remains. Temporal difference learning trains the dynamics model and value function jointly, connecting the model used for near-term planning with the value estimate used beyond it.

Experiments on continuous-control tasks from DMControl and Meta-World cover both state-based and image-based observations. TD-MPC achieves better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than the compared prior work. These findings support dividing the planning problem between explicit short-term trajectory optimization and learned long-term evaluation, reducing reliance on costly long-horizon planning while retaining a model-based component.
summary.tldr: TD-MPC jointly learns a latent dynamics model and terminal value function to combine short-horizon planning with long-term return estimation.

title: Temporal Difference Learning for Model Predictive Control

abstract: In order to deploy deep models in a computationally efficient manner, model quantization approaches have been frequently used. In addition, as new hardware that supports various-bit arithmetic operations, recent research on mixed precision quantization (MPQ) begins to fully leverage the capacity of representation by searching various bitwidths for different layers and modules in a network. However, previous studies mainly search the MPQ strategy in a costly scheme using reinforcement learning, neural architecture search, etc., or simply utilize partial prior knowledge for bitwidth distribution, which might be biased and sub-optimal. In this work, we present a novel Stochastic Differentiable Quantization (SDQ) method that can automatically learn the MPQ strategy in a more flexible and globally-optimized space with a smoother gradient approximation. Particularly, Differentiable Bitwidth Parameters (DBPs) are employed as the probability factors in stochastic quantization between adjacent bitwidth. After the optimal MPQ strategy is acquired, we further train our network with the entropy-aware bin regularization and knowledge distillation. We extensively evaluate our method on different networks, hardwares (GPUs and FPGA), and datasets. SDQ outperforms all other state-of-the-art mixed or single precision quantization with less bitwidth, and are even better than the original full-precision counterparts across various ResNet and MobileNet families, demonstrating the effectiveness and superiority of our method. Code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used by a neural network to make deployment more efficient. Mixed-precision quantization assigns different bitwidths to different layers or modules. Finding those assignments can be costly, while selecting them from partial prior knowledge can introduce bias or yield suboptimal choices.

SDQ learns the precision strategy through stochastic differentiable quantization. Its differentiable bitwidth parameters determine probabilities for quantizing between adjacent bitwidths, providing a smoother gradient approximation for learning the assignments. After acquiring the strategy, the network receives further training with entropy-aware bin regularization and knowledge distillation. The approach thus combines learning where to allocate precision with subsequent refinement of the quantized network.

Across various ResNet and MobileNet families, results even exceed the original full-precision counterparts. These empirical findings support the effectiveness of jointly learning precision choices and refining the resulting low-precision model.
summary.tldr: SDQ learns mixed-precision bitwidths through stochastic differentiable quantization and reports strong accuracy at reduced precision.

title: SDQ: Stochastic Differentiable Quantization with Mixed Precision

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn policies that satisfy certain constraints before deploying them to safety-critical applications. Previous primal-dual style approaches suffer from instability issues and lack optimality guarantees. This paper overcomes the issues from the perspective of probabilistic inference. We introduce a novel Expectation-Maximization approach to naturally incorporate constraints during the policy learning: 1) a provable optimal non-parametric variational distribution could be computed in closed form after a convex optimization (E-step); 2) the policy parameter is improved within the trust region based on the optimal variational distribution (M-step). The proposed algorithm decomposes the safe RL problem into a convex optimization phase and a supervised learning phase, which yields a more stable training performance. A wide range of experiments on continuous robotic tasks shows that the proposed method achieves significantly better constraint satisfaction performance and better sample efficiency than baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/liuzuxin/cvpo-safe-rl.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning seeks policies that satisfy specified constraints before deployment. This paper approaches that problem through probabilistic inference, responding to instability and missing optimality guarantees in earlier primal-dual approaches. Its central idea is to separate finding a suitable constrained distribution from updating the parameterized policy that will act.

The method alternates two stages in an Expectation-Maximization procedure. In the E-step, a convex optimization leads to a closed-form, provably optimal non-parametric variational distribution. In the M-step, the policy is improved using that distribution while remaining within a trust region. The optimality statement concerns the variational distribution computed in the first stage.

This decomposition turns policy learning into a convex optimization phase followed by a supervised learning phase, yielding more stable training. Across the reported continuous robotic tasks, the method achieves better constraint satisfaction and sample efficiency than the evaluated baselines. The practical finding is that the inference-based decomposition can improve both compliance with constraints and how efficiently experience is used.
summary.tldr: An inference-based policy optimizer separates constrained distribution optimization from policy fitting, improving constraint satisfaction and sample efficiency in robotic experiments.

title: Constrained Variational Policy Optimization for Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Attributes skew hinders the current federated learning (FL) frameworks from consistent optimization directions among the clients, which inevitably leads to performance reduction and unstable convergence. The core problems lie in that: 1) Domain-specific attributes, which are non-causal and only locally valid, are indeliberately mixed into global aggregation. 2) The one-stage optimizations of entangled attributes cannot simultaneously satisfy two conflicting objectives, i.e., generalization and personalization. To cope with these, we proposed disentangled federated learning (DFL) to disentangle the domain-specific and cross-invariant attributes into two complementary branches, which are trained by the proposed alternating local-global optimization independently. Importantly, convergence analysis proves that the FL system can be stably converged even if incomplete client models participate in the global aggregation, which greatly expands the application scope of FL. Extensive experiments verify that DFL facilitates FL with higher performance, better interpretability, and faster convergence rate, compared with SOTA FL methods on both manually synthesized and realistic attributes skew datasets.

paragraphs: Clients in federated learning can differ in the attributes present in their local data. The paper argues that this attribute skew creates conflicting optimization directions when locally valid, non-causal attributes enter global aggregation. It also identifies a conflict between generalization and personalization when a single optimization stage handles these attributes together.

Disentangled federated learning separates domain-specific attributes and attributes that remain invariant across domains into two complementary branches. An alternating local-global optimization procedure trains the branches independently. This organization gives the model distinct places to handle local variation and shared information, directly addressing the mixing of attributes that the authors identify as a source of unstable learning.

The convergence analysis establishes that the system can converge stably even when incomplete client models take part in global aggregation. Experiments on both constructed and realistic attribute-skew datasets report higher performance, better interpretability, and faster convergence than the compared state-of-the-art federated methods. These results support separating the two kinds of attributes as a way to improve shared learning while retaining a role for client-specific information.
summary.tldr: DFL separates shared and domain-specific attributes into independently trained branches, improving federated learning under attribute skew in the reported experiments.

title: Disentangled Federated Learning for Tackling Attributes Skew via Invariant Aggregation and Diversity Transferring

abstract: Machine learning models can leak information about the data used to train them. To mitigate this issue, Differentially Private (DP) variants of optimization algorithms like Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) have been designed to trade-off utility for privacy in Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) problems. In this paper, we propose Differentially Private proximal Coordinate Descent (DP-CD), a new method to solve composite DP-ERM problems. We derive utility guarantees through a novel theoretical analysis of inexact coordinate descent. Our results show that, thanks to larger step sizes, DP-CD can exploit imbalance in gradient coordinates to outperform DP-SGD. We also prove new lower bounds for composite DP-ERM under coordinate-wise regularity assumptions, that are nearly matched by DP-CD. For practical implementations, we propose to clip gradients using coordinate-wise thresholds that emerge from our theory, avoiding costly hyperparameter tuning. Experiments on real and synthetic data support our results, and show that DP-CD compares favorably with DP-SGD.

paragraphs: Training a model can expose information about its training data, so private optimization must balance predictive usefulness with privacy protection. This paper proposes differentially private proximal coordinate descent, or DP-CD, for composite empirical risk minimization. Its central idea is to exploit differences between gradient coordinates when designing private optimization steps.

The authors develop an analysis of inexact coordinate descent that yields utility guarantees. Their results show that larger step sizes allow DP-CD to benefit from imbalance across gradient coordinates and potentially outperform private stochastic gradient descent. They also establish lower bounds under coordinate-wise regularity assumptions, which DP-CD nearly matches. These bounds help characterize how much improvement is possible within that setting.

For implementation, the theory supplies separate gradient-clipping thresholds for individual coordinates, avoiding costly tuning of those thresholds. Experiments using real and synthetic data support the theoretical findings and compare favorably with DP-SGD. The contribution ties together an optimization method, an account of when coordinate imbalance helps, and a practical rule for configuring gradient clipping.
summary.tldr: Private coordinate descent can exploit gradient imbalance to improve utility, with near-matching lower bounds and theory-guided clipping thresholds.

title: Differentially Private Coordinate Descent for Composite Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms often suffer from an exponential sample complexity dependence on the number of agents, a phenomenon known as the curse of multiagents . We address this challenge by investigating sample-efficient model-free algorithms in decentralized MARL, and aim to improve existing algorithms along this line. For learning (coarse) correlated equilibria in general-sum Markov games, we propose stage-based V-learning algorithms that significantly simplify the algorithmic design and analysis of recent works, and circumvent a rather complicated no- weighted -regret bandit subroutine. For learning Nash equilibria in Markov potential games, we propose an independent policy gradient algorithm with a decentralized momentum-based variance reduction technique. All our algorithms are decentralized in that each agent can make decisions based on only its local information. Neither communication nor centralized coordination is required during learning, leading to a natural generalization to a large number of agents. Finally, we provide numerical simulations to corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Learning with many interacting agents can require a number of samples that grows exponentially with the number of participants. This paper investigates sample-efficient, model-free reinforcement learning algorithms that work without centralized coordination. It considers different equilibrium objectives in different classes of Markov games rather than proposing one algorithm for every setting.

For general-sum Markov games, the authors develop stage-based V-learning methods for learning correlated or coarse correlated equilibria. These simplify earlier designs and analyses by avoiding a complicated weighted-regret bandit subroutine. For Markov potential games, they instead propose independent policy gradient with a decentralized, momentum-based technique for reducing variance, targeting Nash equilibria.

Each agent uses only local information to make decisions. Learning requires neither communication between agents nor a central coordinator, making the approach naturally applicable to larger groups. Numerical simulations corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution combines simpler algorithms for one equilibrium-learning problem with a variance-reduced method for another, while maintaining the same decentralized information requirement across both.
summary.tldr: The paper develops simpler and sample-efficient equilibrium-learning algorithms in which agents learn from local information without communication.

title: On Improving Model-Free Algorithms for Decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) method has been shown to be a powerful method for solving the optimization problem where explicit expression of the gradients is difficult or infeasible to obtain. Recently, due to the practical value of the constrained problems, a lot of ZO Frank-Wolfe or projected ZO methods have been proposed. However, in many applications, we may have a very large number of nonconvex white/black-box constraints, which makes the existing zeroth-order methods extremely inefficient (or even not working) since they need to inquire function value of all the constraints and project the solution to the complicated feasible set. In this paper, to solve the nonconvex problem with a large number of white/black-box constraints, we proposed a doubly stochastic zeroth-order gradient method (DSZOG) with momentum method and adaptive step size. Theoretically, we prove DSZOG can converge to the $\epsilon$-stationary point of the constrained problem. Experimental results in two applications demonstrate the superiority of our method in terms of training time and accuracy compared with other ZO methods for the constrained problem.

Experimental results in two applications demonstrate the superiority of our method in terms of training time and accuracy compared with other ZO methods for the constrained problem.

paragraphs: Gradient-free optimization is useful when derivatives are difficult or impossible to obtain. Constraints make this harder, especially when there are many nonconvex restrictions defined by explicit formulas or black-box evaluations. Existing approaches can become inefficient because they evaluate every constraint or project candidate solutions onto a complicated feasible set.

The paper proposes DSZOG, a doubly stochastic zeroth-order gradient method for this heavily constrained setting. It combines momentum with an adaptive step size. The method is designed to address the computational obstacles created by numerous white-box or black-box constraints while operating without directly available gradients.

The authors prove convergence to an ε-stationary point of the constrained problem, an approximate stationarity guarantee rather than a guarantee of global optimality. They also evaluate the method in two applications, reporting better training time and accuracy than other constrained zeroth-order methods. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support its use for nonconvex problems where derivative access and constraint-handling costs are both important obstacles.
summary.tldr: DSZOG combines gradient-free stochastic updates, momentum, and adaptive step sizes to handle nonconvex problems with many constraints.

title: Gradient-Free Method for Heavily Constrained Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Large amounts of efforts have been devoted into learning counterfactual treatment outcome under various settings, including binary/continuous/multiple treatments. Most of these literature aims to minimize the estimation error of counterfactual outcome for the whole treatment space. However, in most scenarios when the counterfactual prediction model is utilized to assist decision-making, people are only concerned with the small fraction of treatments that can potentially induce superior outcome (i.e. outcome-oriented treatments). This gap of objective is even more severe when the number of possible treatments is large, for example under the continuous treatment setting. To overcome it, we establish a new objective of optimizing counterfactual prediction on outcome-oriented treatments, propose a novel Outcome-Oriented Sample Re-weighting (OOSR) method to make the predictive model concentrate more on outcome-oriented treatments, and theoretically analyze that our method can improve treatment selection towards the optimal one. Extensive experimental results on both synthetic datasets and semi-synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Counterfactual prediction estimates what outcome a treatment would produce, including treatments that were not actually taken. Many learning objectives seek accurate predictions across the entire treatment space. The paper argues that this can misalign with decision making, where attention often centers on a small set of treatments capable of producing especially good outcomes.

The authors define an objective focused on these outcome-oriented treatments and introduce Outcome-Oriented Sample Re-weighting. The method changes the influence of training samples so that the predictor concentrates more on promising treatments. This objective mismatch becomes especially consequential when many choices are available, as in a continuous treatment space.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method can improve treatment selection toward the optimal choice. Experiments using synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets support its effectiveness. The central contribution is to connect predictive training more closely to the decision it supports: errors around promising options can matter differently from errors spread across all possible treatments.
summary.tldr: Outcome-Oriented Sample Re-weighting focuses counterfactual prediction on promising treatments to improve treatment selection.

title: Counterfactual Prediction for Outcome-Oriented Treatments

abstract: Unlearning algorithms aim to remove deleted data’s influence from trained models at a cost lower than full retraining. However, prior guarantees of unlearning in literature are flawed and don’t protect the privacy of deleted records. We show that when people delete their data as a function of published models, records in a database become interdependent. So, even retraining a fresh model after deletion of a record doesn’t ensure its privacy. Secondly, unlearning algorithms that cache partial computations to speed up the processing can leak deleted information over a series of releases, violating the privacy of deleted records in the long run. To address these, we propose a sound deletion guarantee and show that ensuring the privacy of existing records is necessary for the privacy of deleted records. Under this notion, we propose an optimal, computationally efficient, and sound machine unlearning algorithm based on noisy gradient descent.

This paper argues that prior unlearning guarantees fail to protect deleted records' privacy. It identifies problems that arise when deletion decisions and successive model releases are considered together, expanding the question beyond a single update to a model.

Such decisions create dependencies among records, so even training a fresh model after deletion does not ensure privacy. A second problem concerns algorithms that retain partial computations to accelerate later updates: across a sequence of releases, those cached computations can expose information about deleted records.

The authors propose a deletion guarantee that addresses these issues and show that, under this notion, protecting existing records is necessary to protect deleted ones. They also provide an optimal, computationally efficient unlearning algorithm based on noisy gradient descent. The contribution links deletion privacy to the broader training and release process, rather than assessing only whether the deleted record remains in the current training dataset.
summary.tldr: The paper exposes privacy failures in prior unlearning guarantees and develops a stronger deletion guarantee with an efficient noisy-gradient algorithm.

title: Forget Unlearning: Towards True Data-Deletion in Machine Learning

abstract: This paper studies federated linear contextual bandits under the notion of user-level differential privacy (DP). We first introduce a unified federated bandits framework that can accommodate various definitions of DP in the sequential decision-making setting. We then formally introduce user-level central DP (CDP) and local DP (LDP) in the federated bandits framework, and investigate the fundamental trade-offs between the learning regrets and the corresponding DP guarantees in a federated linear contextual bandits model. For CDP, we propose a federated algorithm termed as $\texttt{ROBIN}$ and show that it is near-optimal in terms of the number of clients $M$ and the privacy budget $\varepsilon$ by deriving nearly-matching upper and lower regret bounds when user-level DP is satisfied. For LDP, we obtain several lower bounds, indicating that learning under user-level $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-LDP must suffer a regret blow-up factor at least $\min\{1/\varepsilon,M\}$ or $\min\{1/\sqrt{\varepsilon},\sqrt{M}\}$ under different conditions.

paragraphs: Federated contextual bandits combine learning across clients with repeated decisions informed by contextual features. This paper asks how much learning performance must suffer when privacy protects an entire user’s contribution. It introduces a common framework for defining privacy in this sequential setting and studies both central and local differential privacy.

For central privacy, the authors propose an algorithm called ROBIN. They derive upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match in their dependence on the number of clients and the privacy budget. This establishes near-optimality with respect to those quantities: the algorithm’s dependence is close to what the accompanying lower bounds permit.

For local privacy, the paper instead establishes several lower bounds on the additional regret required. Under different conditions, the blow-up is at least min{1/ε, M} or min{1/√ε, √M}, where M is the client count and ε is the privacy budget. These are conditional alternatives, not a single universal formula. The results make the learning cost of different user-level privacy definitions mathematically explicit.
summary.tldr: ROBIN nearly matches central user-level privacy regret limits, while lower bounds reveal conditional performance costs under local privacy.

title: Federated Linear Contextual Bandits with User-level Differential Privacy

abstract: In recent years, there has been a significant amount of research focused on expanding the expressivity of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) beyond the Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) framework. While many of these studies have yielded advancements in expressivity, they have frequently come at the expense of decreased efficiency or have been restricted to specific types of graphs. In this study, we investigate the expressivity of GNNs from the perspective of graph search. Specifically, we propose a new vertex colouring scheme and demonstrate that classical search algorithms can efficiently compute graph representations that extend beyond the 1-WL. We show the colouring scheme inherits useful properties from graph search that can help solve problems like graph biconnectivity. Furthermore, we show that under certain conditions, the expressivity of GNNs increases hierarchically with the radius of the search neighbourhood. To further investigate the proposed scheme, we develop a new type of GNN based on two search strategies, breadth-first search and depth-first search, highlighting the graph properties they can capture on top of 1-WL. Our code is available at https://github.com/seanli3/lvc.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often evaluated against the expressive power of the first Weisfeiler–Lehman procedure, or 1-WL. Methods that go beyond this reference can sacrifice efficiency or apply only to particular graph types. This paper approaches the problem through graph search, examining what structural information classical search procedures can contribute to learned graph representations.

The authors propose a vertex-colouring scheme and show that search algorithms can efficiently compute representations exceeding 1-WL. The scheme inherits structural properties of graph search that can help with problems such as graph biconnectivity. They also establish that, under certain conditions, increasing the radius of the searched neighborhood produces a hierarchy of increasing expressive power.

The paper develops graph neural networks using breadth-first and depth-first search to investigate the scheme further. These variants expose graph properties that can be captured beyond 1-WL. The contribution connects familiar search procedures to stronger graph representations while explicitly qualifying the conditions under which a larger search neighborhood increases expressivity.
summary.tldr: Search-based vertex colouring gives graph neural networks expressive power beyond 1-WL, with a conditional hierarchy as search neighborhoods expand.

title: Local Vertex Colouring Graph Neural Networks

abstract: This work considers the fundamental problem of learning an unknown object from training data using a given model class. We introduce a framework that allows for objects in arbitrary Hilbert spaces, general types of (random) linear measurements as training data and general types of nonlinear model classes. We establish a series of learning guarantees for this framework, which provide explicit relations between the amount of training data and the model class to ensure near-best generalization bounds. In doing so, we introduce the key notion of the variation of a model class with respect to a distribution of sampling operators. We show that this framework can accommodate many different types of well-known problems of interest, such as matrix sketching by random sampling, compressed sensing with isotropic vectors, active learning in regression and compressed sensing with generative models. In all cases, known results become straightforward corollaries of our general theory. Hence, this work provides a powerful framework for studying and analyzing many different types of learning problems.

paragraphs: Many learning problems reconstruct an unknown object from measurements while restricting the answer to a chosen model class. This paper builds a common mathematical framework for such problems. It accommodates objects in arbitrary Hilbert spaces, random linear measurements, and nonlinear model classes, allowing different reconstruction settings to be studied within the same theory.

The central guarantees relate the amount of training data to the model class needed for near-best generalization bounds. Near-best performance is relative to what the chosen class can represent. A key concept is the variation of a model class with respect to the sampling-operator distribution, which links the candidate models to the way measurements are collected.

The framework includes matrix sketching through random sampling, compressed sensing with isotropic vectors, active regression learning, and compressed sensing with generative models. Known results in these settings follow as corollaries of the broader theory. Its contribution is therefore a shared analytical foundation: apparently different learning problems can be connected through the relationship between measurements, model structure, and required data.
summary.tldr: A unified theory connects linear measurement schemes and nonlinear model classes to data requirements for near-best generalization.

title: A Unified Framework for Learning with Nonlinear Model Classes from Arbitrary Linear Samples

abstract: While neural networks allow highly accurate predictions in many tasks, their lack of robustness towards even slight input perturbations often hampers their deployment. Adversarial attacks such as the seminal projected gradient descent (PGD) offer an effective means to evaluate a model’s robustness and dedicated solutions have been proposed for attacks on semantic segmentation or optical flow estimation. While they attempt to increase the attack’s efficiency, a further objective is to balance its effect, so that it acts on the entire image domain instead of isolated point-wise predictions. This often comes at the cost of optimization stability and thus efficiency. Here, we propose CosPGD, an attack that encourages more balanced errors over the entire image domain while increasing the attack’s overall efficiency. To this end, CosPGD leverages a simple alignment score computed from any pixel-wise prediction and its target to scale the loss in a smooth and fully differentiable way. It leads to efficient evaluations of a model’s robustness for semantic segmentation as well as regression models (such as optical flow, disparity estimation, or image restoration), and it allows it to outperform the previous SotA attack on semantic segmentation. We provide code for the CosPGD algorithm and example usage at https://github.com/shashankskagnihotri/cospgd.

paragraphs: Models that predict something at every image pixel can be vulnerable to small input changes. Testing that vulnerability requires attacks that meaningfully challenge predictions across the image. Existing approaches can concentrate errors on isolated pixels, while attempts to distribute their effects more broadly can make optimization less stable and less efficient.

CosPGD addresses this trade-off by modifying how the attack loss is weighted. It computes an alignment score between each pixel-wise prediction and its target, then uses that score to scale the loss smoothly. Because this operation is fully differentiable, it fits into gradient-based attack optimization while encouraging errors to be spread more evenly across the image.

The method supports robustness evaluation for semantic segmentation and regression tasks, including optical flow, disparity estimation, and image restoration. The authors report improved attack efficiency and performance beyond the previous leading segmentation attack. Its significance is a shared attack mechanism that works with several forms of pixel-level output, rather than requiring a separate construction for each task.
summary.tldr: CosPGD smoothly reweights pixel-level attack losses to produce more balanced errors and more efficient robustness evaluations.

title: CosPGD: an efficient white-box adversarial attack for pixel-wise prediction tasks

abstract: Despite the rich line of research works on out-of-distribution (OOD) detection on images, the literature on OOD detection for interdependent data, e.g., graphs, is still relatively limited. To fill this gap, we introduce TopoOOD as a principled approach that accommodates graph topology and neighborhood context for detecting OOD node instances on graphs. Meanwhile, we enrich the experiment settings by splitting in-distribution (ID) and OOD data based on distinct topological distributions, which presents new benchmarks for a more comprehensive analysis of graph-based OOD detection. The latter is designed to thoroughly assess the performance of these discriminators under distribution shifts involving structural information, providing a rigorous evaluation of methods in the emerging area of OOD detection on graphs. Our experimental results show the competitiveness of the proposed model across multiple datasets, as evidenced by up to a 15% increase in the AUROC and a 50% decrease in the FPR compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Detecting an unusual node in a graph requires considering its relationships with other nodes. This paper introduces TopoOOD, an approach to out-of-distribution detection that incorporates graph topology and neighborhood context. The goal is to identify node instances that differ from the distribution treated as familiar by the model.

The work also changes how graph detectors are evaluated. The authors construct benchmarks that separate familiar and unfamiliar data according to distinct topological distributions. This explicitly tests distribution shifts involving structural information. Such evaluation matters because a detector’s ability to recognize unfamiliar graph relationships is part of its intended job, and the benchmark makes that ability a direct object of study.

Across multiple datasets, TopoOOD is reported to be competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. The abstract reports improvements of up to 15% in AUROC and reductions of up to 50% in false-positive rate. These are maximum reported gains, rather than uniform improvements across every evaluation. Together, the method and benchmarks put neighborhood structure at the center of both graph anomaly detection and its assessment.
summary.tldr: TopoOOD uses graph structure and neighborhood context to detect unfamiliar nodes, with new benchmarks explicitly testing structural distribution shifts.

title: Graph Out-of-Distribution Detection Goes Neighborhood Shaping

abstract: We introduce the first model-stealing attack that extracts precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s PaLM-2. Specifically, our attack recovers the embedding projection layer (up to symmetries) of a transformer model, given typical API access. For under $20 USD, our attack extracts the entire projection matrix of OpenAI’s Ada and Babbage language models. We thereby confirm, for the first time, that these black-box models have a hidden dimension of 1024 and 2048, respectively. We also recover the exact hidden dimension size of the GPT-3.5-turbo model, and estimate it would cost under \$2,000 in queries to recover the entire projection matrix. We conclude with potential defenses and mitigations, and discuss the implications of possible future work that could extend our attack.

That cost is an estimate, distinct from the completed extractions. The paper also discusses potential defenses and mitigations, along with possible future extensions. Its central finding is that black-box access can expose more internal model information than merely observable behavior.
summary.tldr: Typical API access enabled recovery of production language models’ projection layers up to symmetries and exposed hidden dimensions.

title: Stealing part of a production language model

abstract: In this work, we propose MagicPose, a diffusion-based model for 2D human pose and facial expression retargeting. Specifically, given a reference image, we aim to generate a person’s new images by controlling the poses and facial expressions while keeping the identity unchanged. To this end, we propose a two-stage training strategy to disentangle human motions and appearance (e.g., facial expressions, skin tone, and dressing), consisting of (1) the pre-training of an appearance-control block and (2) learning appearance-disentangled pose control. Our novel design enables robust appearance control over generated human images, including body, facial attributes, and even background. By leveraging the prior knowledge of image diffusion models, MagicPose generalizes well to unseen human identities and complex poses without the need for additional fine-tuning. Moreover, the proposed model is easy to use and can be considered as a plug-in module/extension to Stable Diffusion. The project website is here. The code is available here.

paragraphs: MagicPose addresses the problem of generating new images of a person from a reference image while controlling their pose and facial expression. The intended result preserves the person’s identity as their depicted movement changes. The method uses a diffusion model for this two-dimensional retargeting task, drawing on existing image-generation knowledge.

The authors introduce a two-stage training strategy to separate motion control from appearance. First, they pretrain a block responsible for appearance control. They then learn pose control that is disentangled from appearance. This separation is designed to support changes in movement while retaining control over visual attributes, including the body, face, clothing-related appearance, and even the background.

The paper reports robust appearance control and good generalization to unseen identities and complex poses without additional finetuning. That matters for using a reference image of a new person without separately adapting the model to that individual. MagicPose can also serve as a plug-in or extension to Stable Diffusion, making the proposed control mechanism usable within that image-generation framework.
summary.tldr: MagicPose separates appearance and motion control to retarget human poses and expressions while preserving identity from a reference image.

title: MagicPose: Realistic Human Poses and Facial Expressions Retargeting with Identity-aware Diffusion

abstract: Complex physical systems are often described by partial differential equations (PDEs) that depend on parameters such as the Raynolds number in fluid mechanics. In applications such as design optimization or uncertainty quantification, solutions of those PDEs need to be evaluated at numerous points in the parameter space. While physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a new strong competitor as a surrogate, their usage in this scenario remains underexplored due to the inherent need for repetitive and time-consuming training. In this paper, we address this problem by proposing a novel extension, parameterized physics-informed neural networks (P$^2$INNs). P$^2$INNs enable modeling the solutions of parameterized PDEs via explicitly encoding a latent representation of PDE parameters. With the extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that P$^2$INNs outperform the baselines both in accuracy and parameter efficiency on benchmark 1D and 2D parameterized PDEs and are also effective in overcoming the known “failure modes”.

paragraphs: Many physical equations describe a family of systems whose behavior changes with parameters, such as the Reynolds number in fluid mechanics. Design optimization and uncertainty quantification may require evaluating solutions at many parameter settings. Physics-informed neural networks offer surrogate solutions, but repeated, time-consuming training makes this use case challenging.

Parameterized Physics-informed Neural Networks, or P²INNs, extend the approach by explicitly encoding a latent representation of the equation parameters. This gives parameter dependence a dedicated role in the model's representation. The aim is to model solutions across the parameterized problem, addressing the repeated-training burden that motivates the work.

Extensive experiments on one- and two-dimensional parameterized PDE benchmarks show better accuracy and parameter efficiency than the evaluated baselines. The method also proves effective against known failure modes in those evaluations. These results support explicit parameter encoding as a useful design choice for physics-informed surrogates, particularly when the application requires solutions at numerous points in a parameter space.
summary.tldr: P²INNs explicitly encode equation parameters to improve accuracy and parameter efficiency when modeling families of PDE solutions.

title: Parameterized Physics-informed Neural Networks for Parameterized PDEs

abstract: In this paper, we focus on the problem of conformal prediction with conditional guarantees. Prior work has shown that it is impossible to construct nontrivial prediction sets with full conditional coverage guarantees. A wealth of research has considered relaxations of full conditional guarantees, relying on some predefined uncertainty structures. Departing from this line of thinking, we propose Partition Learning Conformal Prediction (PLCP), a framework to improve conditional validity of prediction sets through learning uncertainty-guided features from the calibration data. We implement PLCP efficiently with alternating gradient descent, utilizing off-the-shelf machine learning models. We further analyze PLCP theoretically and provide conditional guarantees for infinite and finite sample sizes. Finally, our experimental results over four real-world and synthetic datasets show the superior performance of PLCP compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of coverage and length in both classification and regression scenarios.

paragraphs: Prediction sets express uncertainty by returning multiple plausible outcomes rather than one answer. Conditional coverage asks whether their reliability holds under particular input conditions. Full conditional guarantees for nontrivial sets are impossible in general, so researchers study relaxed versions. This paper asks whether learning uncertainty structure can improve those relaxed guarantees.

Partition Learning Conformal Prediction, or PLCP, learns uncertainty-guided features from calibration data. This differs from approaches that start with a predefined uncertainty structure. The framework uses alternating gradient descent and existing machine learning models, making the learned structure part of the procedure for constructing prediction sets rather than something fixed in advance.

The authors analyze PLCP theoretically and establish conditional guarantees for both finite and infinite sample sizes. Experiments across four real-world and synthetic datasets report better coverage and length performance than state-of-the-art methods in classification and regression. These findings support learning how uncertainty varies across inputs. They should be understood within the paper’s conditional-guarantee framework, which does not remove the general impossibility of unrestricted full conditional coverage.
summary.tldr: PLCP learns uncertainty-guided features from calibration data to improve prediction sets and provide conditional coverage guarantees.

title: Conformal Prediction with Learned Features

abstract: This paper studies the performative prediction problem where a learner aims to minimize the expected loss with a decision-dependent data distribution. Such setting is motivated when outcomes can be affected by the prediction model, e.g., in strategic classification. We consider a state-dependent setting where the data distribution evolves according to an underlying controlled Markov chain. We focus on stochastic derivative free optimization (DFO) where the learner is given access to a loss function evaluation oracle with the above Markovian data. We propose a two-timescale DFO($\lambda$) algorithm that features (i) a sample accumulation mechanism that utilizes every observed sample to estimate the overall gradient of performative risk, and (ii) a two-timescale diminishing step size that balances the rates of DFO updates and bias reduction. Under a general non-convex optimization setting, we show that DFO($\lambda$) requires ${\cal O}( 1 /\epsilon^3)$ samples (up to a log factor) to attain a near-stationary solution with expected squared gradient norm less than $\epsilon > 0$. Numerical experiments verify our analysis.
originalAbstract: This paper studies the performative prediction problem where a learner aims to minimize the expected loss with a decision-dependent data distribution. Such setting is motivated when outcomes can be affected by the prediction model, e.g., in strategic classification. We consider a state-dependent setting where the data distribution evolves according to an underlying controlled Markov chain. We focus on stochastic derivative free optimization (DFO) where the learner is given access to a loss function evaluation oracle with the above Markovian data. We propose a two-timescale DFO($\lambda$) algorithm that features (i) a sample accumulation mechanism that utilizes every observed sample to estimate the overall gradient of performative risk, and (ii) a two-timescale diminishing step size that balances the rates of DFO updates and bias reduction. Under a general non-convex optimization setting, we show that DFO($\lambda$) requires ${\cal O}( 1 /\epsilon^3)$ samples (up to a log factor) to attain a near-stationary solution with expected squared gradient norm less than $\epsilon > 0$. Numerical experiments verify our analysis.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a decision changes the data distribution on which its loss is evaluated. This paper studies a setting where the distribution also evolves through a controlled Markov chain, so data depend on the system's state. The learner receives loss evaluations and must optimize without direct access to derivatives.

The proposed DFO(λ) algorithm accumulates samples so that every observed sample contributes to estimating the overall gradient of performative risk. It also uses diminishing step sizes operating on two timescales. These balance the pace of optimization updates with the reduction of estimation bias, addressing the interaction between changing decisions and evolving data.

For the analyzed nonconvex setting, the authors establish a sample requirement of O(1/ε³), up to a logarithmic factor, to obtain an expected squared gradient norm below ε. This is a near-stationarity guarantee, specifying how small the gradient becomes. Numerical experiments verify the analysis. The result gives a quantitative convergence account for derivative-free learning when decisions influence a temporally dependent data-generating process.

title: Two-timescale Derivative Free Optimization for Performative Prediction with Markovian Data

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm that extends the methods of ball smoothing and Gaussian smoothing for noisy derivative-free optimization by accounting for the heterogeneous curvature of the objective function. The algorithm dynamically adapts the shape of the smoothing kernel to approximate the Hessian of the objective function around a local optimum. This approach significantly reduces the error in estimating the gradient from noisy evaluations through sampling. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through numerical experiments on artificial problems. Additionally, we show improved performance when tuning NP-hard combinatorial optimization solvers compared to existing state-ofthe-art heuristic derivative-free and Bayesian optimization methods.

paragraphs: Derivative-free optimization searches for good solutions using function evaluations rather than directly available derivatives. When those evaluations are noisy, estimating a useful gradient from sampled values becomes difficult. This paper develops a smoothing method that accounts for the objective having different curvature in different directions, extending ball and Gaussian smoothing approaches.

The algorithm changes the shape of its smoothing kernel as optimization proceeds. It adapts that shape to approximate the objective's Hessian around a local optimum, using local curvature to guide the smoothing. The stated benefit is a substantial reduction in the error of gradient estimates obtained from noisy samples. The mechanism therefore targets the reliability of the directional information used during optimization.

Numerical experiments on artificial problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also apply it to tuning solvers for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, where it improves performance over the compared heuristic derivative-free and Bayesian optimization methods. These results support adapting smoothing geometry to the objective in the noisy optimization settings studied.
summary.tldr: Adapting a smoothing kernel to local curvature improves gradient estimation from noisy evaluations and performance in reported optimization experiments.

title: Dynamic Anisotropic Smoothing for Noisy Derivative-Free Optimization

abstract: Finding and describing sub-populations that are exceptional in terms of a target property has important applications in many scientific disciplines, from identifying disadvantaged demographic groups in census data to finding conductive molecules within gold nanoparticles. Current approaches to finding such subgroups require pre-discretized predictive variables, do not permit non-trivial target distributions, do not scale to large datasets, and struggle to find diverse results. To address these limitations, we propose SYFLOW, an end-to-end optimizable approach in which we leverage normalizing flows to model arbitrary target distributions and introduce a novel neural layer that results in easily interpretable subgroup descriptions. We demonstrate on synthetic data, real-world data, and via a case study, that SYFLOW reliably finds highly exceptional subgroups accompanied by insightful descriptions.

paragraphs: Subgroup discovery looks for populations whose target properties differ unusually from the broader data. It identifies several obstacles in existing approaches, including requirements to discretize predictive variables beforehand, restrictions on target distributions, scalability problems, and difficulty finding diverse results.

SYFLOW makes subgroup discovery an end-to-end optimization problem centered on maximizing KL divergence. It uses normalizing flows to model arbitrary target distributions, giving the search a way to represent more complex target behavior. A newly introduced neural layer produces interpretable descriptions of the subgroups, connecting the optimization result to understandable population characteristics.

The combination matters because finding an unusual distribution is most useful when the corresponding group can also be described clearly. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data, together with a case study, show that SYFLOW reliably finds highly exceptional subgroups with insightful descriptions. The stated findings support both the discovery of unusual groups and the interpretability of their descriptions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SYFLOW jointly learns exceptional subgroups and interpretable descriptions using flexible distribution models and KL-divergence optimization.

title: Learning Exceptional Subgroups by End-to-End Maximizing KL-Divergence

abstract: Constructing the architecture of a neural network is a challenging pursuit for the machine learning community, and the dilemma of whether to go deeper or wider remains a persistent question. This paper explores a comparison between deeper neural networks (DeNNs) with a flexible number of layers and wider neural networks (WeNNs) with limited hidden layers, focusing on their optimal generalization error in Sobolev losses. Analytical investigations reveal that the architecture of a neural network can be significantly influenced by various factors, including the number of sample points, parameters within the neural networks, and the regularity of the loss function. Specifically, a higher number of parameters tends to favor WeNNs, while an increased number of sample points and greater regularity in the loss function lean towards the adoption of DeNNs. We ultimately apply this theory to address partial differential equations using deep Ritz and physics-informed neural network (PINN) methods, guiding the design of neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to choose between adding more layers to a neural network and making a network with relatively few layers wider. It compares these architecture families through their optimal generalization error under Sobolev losses. The purpose is to connect architectural choices to the mathematical learning problem instead of treating depth or width as universally preferable.

The analysis identifies several factors that influence the comparison: the number of available sample points, the number of network parameters, and the regularity associated with the loss function. More parameters tend to favor the wider networks considered in the study. More sample points and greater loss regularity instead tend to favor deeper networks.

These are directional conclusions within the paper’s analytical setting, so the relevant resources and loss properties must be considered together. The authors apply the theory to neural approaches for partial differential equations, including deep Ritz and physics-informed neural network methods. This gives the comparison a concrete role in guiding architecture design for those applications.
summary.tldr: A theoretical comparison links the benefits of depth and width to sample count, parameter count, and Sobolev-loss regularity.

title: Deeper or Wider: A Perspective from Optimal Generalization Error with Sobolev Loss

abstract: With the growing adoption of data privacy regulations, the ability to erase private or copyrighted information from trained models has become a crucial requirement. Traditional unlearning methods often assume access to the complete training dataset, which is unrealistic in scenarios where the source data is no longer available. To address this challenge, we propose a certified unlearning framework that enables effective data removal without access to the original training data samples. Our approach utilizes a surrogate dataset that approximates the statistical properties of the source data, allowing for controlled noise scaling based on the statistical distance between the two. While our theoretical guarantees assume knowledge of the exact statistical distance, practical implementations typically approximate this distance, resulting in potentially weaker but still meaningful privacy guarantees. This ensures strong guarantees on the model’s behavior post-unlearning while maintaining its overall utility. We establish theoretical bounds, introduce practical noise calibration techniques, and validate our method through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our approach in privacy-sensitive settings.

paragraphs: Removing information from a trained model becomes harder when the original training examples are unavailable. This paper develops a certified unlearning framework for that situation. Its aim is to remove the influence of targeted data while preserving the model’s usefulness, without requiring access to the source training samples.

The approach uses a surrogate dataset that approximates the statistical properties of the original data. The statistical distance between these datasets determines how the method scales noise. This connects the unlearning procedure to the quality of the substitute data: the framework explicitly accounts for a mismatch between the surrogate and the source.

The authors establish theoretical bounds, develop practical noise calibration techniques, and evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets. A central qualification concerns the statistical distance: the theoretical guarantees assume its exact value is known, whereas practical implementations approximate it. Those approximations can weaken the privacy guarantees. The reported experiments support the approach’s effectiveness, while this distinction explains why its formal and practical assurances need to be interpreted separately.
summary.tldr: A certified unlearning framework uses surrogate data and calibrated noise to remove information when original training samples are unavailable.

title: A Certified Unlearning Approach without Access to Source Data

abstract: The goal in thinning is to summarize a dataset using a small set of representative points. Remarkably, sub-Gaussian thinning algorithms like Kernel Halving and Compress can match the quality of uniform subsampling while substantially reducing the number of summary points. However, existing guarantees cover only a restricted range of distributions and kernel-based quality measures and suffer from pessimistic dimension dependence. To address these deficiencies, we introduce a new low-rank analysis of sub-Gaussian thinning that applies to any distribution and any kernel, guaranteeing high-quality compression whenever the kernel or data matrix is approximately low-rank. To demonstrate the broad applicability of the techniques, we design practical sub-Gaussian thinning approaches that improve upon the best known guarantees for approximating attention in transformers, accelerating stochastic gradient training through reordering, and distinguishing distributions in near-linear time.

paragraphs: Thinning summarizes a dataset by selecting a small collection of representative points. Existing sub-Gaussian thinning algorithms can match uniform subsampling quality with substantially fewer points, but their theoretical guarantees have restricted coverage and pessimistic dependence on dimension. This paper develops a low-rank analysis to broaden and sharpen those guarantees.

The analysis applies to any distribution and any kernel. Its high-quality compression guarantee depends on the kernel or data matrix being approximately low-rank, meaning that a lower-dimensional structure captures much of the relevant matrix information. The broad scope of the analysis therefore comes with a meaningful structural condition for the strongest compression conclusion.

The authors also design practical thinning approaches for several computational tasks. These improve the best known guarantees for approximating transformer attention, accelerating stochastic-gradient training through reordering, and distinguishing distributions in near-linear time. The contribution connects representative data selection to these different settings through a shared analysis of low-rank structure, rather than treating each application as an unrelated compression problem.
summary.tldr: A low-rank analysis broadens thinning guarantees and improves theoretical results for attention approximation, training reordering, and distribution comparison.

title: Low-Rank Thinning

abstract: Watermarking is essential for protecting the copyright of AI-generated images. We propose WMAdapter, a diffusion model watermark plugin that embeds user-specified watermark information seamlessly during the diffusion generation process. Unlike previous methods that modify diffusion modules to incorporate watermarks, WMAdapter is designed to keep all diffusion components intact, resulting in sharp, artifact-free images. To achieve this, we introduce two key innovations: (1) We develop a contextual adapter that conditions on the content of the cover image to generate adaptive watermark embeddings. (2) We implement an additional finetuning step and a hybrid finetuning strategy that suppresses noticeable artifacts while preserving the integrity of the diffusion components. Empirical results show that WMAdapter provides strong flexibility, superior image quality, and competitive watermark robustness.

paragraphs: WMAdapter adds user-specified watermark information while a latent diffusion model generates an image. The goal is to support watermarking while preserving image quality. Its plugin design keeps the diffusion components intact, addressing the visual-artifact problem associated with incorporating watermark information into image generation.

The method introduces a contextual adapter that uses the content of the cover image to produce adaptive watermark embeddings. This makes the embedding depend on the image being watermarked. An additional fine-tuning step and a hybrid fine-tuning strategy suppress noticeable artifacts while preserving the integrity of the diffusion components. These mechanisms jointly address how to insert the watermark and how to maintain the visual result.

The authors report strong flexibility, superior image quality, and competitive watermark robustness in their empirical evaluation. They describe the resulting images as sharp and artifact-free. The contribution is a controllable watermarking plugin that combines content-aware embeddings with training strategies aimed at visual quality, while retaining the original diffusion components.
summary.tldr: WMAdapter embeds user-selected watermarks during diffusion generation using content-aware adapters, with strong reported image quality and competitive robustness.

title: WMAdapter: Adding WaterMark Control to Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become increasingly effective at approximating quantum mechanical calculations at a fraction of the computational cost. However, lower errors on held out test sets do not always translate to improved results on downstream physical property prediction tasks. In this paper, we propose testing MLIPs on their practical ability to conserve energy during molecular dynamic simulations. If passed, improved correlations are found between test errors and their performance on physical property prediction tasks. We identify choices which may lead to models failing this test, and use these observations to improve upon highly-expressive models. The resulting model, eSEN, provides state-of-the-art results on a range of physical property prediction tasks, including materials stability prediction, thermal conductivity prediction, and phonon calculations.

However, better accuracy on held-out examples does not always lead to better predictions of physical properties. This paper investigates that mismatch by asking whether a learned potential behaves appropriately during molecular-dynamics simulation, where its predictions are used repeatedly as the system evolves.

The proposed practical check is whether the model conserves energy during those simulations. Among models that pass this test, the authors find a stronger relationship between held-out prediction errors and downstream physical-property performance. Passing the check therefore helps make test error more informative in their study; it does not establish that lower error alone guarantees better results.

The authors identify modeling choices that may cause failures of the energy-conservation test and use those observations to improve highly expressive potentials. The resulting model, eSEN, achieves reported state-of-the-art results for materials stability, thermal conductivity, and phonon calculations. The work connects model development to physical behavior in simulation, making that behavior part of evaluating whether predictive accuracy translates into useful scientific results.
summary.tldr: Energy-conservation testing guides the development of eSEN and makes test errors more informative about downstream physical-property predictions.

title: Learning Smooth and Expressive Interatomic Potentials for Physical Property Prediction

abstract: We present a comprehensive classical and parameterized complexity analysis of decision tree pruning operations, extending recent research on the complexity of learning small decision trees. Thereby, we offer new insights into the computational challenges of decision tree simplification, a crucial aspect of developing interpretable and efficient machine learning models. We focus on fundamental pruning operations of subtree replacement and raising, which are used in heuristics. Surprisingly, while optimal pruning can be performed in polynomial time for subtree replacement, the problem is NP-complete for subtree raising. Therefore, we identify parameters and combinations thereof that lead to fixed-parameter tractability or hardness, establishing a precise borderline between these complexity classes. For example, while subtree raising is hard for small domain size $D$ or number $d$ of features, it can be solved in $D^{2d} \cdot |I|^{O(1)}$ time, where $|I|$ is the input size. We complement our theoretical findings with preliminary experimental results, demonstrating the practical implications of our analysis.
