paragraphs: Pruning simplifies decision trees, helping make models more efficient and interpretable. This paper asks how difficult it is to find an optimal pruning when using two operations common in heuristics: subtree replacement and subtree raising. The authors analyze both classical computational complexity and how difficulty changes with particular properties of the input.

The two operations have sharply different complexity. Optimal subtree replacement is solvable in polynomial time, whereas optimal subtree raising is NP-complete. For raising, the analysis identifies parameter choices and combinations that allow fixed-parameter tractability, as well as choices that leave the problem hard. This gives a more detailed picture than a single worst-case classification.

For example, keeping only the feature-domain size D or only the number of features d small does not remove the stated hardness. Considering them together yields a running time of D^(2d) times a polynomial in input size. Preliminary experiments complement the theory, illustrating its practical implications for choosing pruning procedures and identifying settings where optimal simplification is computationally approachable.
summary.tldr: Optimal decision-tree pruning is polynomial-time for subtree replacement but NP-complete for subtree raising, with tractability depending on combined input parameters.

title: Optimal Decision Tree Pruning Revisited: Algorithms and Complexity

abstract: The generated responses of large language models (LLMs) are often fine-tuned to human preferences through a process called reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). As RLHF relies on a challenging training sequence, whereby a separate reward model is independently learned and then later applied to LLM policy updates, ongoing research effort has targeted more straightforward alternatives. In this regard, direct preference optimization (DPO) and its many offshoots circumvent the need for a separate reward training step. Instead, through the judicious use of a reparameterization trick that induces an implicit reward, DPO and related methods consolidate learning to the minimization of a single loss function. And yet despite demonstrable success in some real-world settings, we prove that DPO-based objectives are nonetheless subject to sub-optimal regularization and counter-intuitive interpolation behaviors, underappreciated artifacts of the reparameterizations upon which they are based. To this end, we introduce an explicit preference optimization framework termed EXPO that requires no analogous reparameterization to achieve an implicit reward. Quite differently, we merely posit intuitively-appealing regularization factors from scratch that transparently avoid the potential pitfalls of key DPO variants, provably satisfying regularization desiderata that prior methods do not. Empirical results serve to corroborate our analyses and showcase the efficacy of EXPO.

paragraphs: Aligning language model responses with human preferences often involves learning a reward model and then updating the language model against it. Direct preference optimization simplifies that sequence by using a reparameterization that produces an implicit reward and a single training loss. This paper examines mathematical consequences of that simplification that can affect how learning behaves.

The authors prove that DPO-based objectives can have suboptimal regularization and counterintuitive interpolation behavior arising from their reparameterizations. Regularization controls how the optimization balances its objectives, so these properties concern the behavior built into the training loss itself. The analysis identifies potential pitfalls despite DPO's demonstrated success in some practical settings.

The proposed EXPO framework instead specifies explicit regularization factors without an analogous implicit-reward reparameterization. The authors prove that it satisfies desired regularization properties that prior methods do not, and experiments support both their analysis and EXPO's effectiveness. The contribution is a more transparent way to construct preference objectives, with theoretical criteria for their behavior and empirical evidence that the resulting design is useful.
summary.tldr: EXPO explicitly designs preference regularization to avoid theoretical pitfalls introduced by DPO's implicit-reward reparameterization.

title: Explicit Preference Optimization: No Need for an Implicit Reward Model

abstract: Node classification is a key task in temporal graph learning (TGL). Real-life temporal graphs often introduce new node classes over time, but existing TGL methods assume a fixed set of classes. This assumption brings limitations, as updating models with full data is costly, while focusing only on new classes results in forgetting old ones. Graph continual learning (GCL) methods mitigate forgetting using old-class subsets but fail to account for their evolution. We define this novel problem as temporal graph continual learning (TGCL), which focuses on efficiently maintaining up-to-date knowledge of old classes. To tackle TGCL, we propose a selective learning framework that substitutes the old-class data with its subsets, Learning Towards the Future (LTF). We derive an upper bound on the error caused by such replacement and transform it into objectives for selecting and learning subsets that minimize classification error while preserving the distribution of the full old-class data. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that LTF effectively addresses the TGCL challenge.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a changing graph becomes harder when new classes appear and existing classes also evolve. Training again on all available data is expensive, while learning only the new classes can erase earlier knowledge. The paper argues that retaining small samples of old classes is insufficient if those samples do not account for how the classes change over time.

The authors formulate temporal graph continual learning around maintaining current knowledge of old classes efficiently. Their framework, Learning Towards the Future, replaces the full old-class data with selected subsets. They derive an upper bound on the error introduced by this replacement and use it to guide both subset selection and learning.

The resulting objectives balance classification accuracy with preserving the distribution represented by the complete old-class data. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that the framework addresses this evolving-class setting effectively. Its contribution is to connect economical data retention with keeping old knowledge up to date, so remembering a class also accounts for its subsequent evolution.
summary.tldr: Learning Towards the Future selects representative data subsets to maintain knowledge of evolving old classes as new graph classes arrive.

title: A Selective Learning Method for Temporal Graph Continual Learning

abstract: Achieving effective unified pretraining on large time series corpora remains an open challenge in developing time series foundation models. Existing methods, such as Moirai, introduce multiple projection layers for time series of different frequencies to account for high data heterogeneity. We identify major drawbacks to this human-imposed frequency-level model specialization. First, frequency is not a reliable indicator for grouping pretraining data. Second, time series can display varied distributions even within a short window. Frequency-level specialization overlooks the diversity at this granularity. To address these issues, this paper introduces Moirai-MoE, excluding human-defined data groupings while delegating the modeling of diverse time series patterns to the sparse mixture of experts (MoE) within Transformers. With this design, Moirai-MoE eliminates reliance on heuristics and enables automatic token-level specialization. Extensive evaluations on 39 datasets demonstrate the superiority of Moirai-MoE over state-of-the-art foundation models. This study also conducts comprehensive model analyses to explore the inner workings of time series MoE foundation models.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models must learn from data with widely differing patterns. Existing approaches such as Moirai use separate projection layers for different sampling frequencies. This paper argues that frequency is an unreliable basis for grouping the training data, and that even a short time window can contain varied distributions that such grouping overlooks.

Moirai-MoE replaces those human-defined groups with a sparse mixture of experts inside a Transformer. The model learns specialization at the token level, allowing its internal experts to handle diverse patterns at a finer granularity than a frequency category. This design delegates the organization of pattern-specific modeling to the learned architecture.

Evaluations across 39 datasets show Moirai-MoE outperforming the compared state-of-the-art foundation models. The paper also analyzes the model to investigate the operation of mixture-of-experts time-series architectures. The findings support automatic, fine-grained specialization as a promising response to heterogeneous time-series data, particularly when the diversity within a sequence is poorly represented by a single externally assigned group.
summary.tldr: Moirai-MoE learns token-level expert specialization for diverse time series, outperforming compared foundation models across 39 datasets.

title: Moirai-MoE: Empowering Time Series Foundation Models with Sparse Mixture of Experts

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a crucial task in reliable and safety-critical applications. Previous studies primarily focus on developing score functions while neglecting the design of decision rules based on these scores. A recent work (Ma et al., 2024) is the first to highlight this issue and proposes the generalized BH (g-BH) algorithm to address it. The g-BH algorithm relies on empirical p-values, with the calibrated set playing a central role in their computation. However, the impact of calibrated set on the performance of g-BH algorithm has not been thoroughly investigated. This paper aims to uncover the underlying mechanisms between them. Theoretically, we demonstrate that conditional expectation of true positive rate (TPR) on calibrated set for the g-BH algorithm follows a beta distribution, which depends on the prescribed level and size of calibrated set. This indicates that a small calibrated set tends to degrade the performance of g-BH algorithm. To address the limitation of g-BH algorithm on small calibrated set, we propose a novel ensemble g-BH (eg-BH) algorithm which integrates various empirical p-values for making decisions. Finally, extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of our theoretical findings and demonstrate the superiority of our method over g-BH algorithm on small calibrated set.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar inputs requires both a score and a rule for deciding when that score warrants an alert. This paper studies the decision rule in the generalized BH algorithm, or g-BH. Its decisions use empirical p-values computed with a calibration set, making that reference data an important part of the detector.

The authors analyze how the calibration set affects detection performance. They show that the conditional expected true positive rate, given the calibration set, follows a beta distribution whose parameters depend on the prescribed level and calibration-set size. This connects variation in the reference data to variation in detection success and indicates that small calibration sets tend to hurt performance.

To address that problem, the paper introduces ensemble g-BH, which combines multiple empirical p-values when making decisions. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and show improvements over g-BH with small calibration sets. The contribution therefore concerns how available scores become decisions, with particular attention to situations where calibration data is scarce.
summary.tldr: Ensemble g-BH combines empirical p-values to improve out-of-distribution detection when calibration sets are small.

title: A Closer Look at Generalized BH Algorithm for Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: We introduce SWE-Lancer, a benchmark of over 1400 freelance software engineering tasks from Upwork, valued at $1 million USD total in real-world payouts. SWE-Lancer encompasses both independent engineering tasks — ranging from $50 bug fixes to $32000 feature implementations — and managerial tasks, where models choose between technical implementation proposals. Independent tasks are graded with end-to-end tests triple-verified by experienced software engineers, while managerial decisions are assessed against the choices of the original hired engineering managers. We evaluate model performance and find that frontier models are still unable to solve the majority of tasks. To facilitate future research, we open-source a unified Docker image and a public evaluation split. By mapping model performance to monetary value, we hope SWE-Lancer enables greater research into the economic impact of AI model development.

paragraphs: SWE-Lancer evaluates language models on more than 1,400 real freelance software engineering tasks from Upwork. The tasks correspond to a total of $1 million in actual payouts, spanning work from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 feature implementations. This ties the evaluation to work that customers paid engineers to complete.

The benchmark includes both independent implementation tasks and managerial decisions. Implementation work is assessed using end-to-end tests that experienced software engineers triple-verified. For managerial tasks, models choose among technical implementation proposals, and their choices are compared with those made by the originally hired engineering managers. These tracks evaluate different forms of engineering work.

The evaluated frontier models cannot solve the majority of tasks. The authors release a unified Docker image and a public evaluation split to support further research. By relating task performance to the original monetary values, the benchmark provides a way to investigate the economic significance of model capabilities while grounding that investigation in concrete software work.
summary.tldr: SWE-Lancer evaluates models on real freelance engineering work worth $1 million, finding that tested frontier models fail most tasks.

title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?

abstract: Pre-trained vision language models still fall short of human visual cognition. In an effort to improve visual cognition and align models with human behavior, we introduce visual stimuli and human judgments on visual cognition tasks, allowing us to systematically evaluate performance across cognitive domains under a consistent environment. We fine-tune models on ground truth data for intuitive physics and causal reasoning and find that this improves model performance in the respective fine-tuning domain. Furthermore, it can improve model alignment with human behavior. However, we find that task-specific fine-tuning does not contribute to robust human-like generalization to data with other visual characteristics or to tasks in other cognitive domains.

paragraphs: Vision-language models still differ from humans in their visual cognition. This paper studies whether task-specific fine-tuning can improve both task performance and agreement with human behavior. The authors introduce visual stimuli and human judgments that allow multiple cognitive domains to be evaluated within a consistent environment.

They fine-tune models using ground-truth data for intuitive physics and causal reasoning. Performance improves within the corresponding training domain, and fine-tuning can also increase alignment with human judgments. These outcomes distinguish two useful forms of progress: giving more correct answers and behaving more similarly to people on the evaluated tasks.

The gains do not extend to robust human-like generalization when visual characteristics change or when evaluation moves to another cognitive domain. This is the paper's central boundary on the benefits of fine-tuning. Better performance within a trained task does not, in these experiments, establish a broadly improved visual reasoning ability. The results therefore show both the value of targeted training and the importance of testing whether its benefits transfer.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning improves visual cognition within trained domains but does not produce robust human-like transfer across visual changes or cognitive tasks.

title: Testing the Limits of Fine-Tuning for Improving Visual Cognition in Vision Language Models

abstract: Score-based Generative Models (SGMs) aim to sample from a target distribution by learning score functions using samples perturbed by Gaussian noise. Existing convergence bounds for SGMs in the $\mathcal{W}_2$-distance rely on stringent assumptions about the data distribution. In this work, we present a novel framework for analyzing $\mathcal{W}_2$-convergence in SGMs, significantly relaxing traditional assumptions such as log-concavity and score regularity. Leveraging the regularization properties of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, we show that weak log-concavity of the data distribution evolves into log-concavity over time. This transition is rigorously quantified through a PDE-based analysis of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation governing the log-density of the forward process. Moreover, we establish that the drift of the time-reversed OU process alternates between contractive and non-contractive regimes, reflecting the dynamics of concavity. Our approach circumvents the need for stringent regularity conditions on the score function and its estimators, relying instead on milder, more practical assumptions. We demonstrate the wide applicability of this framework through explicit computations on Gaussian mixture models, illustrating its versatility and potential for broader classes of data distributions.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn from noise-perturbed data and use learned score functions to generate samples. This paper studies how close their generated distribution gets to the target in Wasserstein-2 distance. Its contribution is an analysis framework that relaxes strong assumptions about the target distribution and the regularity of score functions that earlier convergence bounds require.

The analysis uses the smoothing properties of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Under weak log-concavity of the data distribution, the authors show that its evolution eventually becomes log-concave. They quantify that transition through a partial differential equation for the evolving log-density. They also show that the reversed process has both contractive and non-contractive regimes, connecting sampling dynamics to changes in concavity.

Accounting for these changing regimes allows the framework to work with milder assumptions on scores and their estimators. Explicit calculations for Gaussian mixture models illustrate its applicability. The result broadens the theoretical settings in which convergence can be analyzed; its suggested relevance to wider distribution classes remains a potential extension rather than an unrestricted guarantee.
summary.tldr: A new convergence analysis uses noise-induced regularization to weaken assumptions required for score-based generative models.

title: Beyond Log-Concavity and Score Regularity: Improved Convergence Bounds for Score-Based Generative Models in W2-distance

abstract: Flow matching (FM) models extend ODE sampler based diffusion models into a general framework, significantly reducing sampling steps through learned vector fields. However, the theoretical understanding of FM models, particularly how their sample trajectories interact with underlying data geometry, remains underexplored. A rigorous theoretical analysis of FM ODE is essential for sample quality, stability, and broader applicability. In this paper, we advance the theory of FM models through a comprehensive analysis of sample trajectories. Central to our theory is the discovery that the denoiser, a key component of FM models, guides ODE dynamics through attracting and absorbing behaviors that adapt to the data geometry. We identify and analyze the three stages of ODE evolution: in the initial and intermediate stages, trajectories move toward the mean and local clusters of the data. At the terminal stage, we rigorously establish the convergence of FM ODE under weak assumptions, addressing scenarios where the data lie on a low-dimensional submanifold—cases that previous results could not handle. Our terminal stage analysis offers insights into the memorization phenomenon and establishes equivariance properties of FM ODEs. These findings bridge critical gaps in understanding flow matching models, with practical implications for optimizing sampling strategies and architectures guided by the intrinsic geometry of data.

paragraphs: Flow matching generates samples by following a learned vector field through an ordinary differential equation. This paper studies how those trajectories relate to the geometry of the underlying data. Understanding that relationship helps explain where generated samples move and how the sampling process behaves near its endpoint.

The analysis centers on the denoiser, which guides trajectories through attracting and absorbing behaviors that reflect data geometry. The authors distinguish three stages of evolution. During the initial and intermediate stages, trajectories move toward the data mean and local clusters. At the terminal stage, they establish convergence under weak assumptions, including situations where the data occupy a low-dimensional submanifold.

Handling such low-dimensional structure extends beyond cases covered by earlier results. The terminal analysis also provides insight into memorization and establishes equivariance properties, describing how the dynamics relate to transformations. The contribution is principally theoretical: it connects sampling behavior with data geometry and provides a basis for geometry-informed choices of sampling strategies and model architectures.
summary.tldr: The paper explains flow-matching trajectories through denoiser behavior and proves terminal convergence under weak assumptions, including low-dimensional data settings.

title: Elucidating Flow Matching ODE Dynamics via Data Geometry and Denoisers

abstract: Variational inequalities (VIs) encompass many fundamental problems in diverse areas ranging from engineering to economics and machine learning. However, their considerable expressivity comes at the cost of computational intractability. In this paper, we introduce and analyze a natural relaxation—which we refer to as expected variational inequalities (EVIs)—where the goal is to find a distribution that satisfies the VI constraint in expectation. By adapting recent techniques from game theory, we show that, unlike VIs, EVIs can be solved in polynomial time under general (nonmonotone) operators. EVIs capture the seminal notion of correlated equilibria, but enjoy a greater reach beyond games. We also employ our framework to capture and generalize several existing disparate results, including from settings such as smooth games, and games with coupled constraints or nonconcave utilities.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a common mathematical language for problems in engineering, economics, and machine learning, but their flexibility can make them computationally difficult. This paper introduces expected variational inequalities, which change the object being sought: the goal is a distribution satisfying the inequality constraint in expectation.

That relaxation is the key to the computational result. By adapting techniques from game theory, the authors show that expected variational inequalities can be solved in polynomial time for general, nonmonotone operators. The guarantee concerns the expected constraint under the resulting distribution; it does not assert that each individual outcome separately solves the original variational inequality.

The framework includes correlated equilibria, an established game-theoretic solution concept, while extending beyond games. It also brings together and generalizes results involving smooth games, shared constraints, and nonconcave utilities. Its significance is both computational and conceptual: changing the solution requirement to an expectation makes a broad relaxation tractable and places several previously separate results within one framework.
summary.tldr: Expected variational inequalities relax constraints to hold under a distribution’s expectation, enabling polynomial-time solutions even for general nonmonotone operators.

title: Expected Variational Inequalities

abstract: Humans develop world models that capture the underlying generation process of data. Whether neural networks can learn similar world models remains an open problem. In this work, we present the first theoretical results for this problem, showing that in a multi-task setting, models with a low-degree bias provably recover latent data-generating variables under mild assumptions–even if proxy tasks involve complex, non-linear functions of the latents. However, such recovery is sensitive to model architecture. Our analysis leverages Boolean models of task solutions via the Fourier-Walsh transform and introduces new techniques for analyzing invertible Boolean transforms, which may be of independent interest. We illustrate the algorithmic implications of our results and connect them to related research areas, including self-supervised learning, out-of-distribution generalization, and the linear representation hypothesis in large language models.

paragraphs: A world model captures the underlying process that produces observed data. This paper asks when neural networks can recover the hidden variables of such a process while learning tasks built from them. It gives theoretical results for a multi-task setting, where the same latent variables underlie multiple prediction problems.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that models with a low-degree bias recover those latent variables even when the proxy tasks are complex nonlinear functions of them. The recovery depends on model architecture. Thus, the guarantee identifies a combination of task structure and model bias that supports learning hidden generating factors, with architectural sensitivity remaining part of the result.

The analysis represents Boolean task solutions using the Fourier-Walsh transform and develops techniques for studying invertible Boolean transformations. The paper also illustrates algorithmic implications and connects the theory to self-supervised learning, out-of-distribution generalization, and linear representations in language models. Its contribution is a conditional mathematical account of latent recovery that helps specify when learning several tasks can produce a representation of their shared underlying world.
summary.tldr: The paper proves latent-variable recovery in a multi-task setting for models with a low-degree bias under stated assumptions, with results sensitive to architecture.

title: When do neural networks learn world models?

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that elicit disallowed content, motivating reliable inference-time controls. A popular approach is negative guidance, which subtracts a negative prompt direction with a fixed weight. However, it often forces a safety–fidelity trade-off, causing artifacts or prompt drift when over-applied and failing under attacks when under-applied. Dynamic variants reweight guidance using posterior-odds signals, which can be brittle for open-vocabulary compositional prompts, while lightweight similarity-based methods ignore the evolving image evidence along the denoising trajectory. We introduce Concept Removal Guidance (CRG), a training-free method that estimates unwanted-concept presence at each diffusion step from the model’s noise predictions, and adaptively calibrates negative guidance via a closed-form constrained update enforcing a target presence threshold while minimally perturbing the conditional trajectory. Across red-teaming benchmarks, CRG reduces attack success rates while preserving benign fidelity, and extends to additional suppression targets such as artist style and violence without fine-tuning or external classifiers.

paragraphs: Negative guidance steers a text-to-image diffusion model away from unwanted content by subtracting a direction associated with a negative prompt. A fixed strength can create a difficult balance: excessive guidance damages image quality or changes the intended prompt, while insufficient guidance can fail against adversarial prompts. The paper proposes adapting this strength to the evolving generation.

Concept Removal Guidance, or CRG, estimates the presence of an unwanted concept at each diffusion step using the model's own noise predictions. It then applies a closed-form constrained update that targets a specified presence threshold while minimizing changes to the conditional generation trajectory. The threshold therefore governs the estimated concept presence used by the update.

CRG needs no additional training, fine-tuning, or external classifier. Across red-teaming benchmarks, the authors report lower attack success while preserving fidelity on benign inputs. They also apply it to artist-style and violence suppression. These findings support using evidence from the current denoising process to calibrate intervention, rather than applying the same removal strength throughout generation.
summary.tldr: CRG adapts diffusion guidance to estimated unwanted-concept presence, reducing attack success while preserving benign image fidelity in reported evaluations.

title: Concept Removal Guidance: Evidence-Calibrated Negative Guidance for Safe Diffusion Sampling

abstract: Large language models have transformed many applications but remain expensive to train. Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) addresses this through conditional computation, with Expert Parallel (EP) as the standard distributed training method. However, EP has three limitations: communication cost grows linearly with the number of activated experts $k$, load imbalance affects latency and memory usage, and data-dependent communication requires metadata exchange. We propose Multi-Head LatentMoE and Head Parallel (HP), a new architecture and parallelism that achieve $O(1)$ communication cost regardless of $k$, completely balanced traffic, and deterministic communication, all while remaining compatible with EP. To accelerate Multi-Head LatentMoE, we propose IO-aware routing and expert computation. Compared to MoE with EP, Multi-Head LatentMoE with HP trains up to $1.82\times$ faster while having better performance. With double the granularity, the performance is even better while being $1.08\times$ faster. Our method makes multi-billion-parameter foundation model research more accessible.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models reduce computation by activating only selected experts, but distributed training still requires moving data between devices. With standard Expert Parallel training, communication grows with the number of activated experts. Uneven loads also affect latency and memory, while data-dependent transfers require metadata exchange to coordinate communication.

The paper jointly introduces Multi-Head LatentMoE and Head Parallel, an architecture and parallelization method designed around those bottlenecks. Communication remains constant with respect to the number of activated experts, traffic is completely balanced, and communication is deterministic. The approach remains compatible with Expert Parallel, and the authors add input/output-aware routing and expert computation to accelerate the architecture.

Compared with mixture-of-experts training using Expert Parallel, the reported configuration trains up to 1.82 times faster while achieving better performance. A configuration with double the granularity improves performance further and remains 1.08 times faster. These results show how changing both the model organization and its distributed execution can reduce communication overhead while preserving useful expert computation in the evaluated training settings.
summary.tldr: Multi-Head LatentMoE with Head Parallel makes communication independent of activated-expert count and reports up to 1.82-fold faster training.

title: Multi-Head LatentMoE and Head Parallel: Communication-Efficient and Deterministic MoE Parallelism

abstract: Foundation models have revolutionized AI, yet biological applications often repurpose general architectures without accounting for the intrinsic structural and functional properties of distinct modalities, such as genomic and proteomic sequences. Consequently, these architectures lack the inductive biases required to capture the complex “grammars" inherent to biological data, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce BioArc, a framework utilizing Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to shift from intuition-driven design to automated data-driven discovery. Unlike standard NAS restricted to homogeneous spaces, BioArc navigates a heterogeneous space for open-ended composition of architectural blocks. By systematically analyzing the interplay between architecture, tokenization, and training across modalities, BioArc identifies novel hybrid architectures that surpass state-of-the-art models while being up to 25x smaller. We distill these findings into empirical design principles and validate their biological relevance, demonstrating how our designs hierarchically capture the underlying biological grammar. Additionally, we introduce an agentic framework to predict optimal architectures for new tasks. Overall, BioArc provides a data-driven methodology for developing the next generation of efficient biological foundation models and task-specific networks.

paragraphs: Biological foundation models often reuse general-purpose architectures even though genomic and proteomic sequences have distinct structural and functional patterns. BioArc investigates whether architecture discovery can better match these patterns. Its central idea is to let data guide the composition of a model instead of relying primarily on designers’ intuition about which architecture should work.

The framework uses neural architecture search over a heterogeneous collection of building blocks, allowing hybrid architectures rather than restricting the search to a single uniform design family. It also studies architecture together with tokenization and training across biological modalities. This matters because the way biological inputs are represented and the way a network processes them are treated as interacting design choices.

The discovered architectures surpass state-of-the-art models while being up to 25 times smaller. The authors derive empirical design principles and report evidence that their architectures capture biological patterns hierarchically. They also introduce an agentic framework for predicting suitable architectures for new tasks. Together, these contributions position automated architecture discovery as a route to more efficient biological foundation models and specialized networks.
summary.tldr: BioArc searches heterogeneous neural architectures to discover biological models that outperform existing designs while being up to 25 times smaller.

title: BIOARC: Discovering Optimal Neural Architectures for Biological Foundation Models

abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) alters brain electrophysiology and disrupts multichannel EEG dynamics, making accurate and clinically useful EEG-based diagnosis increasingly important for screening and disease monitoring. However, many existing approaches rely on black-box classifiers and do not explicitly model the latent event timing and cross-channel coordination behind their decisions. To address these limitations, we propose LERD, an end-to-end Bayesian latent event–relational dynamical system that infers latent neural events and their relational structure directly from multichannel EEG without event or interaction annotations. LERD combines a continuous-time event inference module with a stochastic event-generation process to capture flexible temporal patterns, while incorporating an electrophysiology-inspired dynamical prior to guide learning in a principled way. We further provide theoretical analysis that yields a tractable IVP-based KL regularizer and stability guarantees for the inferred relational dynamics. Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks and two real-world AD EEG cohorts demonstrate that LERD consistently outperforms strong baselines and yields physiology-aligned rate, timing, and graph summaries that help characterize group-level dynamical differences.

paragraphs: Alzheimer’s disease changes electrical brain activity and coordination across EEG channels. Many classifiers predict disease status without explicitly describing the event timing or channel relationships behind their decisions. LERD models those hidden dynamics directly, aiming to combine useful classification with summaries that relate to brain physiology.

The system learns latent neural events and their relationships from multichannel EEG without annotations identifying events or interactions. It combines continuous-time event inference with a stochastic process for generating events, allowing flexible timing patterns. An electrophysiology-inspired dynamical prior guides learning. The theoretical analysis provides a tractable regularizer based on an initial-value problem and guarantees concerning stability of the inferred relational dynamics.

On synthetic benchmarks and two real Alzheimer’s EEG cohorts, LERD consistently outperforms the strong baselines evaluated by the authors. It also produces summaries of event rates, timing, and relational graphs that align with physiology and help describe group-level differences. These findings support interpreting classification through learned dynamics, while the stated physiological summaries concern differences between groups.
summary.tldr: LERD learns hidden EEG events and channel relationships to improve Alzheimer’s classification while producing physiology-aligned summaries of group differences.

title: LERD: Latent Event-Relational Dynamics for Neurodegenerative Classification

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose $\textit{Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization}$ (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

paragraphs: Human preference feedback can be inconsistent or subjective, making it an imperfect training signal for language-model alignment. title: Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback

abstract: Recommender systems play a crucial role in internet economies by connecting users with relevant products. However, designing effective recommender systems faces the key challenges: the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in securing incentive to explore new products against user’s self-interested preferences. While prior work addresses Bayesian Incentive Compatibility (BIC) in fixed-design linear bandits (Sellke & Slivkins, 2023), we tackle the challenge of stochastic user covariates sampled online. Unlike standard black-box reductions (Mansour et al., 2020), our two-stage framework exploits the linear reward structure to achieve sublinear regret while satisfying incentive constraints. To address it, we propose a two-stage algorithm that integrates incentivized exploration with any efficient plug-in offline learning algorithms. In the first stage, it explores products while maintaining incentive compatibility to gather optimal samples. The second stage employs inverse proportional gap sampling strategy (IPGS) integrated with any efficient learning methods to secure sublinear regret. Theoretically, we prove that algorithm RCB achieves $O(\sqrt{KdT})$ regret and simultaneously satisfies incentive constraints, and discovers the tradeoff between incentive budget and regret, validating in experiments. We demonstrate RCB’s strong incentive gain, sublinear regret, and robustness through a real application on personalized warfarin dosing and simulations.

paragraphs: A recommender needs to explore unfamiliar products to learn their value, but users have their own preferences and may not want to follow exploratory recommendations. This paper studies that tension when user characteristics arrive randomly over time. Its goal is to learn effectively while maintaining incentive constraints that make the recommendations compatible with users’ interests.

The proposed two-stage framework uses a linear reward structure. First, it conducts incentive-compatible exploration to collect informative samples. Second, it combines an efficient plug-in offline learner with inverse proportional gap sampling, which uses estimated reward gaps to guide sampling. This design links the initial incentive-aware data collection to continued learning and recommendation.

The authors prove that their RCB algorithm achieves O(√KdT) regret while satisfying incentive constraints, and analyze a tradeoff between incentive budget and regret. Sublinear regret means cumulative learning costs grow more slowly than the decision horizon. Experiments involving simulations and personalized warfarin dosing report strong incentive gains, sublinear regret, and robustness, supporting the framework’s ability to balance learning with user incentives.
summary.tldr: RCB combines incentive-compatible exploration with offline learning to achieve sublinear regret when user characteristics arrive stochastically.

title: Incentivized Exploration with Stochastic Covariates: A Two-Stage Mechanism Design for Recommender System

abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has shown notable effectiveness in enhancing large language models (LLMs) reasoning performance, especially in mathematics tasks. However, such improvements often come with reduced outcome diversity, where the model concentrates probability mass on a narrow set of solutions. Motivated by diminishing-returns principles, we introduce a set level diversity objective defined over sampled trajectories using kernelized similarity. Our approach derives a leave-one-out marginal contribution for each sampled trajectory and integrates this objective as a plug-in advantage shaping term for policy optimization. We further investigate the contribution of a single trajectory to language model diversity within a distribution perturbation framework. This analysis theoretically confirms a monotonicity property, proving that rarer trajectories yield consistently higher marginal contributions to the global diversity. Extensive experiments across a range of model scales demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm, consistently outperforming strong baselines in both Pass@1 and Pass@K across various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language model reasoning while concentrating generation on a narrow range of solutions. SetPO addresses this loss of diversity by evaluating sampled reasoning trajectories as a set. Its objective reflects diminishing returns: another trajectory should contribute less when it resembles those already present.

The method measures similarity through a kernel and computes each trajectory's contribution by comparing the set with and without that trajectory. This leave-one-out contribution becomes a plug-in term that shapes the advantage used in policy optimization. Diversity thus affects the learning signal alongside the rewards already driving reasoning performance.

A distribution-perturbation analysis proves a monotonicity property within the proposed framework: rarer trajectories make larger marginal contributions to global diversity. Across model scales and reasoning benchmarks, experiments report improvements over strong baselines in both Pass@1 and Pass@K. These findings support encouraging varied trajectories while improving success with both a single attempt and multiple sampled attempts.
summary.tldr: SetPO rewards each reasoning trajectory's contribution to set diversity, improving both single-attempt and multiple-attempt success.

title: SetPO: Set-Level Policy Optimization for Diversity-Preserving LLM Reasoning

abstract: Large language models are typically optimized for accuracy and, therefore, will guess even when uncertain about their predictions. This problem becomes especially pronounced when the model is fine-tuned on small datasets, which often causes overfitting and results in a tendency toward miscalibration. In this work, we introduce Bayesian-LoRA, which reformulates the deterministic LoRA update as a probabilistic low-rank representation inspired by Sparse Gaussian Processes (SGP). We identify a structural isomorphism between LoRA’s factorization and Kronecker-factored SGP posteriors, and show that LoRA emerges as a limiting case when posterior uncertainty collapses. We conduct extensive experiments on various LLM architectures across commonsense reasoning, language modeling, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. With only approximately 0.42M additional parameters and ${\approx}1.2{\times}$ training cost relative to standard LoRA, Bayesian-LoRA significantly improves calibration across models from 7B up to 30B, achieving up to 84% Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and 76% Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) reduction while maintaining competitive accuracy for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OoD) evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayesian-LoRA addresses confidence errors in fine-tuned language models, especially when limited training data encourages overfitting. A model can produce a confident answer even when its prediction is unreliable. The paper changes the low-rank adaptation itself into a probabilistic representation, giving the adaptation a way to express uncertainty.

The construction draws on sparse Gaussian processes. The authors identify a structural correspondence between LoRA's factorized update and a particular factorized Gaussian-process posterior. Under this view, ordinary LoRA appears as a limiting case in which posterior uncertainty disappears. This connection provides a probabilistic foundation for extending the existing adaptation mechanism.

Across commonsense, language-modeling, and mathematical reasoning evaluations, Bayesian-LoRA improves calibration for models ranging from 7 to 30 billion parameters while retaining competitive accuracy. Reported reductions reach 84% in Expected Calibration Error and 76% in Negative Log-Likelihood, across evaluations including familiar and shifted distributions. The additional cost is approximately 420,000 parameters and 1.2 times standard LoRA's training cost, making uncertainty modeling a relatively compact extension.
summary.tldr: Bayesian-LoRA makes low-rank adaptation probabilistic, improving confidence calibration while maintaining competitive accuracy with modest added training cost.

title: Bayesian-LoRA: Probabilistic Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

abstract: Label Distribution Learning (LDL) is an effective learning paradigm for predicting entire conditional label distributions, improving the trustworthiness of predictions in risk-sensitive tasks. Although previous LDL methods achieve satisfactory performance on conventional evaluation metrics, they generally overlook the divisiveness within label distributions, i.e., the propensity of label distribution to exhibit dissension between semantically opposing labels, which is an essential indicator of the practical decision risk. Therefore, we propose a divisiveness-consistent label distribution learning framework to quantify and preserve the divisiveness information. First, we formalize a divisiveness measure that satisfies the axiomatic property of polarity monotonicity to quantify the divisiveness information. Second, we theoretically demonstrate the inconsistency between conventional loss functions and divisiveness error. Besides, in order to address the adversarial gradient problem arising from directly minimizing the divisiveness error, we propose a pairwise divisiveness loss as an unbiased estimator of the original divisiveness error. Experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how support is spread across labels instead of selecting just one. However, conventional measures of prediction quality can overlook whether that support is divided between semantically opposing labels. The paper calls this property divisiveness and treats it as information relevant to practical decision risk.

The authors define a divisiveness measure with a formal polarity-monotonicity property, giving the concept an explicit mathematical foundation. They then show that conventional loss functions are inconsistent with divisiveness error. Consequently, optimizing familiar distribution losses does not necessarily preserve the particular pattern of disagreement that the new measure captures.

Directly minimizing divisiveness error introduces an adversarial gradient problem. The proposed framework addresses this with a pairwise divisiveness loss that is an unbiased estimator of the original error. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a learning objective that explicitly preserves an aspect of label distributions that standard metrics can miss, making the training target more attentive to disagreement between opposing outcomes.
summary.tldr: This framework measures and preserves disagreement between opposing labels through a divisiveness-aware training objective.

title: Divisiveness-Consistent Label Distribution Learning

abstract: This paper provides data-dependent bounds on the expected error of the Gibbs algorithm in the overparameterized interpolation regime, where low training errors are also obtained for impossible data, such as random labels in classification. The results show that generalization in the low-temperature regime is already signaled by small training errors in the noisier high-temperature regime. The bounds are stable under approximation with Langevin Monte Carlo algorithms. The analysis motivates the design of an algorithm to compute bounds, which on the MNIST, CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets yield nontrivial, close predictions on the test error for true labeled data, while maintaining a correct upper bound on the test error for random labels.

paragraphs: An overparameterized model can fit its training data even when classification labels are random. Consequently, a small training error alone may say little about performance on new examples. This paper studies how to obtain informative error bounds for the Gibbs algorithm in this interpolation regime, using information that depends on the observed data.

The central result links behavior at different temperatures. Small training errors in the noisier, high-temperature regime already signal generalization in the low-temperature regime. This supplies information beyond the ability to fit data under low noise. The bounds also remain stable when the Gibbs algorithm is approximated using Langevin Monte Carlo, connecting the analysis to an implementable sampling procedure.

The theory motivates an algorithm for computing bounds. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN, these give nontrivial predictions close to test error for correctly labeled data, while retaining valid upper bounds for random labels. The significance is their ability to remain informative on learnable data while accounting for the contrasting behavior of models trained on meaningless labels.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent Gibbs error bounds use high-temperature training behavior to assess low-temperature generalization and remain stable under Langevin Monte Carlo approximation.

title: Generalization of Gibbs and Langevin Monte Carlo Algorithms in the Interpolation Regime

abstract: We propose non-parametric estimators for the average run length (ARL) and average detection delay (ADD) in quickest changepoint detection (QCD) under finite and irregular sequence lengths. Although ARL and ADD are widely used as optimality criteria in theoretical and simulation studies, their application to real-world datasets is hindered by limited and irregular sequence lengths. To address this issue, we propose non-parametric estimators for the ARL and ADD, termed KM-ARL and KM-ADD, by drawing an analogy between QCD and survival analysis to model detection probabilities under sequence truncation. We derive estimation bias bounds and prove that they are asymptotically unbiased unless extrapolation is required. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate their practical utility, enhancing robustness against limited and irregular sequence lengths, improving interpretability, and facilitating empirical, intuitive model selection. Our Python code is provided at https://github.com/TaikiMiyagawa/Kaplan-Meier-Average-Run-Length, offering ready-to-use implementations for practitioners.

paragraphs: Quickest changepoint detection concerns recognizing when a sequence changes its behavior. Two common evaluation measures are average run length and average detection delay. These are useful in theory and simulation, but real datasets introduce a complication: sequences may end before detection occurs, and different sequences may have different lengths. An evaluation must account for those unfinished observations.

The paper introduces KM-ARL and KM-ADD, non-parametric estimators built around an analogy with survival analysis. The relevant event is detection, and sequence truncation limits how long that event can be observed. This connection lets the estimators account for detection probabilities when the available observation windows are finite and irregular.

The authors derive bounds on estimation bias and prove asymptotic unbiasedness except when extrapolation is required. That qualification distinguishes estimating from observed follow-up from extending beyond it. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate more robust evaluation under limited sequence lengths, supporting clearer interpretation and practical detector selection.
summary.tldr: Survival-analysis estimators improve changepoint-detector evaluation when observation sequences are short or have unequal lengths.

title: Accurate Evaluation of Quickest Changepoint Detectors via Non-parametric Survival Analysis

abstract: Continual training of deep neural networks under non-stationarity often leads to a progressive loss of plasticity, eventually limiting further learning. We relate plasticity to the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel, and identify dynamical isometry (the condition that layer-wise Jacobian singular values remain close to one) as a key mechanism for preserving plasticity in continual learning. We revisit a class of networks that are almost-everywhere isometric while remaining universal Lipschitz function approximators, demonstrating that near-dynamical isometry is compatible with expressive nonlinear representations. For general architectures, we propose an efficient isometry-promoting regularization scheme and identify a novel mechanism by which it can reactivate dormant ReLU units. Building on this, we introduce AdamO, an Adam-style adaptive optimizer that decouples isometry regularization from gradient updates, analogous to AdamW. We further reinterpret prior plasticity-preserving approaches through the lens of dynamical isometry, showing that they target only a partial measure of isometry. Across supervised and reinforcement-learning continual-learning benchmarks designed to induce plasticity loss, our methods consistently match or outperform existing approaches.

This paper connects that loss of plasticity to the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel and identifies dynamical isometry as a key preservation mechanism. summary.tldr: Encouraging dynamical isometry helps preserve continual-learning plasticity and motivates a regularizer and the AdamO optimizer.

title: Preserving Plasticity in Continual Learning via Dynamical Isometry

abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) for non-verifiable tasks—such as creative writing, dialogue, and ethical reasoning—remains challenging due to the absence of ground-truth labels. While LLM-as-Judge approaches offer a scalable alternative to human feedback, they face a fundamental limitation: performance is constrained by the evaluator’s own quality. If the judge cannot recognize good solutions, it cannot provide useful training signals, and evaluation biases (e.g., favoring verbosity over quality) remain unaddressed. This motivates meta-evaluation—the ability to evaluate and improve the evaluator itself. We introduce CoNL, a framework that unifies generation, evaluation, and meta-evaluation through multi-agent self-play. Our key insight: critique quality can be measured by whether it helps others improve their solutions. In CoNL, multiple agents sharing the same policy engage in structured conversations to propose, critique, and revise solutions. Critiques that enable other agents’ solution improvements earn a diagnostic reward, creating explicit supervision for meta-evaluation and enabling joint optimization of generation and judging capabilities through self-play, without external judges or ground truth. Experiments on various benchmarks show that CoNL achieves consistent improvements over self-rewarding baselines while maintaining stable training.

paragraphs: Creative writing, dialogue, and ethical reasoning lack the straightforward ground-truth labels available for many other tasks. Using a language model as a judge can provide scalable feedback, but that feedback is constrained by the judge's ability to recognize quality. An evaluator that rewards verbosity, for example, can reinforce an unhelpful preference during training.

CoNL addresses this problem by training generation, evaluation, and evaluation of the evaluator together. Multiple agents sharing one policy propose solutions, critique one another, and revise their answers through structured conversations. Its central idea is to assess a critique by whether it helps another agent improve a solution. Helpful critiques receive a diagnostic reward, supplying supervision for the judging process itself.

This self-play framework jointly optimizes solution writing and judging without external judges or ground truth. Across the reported benchmarks, CoNL consistently improves on self-rewarding baselines while keeping training stable. The findings support evaluating feedback through its contribution to revision as a practical training signal for tasks where direct correctness checks are unavailable.
summary.tldr: CoNL trains language models to generate and judge better solutions by rewarding critiques that help other agents improve.

title: Conversation for Non-verifiable Learning: Self-Evolving Large Language Models through Meta-Evaluation

abstract: Compositional diffusion planners aim to solve long-horizon robotic tasks using short training trajectories. Yet, current approaches often rely on the heuristic stitching of local predictions. We show that the resulting stitched update is generally a non-conservative field that does not mathematically correspond to any valid global trajectory log-density function. We propose Energy-based Compositional Diffuser (ECD), a framework that formulates the global trajectory as the minimizer of the sum of local bridge potentials. This energy-based perspective defines a conservative correction field and contains a boundary reaction term that heuristic stitching omits. To enable efficient inference, we further introduce a Markov-based score approximation that computes the reaction term via a single block-tridiagonal solve, maintaining time complexity linear in the planning horizon. Empirically, ECD achieves state-of-the-art success rates on a range of OGBench stitching tasks, while nearly matching the inference speed of heuristic stitching methods. Code is available at https://github.com/GradientSpaces/ECD.

Energy-based Compositional Diffuser addresses this by defining a global trajectory through the sum of local bridge potentials. summary.tldr: ECD replaces heuristic trajectory stitching with a global energy formulation, improving planning success while nearly preserving stitching speed.

title: Energy-based Compositional Diffusion Planning

abstract: RL methods for scaling large reasoning models stall on datasets with low initial success rates, and thus little training signal. We investigate a fundamental question:Can a pretrained LLM leverage latent knowledge to generate an automated curriculum for problems it cannot solve? We explore this with SOAR: An asymmetric self-play framework that uses meta-RL to surface these pedagogical signals. A teacher model proposes synthetic problems for a student model, and is rewarded with its improvement on a subset of hard problems, thus grounding the curriculum in real student progress rather than intrinsic proxy rewards. Our study on the hardest subsets of math benchmarks (0/128 success) reveals three core findings. First, it is possible to realize bilevel meta-RL that unlocks learning under sparse, binary rewards by sharpening a latent capacity of pretrained models to generate useful problems. Second, grounded rewards outperform intrinsic learnability rewards used in prior LLM self-play, reliably avoiding typical instability and diversity collapse modes. Third, the structure and well-posedness of questions are more critical for learning progress than solution correctness. Our results suggest that the ability to generate useful stepping stones does not require the preexisting ability to solve the hard problems, paving a principled path to escape reasoning plateaus without additional curated data.

paragraphs: SOAR investigates how reasoning models can learn when they initially fail so often that reinforcement learning receives little useful reward. It asks whether a pretrained model’s latent knowledge can still produce helpful practice problems for tasks it cannot solve. The study targets difficult math subsets with an initial success rate of 0 out of 128.

This grounds curriculum quality in observed learning progress, making the usefulness of the generated exercises the central training signal.

The experiments show that this two-level training can unlock learning under sparse binary rewards. Progress-based rewards outperform intrinsic learnability rewards and avoid the instability and diversity collapse observed with those alternatives. The study also finds question structure and well-posedness more important for progress than solution correctness. These results suggest that generating useful stepping stones need not require already solving the target problems.
summary.tldr: SOAR rewards a teacher for a student’s actual progress, enabling useful curricula even when target math problems initially remain unsolved.

title: Teaching Models to Teach Themselves: Reasoning at the Edge of Learnability

abstract: Wearable accelerometers enable large-scale health monitoring, yet learning robust human-activity representations has been constrained by scarce labeled data. While self-supervised learning offers a remedy, existing methods treat sensor streams as unstructured time series, overlooking the underlying biological structure of human movement, a factor we argue is critical for effective Human Activity Recognition (HAR). We introduce a novel tokenization strategy grounded in the submovement theory of motor control, which posits that continuous wrist motion is composed of elementary basis functions called submovements. We define our token as the movement segment, a computationally tractable unit of motion composed of a finite sequence of submovements. By pretraining a Transformer encoder via masked reconstruction of these tokens, we shift the learning focus from local waveform morphology to high-level structural and temporal organization. Pretrained on the NHANES corpus ($\approx$ 28k hours; $\approx$ 11k participants), our representations outperform strong wearable SSL baselines across six subject-disjoint HAR benchmarks. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://prithvitarale.github.io/biopm-site/.

paragraphs: Wrist accelerometers collect large amounts of movement data, but labeling those recordings with human activities is costly. This paper studies how to learn useful representations without those labels. Its central proposal is to organize the learning process around the biological structure of movement rather than treating recordings as an undifferentiated sequence of sensor measurements.

The method draws on submovement theory, which describes continuous wrist motion as a combination of elementary movement components. The authors group finite sequences of these components into movement segments and use those segments as tokens. A Transformer learns by reconstructing masked tokens. This design shifts the prediction task toward the organization and timing of movement, rather than concentrating on the detailed shape of short waveform fragments.

The resulting representations outperform strong wearable self-supervised learning baselines on six activity-recognition benchmarks with separate subjects across evaluation splits. The findings support movement-informed tokenization as a useful way to learn activity representations from large, unlabeled wearable datasets.
summary.tldr: Movement-based tokens help a self-supervised Transformer learn wrist-sensor representations that improve activity recognition across six benchmarks.

title: Bio-Inspired Self-Supervised Learning for Wrist-worn Accelerometer Data

abstract: Few-shot point cloud semantic segmentation (FS-PCSS) aims to achieve precise segmentation of novel categories using only limited labeled samples. Existing prototype-based methods rely on shallow feature fusion, failing to adequately model the feature distribution shift between support and query sets, resulting in insufficient prototype adaptation. To address this, we propose the Deep Prototype Refinement Network (DPR-Net), which systematically achieves progressive adaptation by constructing a coarse-to-fine prototype evolution trajectory. Our core Dynamic Prototype Refinement (DPR) module decomposes features into common and distinctive subspaces based on channel activation, enabling targeted adjustment of domain-sensitive features while preserving class-shared semantics. By cascading multiple refinement modules, we construct a prototype trajectory transitioning from support-biased to query-adapted representations, mitigating both under- and over-adaptation. Furthermore, our Mixture of Prototype Experts (MoPE) mechanism treats prototypes at different stages as experts and ensembles their predictions through confidence-driven weighting. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance with high efficiency. Our code will be available at https://github.com/changshuowang/DPR-Net.

paragraphs: Few-shot point cloud segmentation assigns semantic categories to 3D points using only a small number of labeled examples for new categories. Prototype-based methods summarize those examples into class representations, but a prototype fitted to the labeled support set may not match the query data. DPR-Net addresses this mismatch through a sequence of refinements.

Its Dynamic Prototype Refinement module separates features into common and distinctive subspaces based on channel activation. It can then adjust features that are sensitive to the support-query shift while preserving class-shared information. Stacking these modules creates a progression from support-biased prototypes toward query-adapted ones, aiming to avoid both insufficient adjustment and excessive adaptation.

The method also retains information from several stages through a Mixture of Prototype Experts. Each stage’s prototypes produce predictions, and confidence-based weighting combines them. This means prediction can draw on the full refinement trajectory instead of relying only on its endpoint. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance with high efficiency, supporting progressive adaptation and confidence-weighted combination as complementary ways to improve few-shot segmentation.
summary.tldr: DPR-Net progressively adapts class prototypes to query point clouds and combines predictions across refinement stages, improving few-shot semantic segmentation.

title: From Coarse to Fine: Deep Prototype Refinement Network for Few-Shot Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Key–value (KV) caching is essential for large language model inference, yet its memory overhead poses a critical bottleneck for long-context generation. Existing eviction policies predominantly rely on empirical heuristics, lacking a rigorous theoretical foundation. This work rethinks KV cache eviction through the lens of the Information Bottleneck principle. Under a linear–Gaussian surrogate of attention, we derive a closed-form mutual information objective that characterizes the effective information capacity of a retained KV cache subset. This formulation reveals that a wide range of existing eviction strategies can be interpreted as different approximations of the same capacity-maximization principle. Guided by this insight, we introduce CapKV, a capacity-aware eviction method that directly targets information preservation via a log-determinant approximation using statistical leverage scores. This approach replaces heuristic selection with a theoretically grounded mechanism that preserves the maximum predictive signal. Extensive experiments across multiple models and long-context benchmarks show that CapKV consistently outperforms prior methods, achieving a better trade-off between memory efficiency and generational fidelity.

paragraphs: A language model’s key–value cache helps reuse prior computation, but its memory cost becomes a bottleneck for long contexts. This paper frames eviction as a problem of preserving useful information within a smaller retained cache. It seeks a shared theoretical objective behind policies that are often designed as empirical heuristics.

Under a linear–Gaussian surrogate for attention, the authors derive a closed-form mutual-information objective describing a retained subset’s effective information capacity. The formulation interprets several existing eviction strategies as approximations to capacity maximization. This theoretical connection depends on the surrogate model used in the derivation.

The proposed CapKV method targets information preservation through a log-determinant approximation using statistical leverage scores. These tools translate the capacity objective into a practical selection mechanism. Across multiple models and long-context benchmarks, CapKV consistently outperforms prior approaches in the reported experiments, offering a better balance between memory use and generation fidelity. The findings support using an explicit information objective to guide which cached content remains available.
summary.tldr: CapKV uses an information-capacity objective derived under a linear–Gaussian attention surrogate to improve the memory–quality trade-off in cache eviction.

title: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction via a Unified Information-Theoretic Objective

abstract: Reward feedback learning (ReFL) is effective for both text-to-image (T2I) and text-to-video (T2V) generation with image reward models (RMs). However, image RMs are misaligned with temporal objectives of T2V, motivating ReFL with video reward models. Nevertheless, directly deploying video RMs is impractical due to their large parameter size and the prohibitive cost of memory. To address this, we propose VELR: an efficient framework that employs ensemble latent reward models (LRMs) to predict rewards directly in latent space, bypassing expensive backpropagation through VAE decoders and video RMs. Specifically, we introduce the ensemble technique for the LRM, which enhances capacity, quantifies uncertainty, and mitigates reward hacking. VELR achieves a reduction of up to 150GB in memory, requiring as little as 12.4% of the memory compared to standard ReFL. Experiments on OpenSora-1.2, CogVideoX-1.5, and Wan-2.1 with large-scale video RMs demonstrate that VELR achieves comparable performance as standard ReFL and enables efficient and robust video RM-based ReFL at scales previously unattainable.

paragraphs: Reward feedback learning can improve video generation, but image reward models do not align well with video’s temporal objectives. Video reward models address that mismatch at a substantial memory cost. VELR aims to make their feedback practical by predicting rewards directly from latent representations used in generation.

The framework uses an ensemble of latent reward models, avoiding expensive backpropagation through video decoders and full video reward models. The ensemble increases predictive capacity, provides uncertainty estimates, and helps mitigate reward hacking. These roles matter together: an efficient reward predictor must remain useful when the generator is being optimized against its feedback.

Experiments with OpenSora-1.2, CogVideoX-1.5, and Wan-2.1 report performance comparable to standard reward feedback learning using large video reward models. Memory savings reach up to 150 GB, with usage as low as 12.4% of the standard approach. Those extrema describe the reported settings. The findings support latent reward ensembles as a way to retain useful video-level feedback while enabling training at scales previously constrained by memory requirements.
summary.tldr: VELR uses ensembles of latent reward models to preserve comparable video reward-learning performance while substantially reducing memory requirements.

title: VELR: Efficient Video Reward Feedback via Ensemble Latent Reward Models

abstract: We present the first theoretical convergence analysis of machine learning training under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), combined with a differentially private (DP) training algorithm tailored to encrypted computation. Our approach improves computational efficiency over standard differentially private gradient descent (DP-GD) while achieving comparable utility. In particular, we prove convergence of approximate gradient descent using polynomial approximations of activation and loss functions, which are required for FHE compatibility. To preserve privacy in downstream tasks, we integrate differential privacy without relying on costly per-sample gradient clipping, enabling scalable encrypted learning. We also provide data-independent hyperparameter selection and theoretically grounded strategies for polynomial approximation which can be of independent interest. Together, these contributions advance the feasibility of efficient, private, and secure machine learning on sensitive data.

paragraphs: Training under fully homomorphic encryption requires adapting machine-learning computations to operations compatible with encrypted data. This paper provides a theoretical convergence analysis for that setting and develops a differentially private training algorithm suited to encrypted computation. It addresses both the behavior of the optimization procedure and privacy in downstream uses.

The analysis studies approximate gradient descent when activation and loss functions are replaced with polynomial approximations required for FHE compatibility. Establishing convergence matters because these substitutions alter the training computation. The authors also provide theoretically grounded choices for polynomial approximation and a method for selecting hyperparameters independently of the training data.

The privacy component avoids costly per-sample gradient clipping and improves computational efficiency compared with standard differentially private gradient descent while maintaining comparable utility. Together, these contributions connect encrypted arithmetic, optimization guarantees, and differential privacy in one training approach. The result supports the feasibility of learning from sensitive data by addressing mathematical approximation and computational cost alongside privacy protection.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes convergence of encrypted training and introduces a more efficient differentially private algorithm tailored to FHE.

title: Revisiting ML Training under Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Convergence Guarantees, Differential Privacy, and Efficient Algorithms

abstract: Crowdsourcing has been widely adopted for large-scale data collection and problem solving, yet its outcomes are often noisy and inconsistent, making quality control and aggregation central concerns. Meanwhile, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in generation, annotation, evaluation, and reasoning. These developments can be framed as an emerging paradigm at the intersection of crowdsourcing and LLMs, encompassing two directions: (1) Crowd-LLM-Sourcing, where humans and LLMs jointly participate in workflows, and (2) LLM-Sourcing Inspired by Crowdsourcing, where crowdsourcing principles guide LLM-driven generation, annotation, evaluation, and inference. Many existing studies on LLMs overlook decades of prior work in crowdsourcing, even though the two domains are grounded in closely related principles on some topics. The central position of this paper is that, in scenarios where an LLM can be regarded as an LLM worker, LLM research should draw upon the rich body of crowdsourcing literature. At the same time, LLM workers differ from human workers in their correlated errors and context-dependent capabilities. This paper therefore highlights not only the relevance of crowdsourcing, but also the need to adapt its mechanisms for collective intelligence with model-based agents.
