The central position of this paper is that, in scenarios where an LLM can be regarded as an LLM worker, LLM research should draw upon the rich body of crowdsourcing literature. At the same time, LLM workers differ from human workers in their correlated errors and context-dependent capabilities. This paper therefore highlights not only the relevance of crowdsourcing, but also the need to adapt its mechanisms for collective intelligence with model-based agents.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing has long dealt with the challenge of combining contributions that vary in quality and consistency. This paper argues that language-model research can benefit from that experience when a model can meaningfully be treated as a worker. The connection covers activities such as producing content, assigning labels, evaluating outputs, and solving problems.

The authors distinguish two directions. In Crowd-LLM-Sourcing, humans and models participate together in a workflow. In LLM-Sourcing inspired by crowdsourcing, established principles for organizing contributions guide work carried out by models. This framing brings quality control and aggregation into a shared discussion instead of treating each use of multiple model contributions as an entirely new problem.

The proposed transfer requires adaptation. Model workers can make correlated errors, and their capabilities depend on context, so mechanisms designed around human workers cannot simply be assumed to behave the same way. The paper’s position is therefore conditional and practical: use crowdsourcing knowledge where the worker analogy fits, while redesigning mechanisms around the distinctive behavior of model-based contributors.
summary.tldr: LLM workflows should adapt crowdsourcing principles when models act as workers, accounting for correlated errors and context-dependent abilities.

abstract: The problem of learning a transduction, that is a string-to-string mapping, is a common problem arising in natural language processing and computational biology. Previous methods proposed for learning such mappings are based on classification techniques. This paper presents a new and general regression technique for learning transductions and reports the results of experiments showing its effectiveness. Our transduction learning consists of two phases: the estimation of a set of regression coefficients and the computation of the pre-image corresponding to this set of coefficients. A novel and conceptually cleaner formulation of kernel dependency estimation provides a simple framework for estimating the regression coefficients, and an efficient algorithm for computing the pre-image from the regression coefficients extends the applicability of kernel dependency estimation to output sequences. We report the results of a series of experiments illustrating the application of our regression technique for learning transductions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a mapping from one string to another, a task called transduction. Such mappings arise in natural language processing and computational biology. Earlier approaches described in the abstract use classification techniques. This work instead develops a general regression approach, making the prediction of an output sequence part of a regression framework.

The method separates learning into two stages. First, it estimates regression coefficients through a reformulation of kernel dependency estimation. Second, it computes the corresponding pre-image: the output string associated with those coefficients. This second step connects the numerical representation produced by regression to the structured answer the application actually needs.

The authors contribute both a cleaner formulation for estimating the coefficients and an efficient algorithm for recovering output sequences. Together, these developments extend the applicability of kernel dependency estimation to sequence outputs. A series of experiments illustrates the method and supports its effectiveness for learning transductions, establishing regression as a workable approach to this string-to-string prediction problem.
summary.tldr: A two-stage regression method learns string-to-string mappings by estimating coefficients and efficiently recovering an output sequence.

title: A general regression technique for learning transductions

abstract: The introduction of relational reinforcement learning and the RRL algorithm gave rise to the development of several first order regression algorithms. So far, these algorithms have employed either a model-based approach or an instance-based approach. As a consequence, they suffer from the typical drawbacks of model-based learning such as coarse function approximation or those of lazy learning such as high computational intensity. In this paper we develop a new regression algorithm that combines the strong points of both approaches and tries to avoid the normally inherent draw-backs. By combining model-based and instance-based learning, we produce an incremental first order regression algorithm that is both computationally efficient and produces better predictions earlier in the learning experiment.

paragraphs: The paper develops a regression algorithm in the context of first-order learning, motivated by relational reinforcement learning. Existing approaches described in the abstract follow either a model-based or an instance-based strategy. Each has a characteristic drawback: model-based methods can approximate the target function too coarsely, while instance-based methods can require substantial computation.

The proposed algorithm combines the two strategies to draw on their strengths. It is incremental, so learning proceeds as examples become available. The design aims to retain computational efficiency while improving the quality of the predictions, addressing the tradeoff that arises when either strategy is used on its own.

The authors report that the combined method is computationally efficient and produces better predictions earlier in the learning experiment. The timing of that improvement matters because an incremental learner makes predictions while its experience is still accumulating. The stated contribution is therefore both a hybrid approach to first-order regression and evidence that the combination can improve early learning behavior.
summary.tldr: An incremental first-order regression algorithm combines model-based and instance-based learning for efficient computation and better early predictions.

title: Combining model-based and instance-based learning for first order regression

abstract: Sensorimotor data from many interesting physical interactions comprises discontinuities. While existing locally weighted learning approaches aim at learning smooth functions, we propose a model that learns how to switch discontinuously between local models. The local responsibilities, usually represented by Gaussian kernels, are learned by a product of local sigmoidal classifiers that can represent complex shaped and sharply bounded regions. Local models are incrementally added. A locality prior constrains them to learn only local data—which is the key ingredient for incremental learning with local models.

paragraphs: Sensorimotor data from physical interactions can contain abrupt changes, while locally weighted learning approaches often aim to fit smooth functions. This paper proposes a model that learns to switch discontinuously between local models. Its focus is the rule that decides which local model is responsible for a particular part of the data.

Instead of representing those responsibilities with Gaussian kernels, the method learns products of local sigmoid classifiers. Combining the classifiers allows responsibility regions to have complex shapes and sharp boundaries. This gives the model a way to separate neighboring regions whose behavior changes abruptly, while preserving a collection of local models for describing the behavior within those regions.

The system adds local models incrementally. A locality prior constrains each model to learn only from local data, which the abstract identifies as the key ingredient for incremental learning with local models. The contribution therefore links two design choices: sharply bounded switching regions represent discontinuities, and locality constraints support the addition of models over time.
summary.tldr: Products of sigmoid classifiers learn sharply bounded responsibility regions so incrementally added local models can capture discontinuous behavior.

title: Learning discontinuities with products-of-sigmoids for switching between local models

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of active model selection for nonlinear dynamical systems. We propose a novel learning approach that selects the most informative subset of time-dependent variables for the purpose of Bayesian model inference. The model selection criterion maximizes the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between the prior and the posterior probabilities over the models. The proposed strategy generalizes the standard D-optimal design, which is obtained from a uniform prior with Gaussian noise. In addition, our approach allows us to determine an information halting criterion for model identification. We illustrate the benefits of our approach by differentiating between 18 published biochemical models of the TOR signaling pathway, a model selection problem in systems biology. By generating pivotal selection experiments, our strategy outperforms the standard A-optimal, D-optimal and E-optimal sequential design techniques.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose observations that distinguish competing models of a nonlinear dynamical system. Its approach selects an informative subset of time-dependent variables for Bayesian model inference. The decision concerns which observations are expected to help identify the model, making experimental selection part of the inference process.

The selection criterion maximizes expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between prior and posterior model probabilities. In plain language, it favors observations expected to change beliefs about the candidate models most informatively. The strategy generalizes standard D-optimal design, which arises under a uniform prior and Gaussian noise. It also provides an information-based criterion for halting model identification.

The authors illustrate the approach by distinguishing among eighteen published biochemical models of the TOR signaling pathway. In that model-selection problem, the strategy generates pivotal experiments and outperforms standard A-optimal, D-optimal, and E-optimal sequential design methods. The result supports directly optimizing expected information about model identity when deciding what to observe in this application.
summary.tldr: Selecting observations by expected information gain improves discrimination among eighteen biochemical models in the reported application.

title: Optimized expected information gain for nonlinear dynamical systems

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find graph modes, understood as dense subgraphs that capture compact patterns in the data. The challenge is to locate these patterns reliably when noise and outliers are present. The authors begin by defining modes through a graph density function, giving the search a mathematical target.

Their graph shift algorithm starts from each vertex and follows an iterative trajectory toward the nearest mode. This provides a way to search for dense patterns from different starting locations across the graph. The mode definition and the movement rule work together: density specifies the pattern of interest, while shifting supplies the procedure for reaching it.

Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the algorithm's efficiency and robustness, especially in settings containing substantial noise and many outliers. These findings matter because dense patterns need to remain recoverable amid distracting graph structure. The paper's contribution is a density-based definition paired with an iterative search algorithm and evidence that the combination remains effective under corruption.
summary.tldr: Graph shift iteratively moves from graph vertices toward dense-subgraph modes, with theoretical and experimental support for efficiency and robustness.

title: Robust Graph Mode Seeking by Graph Shift

abstract: Latent variable models are powerful tools for probabilistic modeling, and have been successfully applied to various domains, such as speech analysis and bioinformatics. However, parameter learning algorithms for latent variable models have predominantly relied on local search heuristics such as expectation maximization (EM). We propose a fast, local-minimum-free spectral algorithm for learning latent variable models with arbitrary tree topologies, and show that the joint distribution of the observed variables can be reconstructed from the marginals of triples of observed variables irrespective of the maximum degree of the tree. We demonstrate the performance of our spectral algorithm on synthetic and real datasets; for large training sizes, our algorithm performs comparable to or better than EM while being orders of magnitude faster.
originalAbstract: Latent variable models are powerful tools for probabilistic modeling, and have been successfully applied to various domains, such as speech analysis and bioinformatics. However, parameter learning algorithms for latent variable models have predominantly relied on local search heuristics such as expectation maximization (EM). We propose a fast, local-minimum-free spectral algorithm for learning latent variable models with arbitrary tree topologies, and show that the joint distribution of the observed variables can be reconstructed from the marginals of triples of observed variables irrespective of the maximum degree of the tree. We demonstrate the performance of our spectral algorithm on synthetic and real datasets; for large training sizes, our algorithm performs comparable to or better than EM while being orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Latent variable models explain observed data through variables that are not directly measured. Learning their parameters often relies on methods such as expectation maximization, which search locally and can settle at local optima. This paper proposes a fast spectral learning algorithm for latent variable models arranged in arbitrary tree structures.

A central result concerns how much observed information is needed to reconstruct the model's observable behavior. The authors show that the joint distribution of observed variables can be recovered from marginal distributions involving triples of observed variables, regardless of the tree's maximum degree. In other words, the reconstruction does not require larger observed groups simply because some tree nodes have many connections.

The algorithm avoids local minima and is evaluated on synthetic and real data. With large training sets, its performance is comparable to or better than expectation maximization while running orders of magnitude faster. The training-size qualification matters: the reported comparison specifically supports the method's combination of speed and performance in that setting.

abstract: The web offers large amounts of information most of which is just copied or rephrased, a phenomenon that is often called trend. A central problem in the context of web data mining is to detect those web sources that publish information which will give rise to a trend first. Here we present a simple and efficient method for finding trends dominating a pool of web sources and identifying those web sources that publish the information relevant to this trend before other websites do so. We validate our approach on real data collected from the most influential technology news feeds.

paragraphs: Web sources often publish information that is copied or rephrased elsewhere. As related material spreads, it can become a trend across a collection of sites. This paper addresses the problem of finding sources that publish information relevant to such a trend before other sources do, making timing central to the identification of trend setters.

The proposed method has two connected purposes: finding trends that dominate a pool of web sources and identifying early publishers of information associated with those trends. Linking these tasks gives the early-publication question a specific context. A source is examined in relation to a shared trend, allowing publication order to help distinguish its role within that trend.

The authors describe the method as simple and efficient and validate it using real data from influential technology news feeds. This provides evidence for applying the approach to actual web publishing activity. The contribution is a way to organize repeated information into trends and then identify which sources were early in publishing the material relevant to them.
summary.tldr: A simple method identifies dominant web trends and the sources that publish related information earliest.

title: Canonical Trends: Detecting Trend Setters in Web Data
